abstract: We develop a model-independent method for characterizing the reliability of neural responses to brief stimuli. This approach allows us to measure the discriminability of similar stimuli, based on the real-time response of a single neuron. Neurophysiological data were obtained from a movement(cid:173) sensitive neuron (HI) in the visual system of the blowfly Calliphom ery(cid:173) throcephala. Furthermore, recordings were made from blowfly photore(cid:173) ceptor cells to quantify the signal to noise ratios in the peripheral visual system. As photoreceptors form the input to the visual system, the reli(cid:173) ability of their signals ultimately determines the reliability of any visual discrimination task. For the case of movement detection, this limit can be computed, and compared to the HI neuron's reliability. Under favor(cid:173) able conditions, the performance of the HI neuron closely approaches the theoretical limit, which means that under these conditions the nervous system adds little noise in the process of computing movement from the correlations of signals in the photoreceptor array.

paragraphs: This paper develops a model-independent method for measuring how reliably a single neuron distinguishes similar brief stimuli. The method uses the neuron's response as it unfolds in real time. The authors apply it to recordings from a movement-sensitive neuron in the blowfly visual system.

They also record photoreceptor responses to quantify the signal-to-noise ratio at the visual system's input. Noise already present there constrains the reliability of later visual judgments. For movement detection, the authors calculate the resulting theoretical limit and compare it with the reliability of the movement-sensitive neuron's responses.

Under favorable conditions, that neuron performs close to the calculated limit. This means that, in those conditions, the intervening processing adds little noise while extracting movement from correlations among photoreceptor signals. The result ties an individual neuron's discrimination ability to the quality of its sensory inputs, providing a way to assess how faithfully a neural computation preserves the information available to it.
summary.tldr: Under favorable conditions, a blowfly movement-sensitive neuron approaches the discrimination limit imposed by photoreceptor noise.

title: Statistical Reliability of a Blowfly Movement-Sensitive Neuron

abstract: The Minimum Description Length principle (MDL) can be used to train the hidden units of a neural network to extract a representa(cid:173) tion that is cheap to describe but nonetheless allows the input to be reconstructed accurately. We show how MDL can be used to develop highly redundant population codes. Each hidden unit has a location in a low-dimensional implicit space. If the hidden unit activities form a bump of a standard shape in this space, they can be cheaply encoded by the center ofthis bump. So the weights from the input units to the hidden units in an autoencoder are trained to make the activities form a standard bump. The coordinates of the hidden units in the implicit space are also learned, thus allow(cid:173) ing flexibility, as the network develops a discontinuous topography when presented with different input classes. Population-coding in a space other than the input enables a network to extract nonlinear higher-order properties of the inputs. Most existing unsupervised learning algorithms can be understood using the Min(cid:173) imum Description Length (MDL) principle (Rissanen, 1989). Given an ensemble of input vectors, the aim of the learning algorithm is to find a method of coding each input vector that minimizes the total cost, in bits, of communicating the input vectors to a receiver. There are three terms in the total description length: • The code-cost is the number of bits required to communicate the code that the algorithm assigns to each input vector.

paragraphs: This paper uses minimum description length to learn representations that are economical to describe while preserving enough information to reconstruct the input accurately. Its distinctive idea is that a highly redundant population of active neurons can still have a compact description. What matters is the structure of the collective activity, rather than simply how many units participate.

Each hidden unit receives a position in a low-dimensional implicit space. Training encourages their activities to form a bump with a standard shape in that space. Once the shape is fixed, its center provides a cheap way to describe the activity pattern. An autoencoder's input-to-hidden weights are adjusted to create these structured responses.

The hidden units' positions are learned too, giving the representation flexibility beyond adjusting connection weights. With different input classes, the network develops a discontinuous topography. Because the population code occupies a learned space distinct from the original input space, it can express nonlinear, higher-order input properties while retaining a compact description of its activity.
summary.tldr: Minimum description length trains redundant population codes whose activity can be compactly described by a bump's location in a learned space.

title: Developing Population Codes by Minimizing Description Length

abstract: We prove that except possibly for small exceptional sets, discrete(cid:173) time analog neural nets are globally observable, i.e. all their cor(cid:173) rupted pseudo-orbits on computer simulations actually reflect the true dynamical behavior of the network. Locally finite discrete (boolean) neural networks are observable without exception.
originalAbstract: We prove that except possibly for small exceptional sets, discrete(cid:173) time analog neural nets are globally observable, i.e. all their cor(cid:173) rupted pseudo-orbits on computer simulations actually reflect the true dynamical behavior of the network. Locally finite discrete (boolean) neural networks are observable without exception.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether the behavior seen in a computer simulation reflects the true dynamics of a neural network. The issue is framed in terms of corrupted pseudo-orbits: simulated sequences that contain perturbations rather than following the system's mathematical evolution exactly. The authors use observability to describe the connection between these sequences and genuine network behavior.

For discrete-time analog neural networks, they prove global observability except possibly on small exceptional sets. In the sense stated by the abstract, corrupted simulation trajectories still reflect the network's true dynamical behavior. The exception is part of the theorem's scope and distinguishes the result from an unconditional guarantee for every analog network case.

For locally finite discrete Boolean networks, the paper gives an observability result without exceptions. The two findings provide mathematical support for interpreting simulated neural dynamics despite corruption in the simulated trajectories. Their significance lies in establishing when observed computation represents the underlying dynamical system, with a stronger unconditional statement for the specified Boolean setting.
summary.tldr: Observability theorems connect corrupted simulation trajectories to true neural dynamics, with possible small exceptions for analog networks.

title: Observability of Neural Network Behavior

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new particle filter based on sequential importance sampling. The algorithm uses a bank of unscented fil(cid:173) ters to obtain the importance proposal distribution. This proposal has two very "nice" properties. Firstly, it makes efficient use of the latest available information and, secondly, it can have heavy tails. As a result, we find that the algorithm outperforms stan(cid:173) dard particle filtering and other nonlinear filtering methods very substantially. This experimental finding is in agreement with the theoretical convergence proof for the algorithm. The algorithm also includes resampling and (possibly) Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) steps.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a particle filter based on sequential importance sampling. Its main change concerns the proposal distribution, which determines where candidate particles are drawn. The algorithm uses a bank of unscented filters to construct that distribution, placing the proposal mechanism at the center of the filtering method.

The authors emphasize two properties of the proposal: it uses the latest available information efficiently, and it can have heavy tails. These properties concern both how current evidence guides sampling and how probability extends away from the distribution's central region. The algorithm also includes resampling and may include Markov chain Monte Carlo steps.

The reported experiments show substantial improvements over standard particle filtering and other nonlinear filtering methods. The authors describe this empirical result as consistent with their theoretical convergence proof. The paper thus combines a new construction of the importance proposal, experimental comparisons, and a convergence result. The experimental performance claim and the proof provide different forms of support for the same filtering algorithm.
summary.tldr: Unscented filters construct informed, potentially heavy-tailed particle proposals, yielding substantial improvements in the reported filtering experiments.

title: The Unscented Particle Filter

abstract: Training a learning algorithm is a costly task. A major goal of active learning is to reduce this cost. In this paper we introduce a new algorithm, KQBC, which is capable of actively learning large scale problems by using selective sampling. The algorithm overcomes the costly sampling step of the well known Query By Committee (QBC) algorithm by projecting onto a low dimensional space. KQBC also enables the use of kernels, providing a simple way of extending QBC to the non-linear scenario. Sampling the low dimension space is done using the hit and run random walk. We demonstrate the success of this novel algorithm by applying it to both artificial and a real world problems.

paragraphs: Active learning aims to reduce the cost of training by selecting which examples to use. This paper introduces KQBC, an algorithm designed to make selective sampling practical for large-scale problems. It builds on Query By Committee, whose sampling step can be computationally expensive and therefore obstruct its use at scale.

KQBC addresses that bottleneck by projecting onto a low-dimensional space and performing sampling there. The sampling procedure uses a hit-and-run random walk. Moving the costly operation into this smaller space is the central computational change, allowing the algorithm to retain a selective-sampling approach while overcoming the expensive step identified in the original method.

The algorithm also supports kernels, providing a way to extend Query By Committee to nonlinear problems. The authors demonstrate successful applications to artificial problems and a real-world problem. Together, the low-dimensional sampling construction and kernel extension broaden the practical scope of the method, addressing both computational scale and the kinds of relationships the learner can represent.
summary.tldr: KQBC makes Query By Committee more practical through low-dimensional sampling and adds kernel support for nonlinear learning.

title: Query by Committee Made Real

abstract: A reliable motion estimation algorithm must function under a wide range of con- ditions. One regime, which we consider here, is the case of moving objects with contours but no visible texture. Tracking distinctive features such as corners can disambiguate the motion of contours, but spurious features such as T-junctions can be badly misleading. It is difﬁcult to determine the reliability of motion from local measurements, since a full rank covariance matrix can result from both real and spurious features. We propose a novel approach that avoids these points al- together, and derives global motion estimates by utilizing information from three levels of contour analysis: edgelets, boundary fragments and contours. Boundary fragment are chains of orientated edgelets, for which we derive motion estimates from local evidence. The uncertainties of the local estimates are disambiguated after the boundary fragments are properly grouped into contours. The grouping is done by constructing a graphical model and marginalizing it using importance sampling. We propose two equivalent representations in this graphical model, re- versible switch variables attached to the ends of fragments and fragment chains, to capture both local and global statistics of boundaries. Our system is success- fully applied to both synthetic and real video sequences containing high-contrast boundaries and textureless regions. The system produces good motion estimates along with properly grouped and completed contours.

paragraphs: Estimating motion is difficult when objects have clear outlines but little visible texture. Corners can help resolve movement, yet apparent features such as T-junctions can suggest misleading motion. The paper explains that local covariance information alone cannot reliably distinguish real features from these spurious ones, motivating an approach that avoids relying on such points.

The method combines three levels of boundary information: small oriented edge elements, chains of those elements called boundary fragments, and complete contours. It estimates fragment motion from local evidence, then resolves uncertainty by grouping fragments into contours. Thus, interpreting which boundary pieces belong together helps determine how they move.

Grouping uses a graphical model whose uncertainty is handled through importance sampling. Two equivalent representations, based on switches at fragment ends and on fragment chains, capture local and global boundary statistics. Tests on synthetic and real video with strong boundaries and textureless regions produce good motion estimates alongside grouped and completed contours. The results support jointly reasoning about boundary organization and movement.
summary.tldr: A contour-based motion method resolves ambiguous local movement by grouping boundary fragments into coherent contours.

title: Analysis of Contour Motions

abstract: Spectral clustering methods are common graph-based approaches to clustering of data. Spectral clustering algorithms typically start from local information encoded in a weighted graph on the data and cluster according to the global eigenvectors of the corresponding (normalized) similarity matrix. One contribution of this paper is to present fundamental limitations of this general local to global approach. We show that based only on local information, the normalized cut functional is not a suitable measure for the quality of clustering. Further, even with a suitable similarity measure, we show that the first few eigenvectors of such adjacency matrices cannot successfully cluster datasets that contain structures at different scales of size and density. Based on these findings, a second contribution of this paper is a novel diffusion based measure to evaluate the coherence of individual clusters. Our measure can be used in conjunction with any bottom-up graph-based clustering method, it is scale-free and can determine coherent clusters at all scales. We present both synthetic examples and real image segmentation problems where various spectral clustering algorithms fail. In contrast, using this coherence measure finds the expected clusters at all scales. Keywords: Clustering, kernels, learning theory.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering often builds a graph from local similarities and uses a few global eigenvectors to divide the data into groups. This paper examines limitations of that progression from local relationships to a global partition. It shows that local information alone does not make the normalized cut objective a suitable measure of clustering quality.

A separate problem persists even with a suitable similarity measure: the first few eigenvectors can fail to recover groups that differ in size and density. The issue is therefore not solely how similarities are chosen. It also concerns which structures the limited spectral representation can capture when several scales coexist.

The authors propose a diffusion-based measure of the coherence of individual clusters. It is scale-free and can be paired with any bottom-up graph-based clustering method to identify coherent groups across scales. Synthetic examples and image segmentation problems illustrate failures of several spectral methods, while the proposed coherence measure finds the expected groups at all scales in those examples. The contribution combines a diagnosis of spectral limitations with a different criterion for evaluating clusters.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies multiscale failures of spectral clustering and proposes a diffusion-based measure of cluster coherence.

title: Fundamental Limitations of Spectral Clustering

abstract: In this paper we present two transductive bounds on the risk of the majority vote estimated over partially labeled training sets. Our first bound is tight when the additional unlabeled training data are used in the cases where the voted classifier makes its errors on low margin observations and where the errors of the associated Gibbs classifier can accurately be estimated. In semi-supervised learning, considering the margin as an indicator of confidence constitutes the working hypothesis of algorithms which search the decision boundary on low density regions. In this case, we propose a second bound on the joint probability that the voted classifier makes an error over an example having its margin over a fixed threshold. As an application we are interested on self-learning algorithms which assign iteratively pseudo-labels to unlabeled training examples having margin above a threshold obtained from this bound. Empirical results on different datasets show the effectiveness of our approach compared to the same algorithm and the TSVM in which the threshold is fixed manually.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to assess a majority-vote classifier when only some training examples have labels. It derives two transductive risk bounds, using the partially labeled collection to reason about prediction errors. A central quantity is the margin: the strength of the vote supporting a prediction, used here as an indicator of confidence.

The first bound is tight under specific circumstances: voting errors occur on low-margin observations, and the associated Gibbs classifier's errors can be estimated accurately. The second bound addresses the joint event that a prediction is wrong and its margin exceeds a chosen threshold. This focuses directly on errors among predictions that appear confident.

The authors apply the second bound to self-learning, which repeatedly assigns provisional labels to unlabeled examples. Rather than choosing a confidence threshold manually, the algorithm derives one from the bound. Experiments on several datasets support the approach compared with the same algorithm and TSVM using manually fixed thresholds. The findings support principled threshold selection within a framework that treats margin as meaningful evidence of confidence.
summary.tldr: Two bounds on voting-classifier errors support a theoretically guided confidence threshold for assigning pseudo-labels in semi-supervised learning.

title: A Transductive Bound for the Voted Classifier with an Application to Semi-supervised Learning

abstract: The use of context is critical for scene understanding in computer vision, where the recognition of an object is driven by both local appearance and the objects relationship to other elements of the scene (context). Most current approaches rely on modeling the relationships between object categories as a source of context. In this paper we seek to move beyond categories to provide a richer appearance-based model of context. We present an exemplar-based model of objects and their relationships, the Visual Memex, that encodes both local appearance and 2D spatial context between object instances. We evaluate our model on Torralbas proposed Context Challenge against a baseline category-based system. Our experiments suggest that moving beyond categories for context modeling appears to be quite beneficial, and may be the critical missing ingredient in scene understanding systems.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object in a scene depends on both its own appearance and its relationship to surrounding objects. The paper argues that representing those relationships only through object categories may leave useful contextual information unused. Two individual objects can carry appearance and spatial information that a category-level relationship does not explicitly retain.

The Visual Memex represents objects through exemplars and records relationships between individual instances. Its representation combines local visual appearance with two-dimensional spatial context. This gives scene reasoning access to what particular objects look like and how they are positioned relative to one another, extending the contextual description beyond category identities.

The authors evaluate the model on Torralba's Context Challenge against a category-based baseline. Their experiments suggest that appearance-based, instance-level context is beneficial. They further propose that this richer context may be an important missing ingredient in scene understanding. The evidence supports the direction of the approach, while the broader claim about its role in scene understanding remains a possibility.
summary.tldr: Visual Memex models appearance and spatial relationships between individual objects, with experiments suggesting benefits over category-based context.

title: Beyond Categories: The Visual Memex Model for Reasoning About Object Relationships

abstract: We introduce a new family of distributions, called $L_p${\em -nested symmetric distributions}, whose densities access the data exclusively through a hierarchical cascade of $L_p$-norms. This class generalizes the family of spherically and $L_p$-spherically symmetric distributions which have recently been successfully used for natural image modeling. Similar to those distributions it allows for a nonlinear mechanism to reduce the dependencies between its variables. With suitable choices of the parameters and norms, this family also includes the Independent Subspace Analysis (ISA) model, which has been proposed as a means of deriving filters that mimic complex cells found in mammalian primary visual cortex. $L_p$-nested distributions are easy to estimate and allow us to explore the variety of models between ISA and the $L_p$-spherically symmetric models. Our main findings are that, without a preprocessing step of contrast gain control, the independent subspaces of ISA are in fact more dependent than the individual filter coefficients within a subspace and, with contrast gain control, where ISA finds more than one subspace, the filter responses were almost independent anyway.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a family of probability distributions that describes data through a hierarchy of Lp norms. Each norm summarizes part of the input, and these summaries feed into further norms. The resulting Lp-nested symmetric distributions extend spherical and Lp-spherical models previously used to represent natural-image statistics.

The family includes Independent Subspace Analysis, or ISA, for suitable parameter and norm choices. This provides a common framework for exploring models between ISA and Lp-spherical symmetry. The authors describe the distributions as easy to estimate and show that, like related models, they permit a nonlinear mechanism for reducing dependence among variables.

Their main findings examine whether ISA's proposed independent groups actually separate dependencies in image features. Without contrast gain control, dependencies between these groups were stronger than dependencies among individual coefficients within a group. With contrast gain control, when ISA identified multiple groups, the filter responses were already almost independent. These findings make preprocessing central to interpreting the apparent independence structure, rather than treating the groups discovered by ISA as automatically independent.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Lp distributions unify image-feature models and reveal that ISA's dependence structure changes substantially with contrast gain control.

title: Hierarchical Modeling of Local Image Features through $L_p$-Nested Symmetric Distributions

abstract: We show that the lambda-return target used in the TD(lambda) family of algorithms is the maximum likelihood estimator for a specific model of how the variance of an n-step return estimate increases with n. We introduce the gamma-return estimator, an alternative target based on a more accurate model of variance, which defines the TD gamma family of complex-backup temporal difference learning algorithms. We derive TD gamma, the gamma-return equivalent of the original TD(lambda) algorithm, which eliminates the lambda parameter but can only perform updates at the end of an episode and requires time and space proportional to the episode length. We then derive a second algorithm, TD gamma(C), with a capacity parameter C. TD gamma(C) requires C times more time and memory than TD(lambda) and is incremental and online. We show that TD gamma outperforms TD(lambda) for any setting of lambda on 4 out of 5 benchmark domains, and that TD gamma(C) performs as well as or better than TD_gamma for intermediate settings of C.

paragraphs: Temporal difference methods can combine return estimates spanning different numbers of steps. The authors show that the lambda-return used in TD(lambda) is a maximum likelihood estimator under a particular model of how return variance grows with the number of steps. This gives its weighting scheme a specific statistical interpretation.

They introduce a gamma-return based on a more accurate variance model and derive the TD gamma algorithm. It removes the lambda parameter, but updates only when an episode ends and requires time and memory proportional to episode length. A second version, TD gamma(C), introduces a capacity parameter C to enable incremental, online updates, using C times the time and memory of TD(lambda).

Across five benchmark domains, TD gamma outperforms TD(lambda) at every lambda setting on four domains. At intermediate capacity settings, TD gamma(C) performs as well as or better than TD gamma. These findings support revisiting how returns are combined, while the two algorithms expose different computational requirements for episodic and online use.
summary.tldr: A revised variance model yields TD gamma return estimators with strong reported benchmark performance and distinct episodic and online computation tradeoffs.

title: TD_gamma: Re-evaluating Complex Backups in Temporal Difference Learning

abstract: Given pairwise dissimilarities between data points, we consider the problem of finding a subset of data points called representatives or exemplars that can efficiently describe the data collection. We formulate the problem as a row-sparsity regularized trace minimization problem which can be solved efficiently using convex programming. The solution of the proposed optimization program finds the representatives and the probability that each data point is associated to each one of the representatives. We obtain the range of the regularization parameter for which the solution of the proposed optimization program changes from selecting one representative to selecting all data points as the representatives. When data points are distributed around multiple clusters according to the dissimilarities, we show that the data in each cluster select only representatives from that cluster. Unlike metric-based methods, our algorithm does not require that the pairwise dissimilarities be metrics and can be applied to dissimilarities that are asymmetric or violate the triangle inequality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm on synthetic data as well as real-world datasets of images and text.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to select representative data points when the available information consists of pairwise dissimilarities. These exemplars should describe the larger collection efficiently. The proposed method jointly chooses the representatives and assigns probabilities describing how strongly each data point is associated with each selected exemplar.

The authors formulate this as a convex optimization problem with a row-sparsity regularizer. Encouraging sparse rows favors using a limited set of representatives across the collection. They characterize the regularization range over which the solution moves between selecting a single representative and selecting every point, clarifying how the penalty controls the extent of compression.

The method accepts dissimilarities that are asymmetric or violate the triangle inequality, so its inputs need not satisfy ordinary metric rules. For data distributed around multiple clusters according to the dissimilarities, the authors show that points choose representatives from their own cluster. Experiments on synthetic data, images, and text demonstrate effectiveness. Together, these results connect representative selection, probabilistic association, and flexible similarity information in one optimization framework.
summary.tldr: A convex sparse optimization method selects exemplars and association probabilities from pairwise dissimilarities, including nonmetric ones.

title: Finding Exemplars from Pairwise Dissimilarities via Simultaneous Sparse Recovery

abstract: We provide a unified framework for the high-dimensional analysis of “superposition-structured” or “dirty” statistical models: where the model parameters are a “superposition” of structurally constrained parameters. We allow for any number and types of structures, and any statistical model. We consider the general class of $M$-estimators that minimize the sum of any loss function, and an instance of what we call a “hybrid” regularization, that is the infimal convolution of weighted regularization functions, one for each structural component. We provide corollaries showcasing our unified framework for varied statistical models such as linear regression, multiple regression and principal component analysis, over varied superposition structures.

paragraphs: A statistical model can contain several kinds of structure at once. This paper studies parameters represented as a sum of components, each subject to its own structural constraint. The term “dirty” describes this combination of structures: the overall parameter need not fit a single structural description even when its individual components do.

The authors develop a unified framework for analyzing these models in high dimensions. Their estimators combine a loss function with a hybrid regularizer built from weighted penalties for the separate components. Technically, the hybrid penalty is an infimal convolution: it considers ways to split a parameter into components and uses the least total weighted penalty across those splits.

The framework allows any number and types of structures and accommodates different statistical models and loss functions. Corollaries demonstrate its application to linear regression, multiple regression, and principal component analysis with varied superpositions. The contribution is a common analytical treatment of these combinations, allowing structurally different estimation problems to be studied through the same framework.
summary.tldr: The paper provides a unified framework for analyzing statistical models whose parameters combine multiple separately constrained structures.

title: Dirty Statistical Models

abstract: The macaque Superior Temporal Sulcus (STS) is a brain area that receives and integrates inputs from both the ventral and dorsal visual processing streams (thought to specialize in form and motion processing respectively). For the processing of articulated actions, prior work has shown that even a small population of STS neurons contains sufficient information for the decoding of actor invariant to action, action invariant to actor, as well as the specific conjunction of actor and action. This paper addresses two questions. First, what are the invariance properties of individual neural representations (rather than the population representation) in STS? Second, what are the neural encoding mechanisms that can produce such individual neural representations from streams of pixel images? We find that a baseline model, one that simply computes a linear weighted sum of ventral and dorsal responses to short action “snippets”, produces surprisingly good fits to the neural data. Interestingly, even using inputs from a single stream, both actor-invariance and action-invariance can be produced simply by having different linear weights.

The model takes responses from ventral and dorsal processing streams to short action snippets and combines them through a linear weighted sum. It is fitted to neural recordings to assess whether this modest computation reproduces individual response patterns. The study separates representing an actor regardless of action from representing an action regardless of actor.

The contribution suggests that sophisticated population behavior need not require a correspondingly elaborate mechanism at every unit: selective weighting of short visual snippets can already account for important aspects of the observed representations.
summary.tldr: Linear combinations of short action-snippet responses explain substantial STS neural behavior, including actor and action invariance.

title: Neural representation of action sequences: how far can a simple snippet-matching model take us?

abstract: We study the problem of recovering an incomplete $m\times n$ matrix of rank $r$ with columns arriving online over time. This is known as the problem of life-long matrix completion, and is widely applied to recommendation system, computer vision, system identification, etc. The challenge is to design provable algorithms tolerant to a large amount of noises, with small sample complexity. In this work, we give algorithms achieving strong guarantee under two realistic noise models. In bounded deterministic noise, an adversary can add any bounded yet unstructured noise to each column. For this problem, we present an algorithm that returns a matrix of a small error, with sample complexity almost as small as the best prior results in the noiseless case. For sparse random noise, where the corrupted columns are sparse and drawn randomly, we give an algorithm that exactly recovers an $\mu_0$-incoherent matrix by probability at least $1-\delta$ with sample complexity as small as $O(\mu_0rn\log(r/\delta))$. This result advances the state-of-the-art work and matches the lower bound in a worst case. We also study the scenario where the hidden matrix lies on a mixture of subspaces and show that the sample complexity can be even smaller. Our proposed algorithms perform well experimentally in both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Life-long matrix completion reconstructs a low-rank matrix as incomplete columns arrive over time. The paper studies how to do this with few observations while tolerating corruption. It develops adaptive sampling algorithms for two distinct noise models, with different recovery guarantees reflecting the different kinds of corruption allowed.

For bounded deterministic noise, an adversary may add arbitrary bounded, unstructured noise to each column. The proposed algorithm returns a reconstruction with small error while using almost as few samples as the best prior noiseless results. The latter sample bound matches a worst-case lower bound, making its efficiency meaningful under the specified assumptions. The paper also considers matrices whose hidden structure is a mixture of subspaces and shows that sample requirements can be smaller still. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the algorithms' practical performance alongside these noise-specific theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: Adaptive sampling enables online low-rank matrix recovery with strong, noise-specific guarantees and low sample requirements.

title: Noise-Tolerant Life-Long Matrix Completion via Adaptive Sampling

abstract: Learning with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) on long sequences is a notoriously difficult task. There are three major challenges: 1) complex dependencies, 2) vanishing and exploding gradients, and 3) efficient parallelization. In this paper, we introduce a simple yet effective RNN connection structure, the DilatedRNN, which simultaneously tackles all of these challenges. The proposed architecture is characterized by multi-resolution dilated recurrent skip connections and can be combined flexibly with diverse RNN cells. Moreover, the DilatedRNN reduces the number of parameters needed and enhances training efficiency significantly, while matching state-of-the-art performance (even with standard RNN cells) in tasks involving very long-term dependencies. To provide a theory-based quantification of the architecture's advantages, we introduce a memory capacity measure, the mean recurrent length, which is more suitable for RNNs with long skip connections than existing measures. We rigorously prove the advantages of the DilatedRNN over other recurrent neural architectures. The code for our method is publicly available at https://github.com/code-terminator/DilatedRNN.

paragraphs: Long sequences challenge recurrent neural networks because relevant information can span many steps, gradients can shrink or grow excessively, and computation can be difficult to parallelize. This paper introduces DilatedRNN, a connection structure designed to address these problems together.

Its distinguishing feature is recurrent skip connections operating at multiple resolutions. These connections link recurrent computations across different temporal distances, giving the architecture a way to handle dependencies at several scales. The structure can be combined with different recurrent cell types. The authors report fewer required parameters and substantially improved training efficiency while matching leading performance on tasks with very long dependencies, even with standard recurrent cells.

The paper also introduces mean recurrent length as a measure of memory capacity suited to architectures with long skip connections. This supplies a theoretical basis for comparing the proposed structure with other recurrent networks, and the authors prove advantages in that analysis. The empirical and theoretical contributions together support changing recurrent connectivity as a useful route to learning from long sequences.
summary.tldr: DilatedRNN uses recurrent skip connections at multiple scales to improve long-sequence learning efficiency while matching leading task performance.

title: Dilated Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We propose new algorithms for topic modeling when the number of topics is unknown. Our approach relies on an analysis of the concentration of mass and angular geometry of the topic simplex, a convex polytope constructed by taking the convex hull of vertices representing the latent topics. Our algorithms are shown in practice to have accuracy comparable to a Gibbs sampler in terms of topic estimation, which requires the number of topics be given. Moreover, they are one of the fastest among several state of the art parametric techniques. Statistical consistency of our estimator is established under some conditions.

paragraphs: Topic modeling seeks underlying topics in a collection of data, but choosing how many topics to use can itself be part of the problem. This paper proposes algorithms that operate when that number is unknown. Their design comes from examining the geometry of the structure formed by the hidden topics.

The authors represent topics as vertices of a simplex, a convex shape containing mixtures of its vertices. They analyze how mass concentrates within this structure and how its angular geometry can help identify topics. This geometric perspective supplies the basis for their scan-and-cover algorithms and makes the unknown topic count part of the modeling setting.

In practical evaluations, topic-estimation accuracy is comparable to a Gibbs sampler that requires the topic count as input. The algorithms also rank among the fastest of the compared state-of-the-art parametric techniques. The paper establishes statistical consistency under certain conditions, adding a conditional theoretical guarantee to the empirical findings on speed and estimation quality.
summary.tldr: Geometric topic-modeling algorithms handle an unknown topic count while showing competitive accuracy and speed.

title: Conic Scan-and-Cover algorithms for nonparametric topic modeling

abstract: Deep learning has become increasingly popular in both supervised and unsupervised machine learning thanks to its outstanding empirical performance. However, because of their intrinsic complexity, most deep learning methods are largely treated as black box tools with little interpretability. Even though recent attempts have been made to facilitate the interpretability of deep neural networks (DNNs), existing methods are susceptible to noise and lack of robustness. Therefore, scientists are justifiably cautious about the reproducibility of the discoveries, which is often related to the interpretability of the underlying statistical models. In this paper, we describe a method to increase the interpretability and reproducibility of DNNs by incorporating the idea of feature selection with controlled error rate. By designing a new DNN architecture and integrating it with the recently proposed knockoffs framework, we perform feature selection with a controlled error rate, while maintaining high power. This new method, DeepPINK (Deep feature selection using Paired-Input Nonlinear Knockoffs), is applied to both simulated and real data sets to demonstrate its empirical utility.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks can make strong predictions while remaining difficult to interpret. For scientific applications, explanations that are sensitive to noise also raise concerns about whether discoveries will be reproducible. This paper addresses that problem through feature selection: identifying relevant inputs while explicitly controlling errors in the selection process.

The proposed method, DeepPINK, combines a new neural-network architecture with the knockoffs framework. This integration lets the model perform nonlinear feature selection with a controlled error rate while maintaining high power, meaning an ability to identify relevant features. Error control and power serve complementary purposes: limiting mistaken selections and preserving useful discoveries.

The authors apply DeepPINK to simulated and real datasets to demonstrate its empirical utility. Its contribution is to connect neural-network interpretation with a statistical selection criterion, giving feature discoveries an explicit error-control objective. The stated results support this approach to interpretability and reproducibility through selected inputs, rather than claiming a complete explanation of every internal computation in a deep network.
summary.tldr: DeepPINK combines a neural-network architecture with knockoffs to select features with controlled errors while maintaining high power.

title: DeepPINK: reproducible feature selection in deep neural networks

abstract: The vulnerability of deep image classification networks to adversarial attack is now well known, but less well understood. Via a novel experimental analysis, we illustrate some facts about deep convolutional networks for image classification that shed new light on their behaviour and how it connects to the problem of adversaries. In short, the celebrated performance of these networks and their vulnerability to adversarial attack are simply two sides of the same coin: the input image-space directions along which the networks are most vulnerable to attack are the same directions which they use to achieve their classification performance in the first place. We develop this result in two main steps. The first uncovers the fact that classes tend to be associated with specific image-space directions. This is shown by an examination of the class-score outputs of nets as functions of 1D movements along these directions. This provides a novel perspective on the existence of universal adversarial perturbations. The second is a clear demonstration of the tight coupling between classification performance and vulnerability to adversarial attack within the spaces spanned by these directions. Thus, our analysis resolves the apparent contradiction between accuracy and vulnerability. It provides a new perspective on much of the prior art and reveals profound implications for efforts to construct neural nets that are both accurate and robust to adversarial attack.

Its central finding connects the two behaviors: the image-space directions that contribute to classification performance are also directions along which the examined networks are especially vulnerable. This links successful prediction and adversarial sensitivity through the same aspects of the input.

The analysis proceeds in two steps. First, the authors show that classes tend to be associated with particular directions in image space. They examine how class scores change as an input moves along one such direction at a time. This viewpoint also offers an explanation of universal adversarial perturbations through the directional structure of class responses.

Second, the authors demonstrate a tight relationship between classification performance and attack vulnerability within spaces spanned by these directions. The finding explains how accuracy and vulnerability can coexist in the studied networks. It also gives efforts to improve robustness a specific relationship to consider: changes to sensitivity in these spaces interact with information the classifier uses for prediction.
summary.tldr: Experiments link adversarial vulnerability to the same image-space directions that support classification performance in deep convolutional networks.

title: With Friends Like These, Who Needs Adversaries?

abstract: Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL) is generally achieved via aligning the semantic relationships between the visual features and the corresponding class semantic descriptions. However, using the global features to represent fine-grained images may lead to sub-optimal results since they neglect the discriminative differences of local regions. Besides, different regions contain distinct discriminative information. The important regions should contribute more to the prediction. To this end, we propose a novel stacked semantics-guided attention (S2GA) model to obtain semantic relevant features by using individual class semantic features to progressively guide the visual features to generate an attention map for weighting the importance of different local regions. Feeding both the integrated visual features and the class semantic features into a multi-class classification architecture, the proposed framework can be trained end-to-end. Extensive experimental results on CUB and NABird datasets show that the proposed approach has a consistent improvement on both fine-grained zero-shot classification and retrieval tasks.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning connects visual features with semantic descriptions of classes. For fine-grained recognition, a single representation of the whole image may miss the local differences that distinguish similar categories. The paper also emphasizes that regions differ in how much useful discriminative information they contain, so their contributions to prediction should vary.

The proposed stacked semantics-guided attention model uses individual class semantic features to progressively guide visual attention. The resulting integrated visual representation is fed into a multiclass classification architecture together with class semantic features, and the complete framework is trained end to end.

Experiments on CUB and NABird report consistent improvements in both fine-grained zero-shot classification and retrieval. These results support using class semantics to guide where the model looks within an image, as well as to connect images with class descriptions. The contribution is a progressively guided attention mechanism that makes local visual information more responsive to the semantic distinctions involved in prediction.
summary.tldr: Class descriptions progressively guide attention toward informative image regions, improving reported fine-grained zero-shot classification and retrieval.

title: Stacked Semantics-Guided Attention Model for Fine-Grained Zero-Shot Learning

abstract: Causal discovery from empirical data is a fundamental problem in many scientific domains. Observational data allows for identifiability only up to Markov equivalence class. In this paper we first propose a polynomial time algorithm for learning the exact correctly-oriented structure of the transitive reduction of any causal Bayesian network with high probability, by using interventional path queries. Each path query takes as input an origin node and a target node, and answers whether there is a directed path from the origin to the target. This is done by intervening on the origin node and observing samples from the target node. We theoretically show the logarithmic sample complexity for the size of interventional data per path query, for continuous and discrete networks. We then show how to learn the transitive edges using also logarithmic sample complexity (albeit in time exponential in the maximum number of parents for discrete networks), which allows us to learn the full network. We further extend our work by reducing the number of interventional path queries for learning rooted trees. We also provide an analysis of imperfect interventions.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave several causal networks indistinguishable because different edge directions may encode the same observational relationships. This paper uses interventions to resolve causal structure through path queries. A query asks whether one variable can reach another along directed edges, and is answered by intervening on the origin variable and sampling the target.

The authors first give a polynomial-time algorithm that recovers the correctly oriented transitive reduction with high probability. This reduction preserves directed reachability while removing edges made redundant by other paths. For both continuous and discrete networks, they establish logarithmic sample complexity for the interventional data needed by each path query.

They then recover the additional transitive edges to obtain the full network, again with logarithmic sample complexity. For discrete networks, this stage takes time exponential in the maximum number of parents, separating statistical efficiency from computational cost. The paper also reduces the number of queries for rooted trees and analyzes imperfect interventions. Together, these results make intervention-based reachability a useful intermediate step toward recovering complete causal structure.
summary.tldr: Interventional path queries enable efficient recovery of causal reachability and, with additional computation, the full network.

title: Computationally and statistically efficient learning of causal Bayes nets using path queries

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have recently shown state of the art performance on semantic segmentation tasks, however, they still suffer from problems of poor boundary localization and spatial fragmented predictions. The difficulties lie in the requirement of making dense predictions from a long path model all at once since details are hard to keep when data goes through deeper layers. Instead, in this work, we decompose this difficult task into two relative simple sub-tasks: seed detection which is required to predict initial predictions without the need of wholeness and preciseness, and similarity estimation which measures the possibility of any two nodes belong to the same class without the need of knowing which class they are. We use one branch network for one sub-task each, and apply a cascade of random walks base on hierarchical semantics to approximate a complex diffusion process which propagates seed information to the whole image according to the estimated similarities. The proposed DifNet consistently produces improvements over the baseline models with the same depth and with the equivalent number of parameters, and also achieves promising performance on Pascal VOC and Pascal Context dataset. OurDifNet is trained end-to-end without complex loss functions.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories across an image, but deep networks can produce fragmented regions and poorly located boundaries. The paper attributes part of this difficulty to predicting a complete, detailed segmentation after information has passed through many layers. DifNet divides the work into two simpler prediction tasks.

One network branch detects seeds: initial class predictions that do not need to be complete or precisely localized. The other estimates whether pairs of nodes belong to the same class, without needing to identify that class. A cascade of random walks then spreads the seed information through the image according to these similarities, using semantics from multiple levels.

This diffusion process connects local class evidence with information about which locations should share a label. The entire system is trained end to end without complex loss functions. The authors report consistent improvements over baselines matched in depth and parameter count, along with promising results on Pascal VOC and Pascal Context. These comparisons support the usefulness of the task decomposition and propagation mechanism within the evaluated segmentation settings.
summary.tldr: DifNet improves segmentation by learning initial class seeds and pairwise similarities, then diffusing the seeds across the image.

title: DifNet: Semantic Segmentation by Diffusion Networks

abstract: Neural Processes combine the strengths of neural networks and Gaussian processes to achieve both flexible learning and fast prediction in stochastic processes. However, a large class of problems comprise underlying temporal dependency structures in a sequence of stochastic processes that Neural Processes (NP) do not explicitly consider. In this paper, we propose Sequential Neural Processes (SNP) which incorporates a temporal state-transition model of stochastic processes and thus extends its modeling capabilities to dynamic stochastic processes. In applying SNP to dynamic 3D scene modeling, we introduce the Temporal Generative Query Networks. To our knowledge, this is the first 4D model that can deal with the temporal dynamics of 3D scenes. In experiments, we evaluate the proposed methods in dynamic (non-stationary) regression and 4D scene inference and rendering.

paragraphs: Neural Processes combine neural-network flexibility with ideas from Gaussian processes to model uncertain functions and predict quickly. This paper addresses situations where the underlying stochastic process itself changes over time. Ordinary Neural Processes do not explicitly represent the temporal dependencies across such a sequence of processes.

Sequential Neural Processes add a temporal state-transition model. This extends the modeling framework so that changes in the underlying process can be represented as part of a temporal sequence. The distinction matters for dynamic settings: the model must account for how the process evolves, in addition to predicting observations associated with it.

For dynamic three-dimensional scenes, the authors introduce Temporal Generative Query Networks as an application of this idea. They describe it, to their knowledge, as the first four-dimensional model capable of handling temporal dynamics of 3D scenes. Evaluations cover non-stationary regression and scene inference and rendering over time. The stated contribution is the extension to dynamic stochastic processes and its evaluation in these settings, rather than a reported numerical performance advantage.
summary.tldr: Sequential Neural Processes add temporal transitions to Neural Processes, enabling models of changing functions and dynamic 3D scenes.

title: Sequential Neural Processes

abstract: Recently a new feature representation and data analysis methodology based on a topological tool called persistent homology (and its persistence diagram summary) has gained much momentum. A series of methods have been developed to map a persistence diagram to a vector representation so as to facilitate the downstream use of machine learning tools. In these approaches, the importance (weight) of different persistence features are usually pre-set. However often in practice, the choice of the weight-function should depend on the nature of the specific data at hand. It is thus highly desirable to learn a best weight-function (and thus metric for persistence diagrams) from labelled data. We study this problem and develop a new weighted kernel, called WKPI, for persistence summaries, as well as an optimization framework to learn the weight (and thus kernel). We apply the learned kernel to the challenging task of graph classification, and show that our WKPI-based classification framework obtains similar or (sometimes significantly) better results than the best results from a range of previous graph classification frameworks on a collection of benchmark datasets.

To use these summaries in machine learning, methods often convert them into vectors and assign different importance to different persistence features. This paper questions the use of fixed importance weights when the useful features may depend on the particular labeled dataset.

The authors introduce a weighted kernel called WKPI and an optimization framework for learning its weights. A kernel determines how summaries are compared, so learning these weights also learns a task-informed notion of similarity. This allows labels to influence which aspects of the topological representation matter most for the prediction problem.

They apply the learned kernel to graph classification and evaluate it on a collection of benchmark datasets. The resulting framework matches or improves on the best results from a range of earlier graph-classification approaches, with improvements sometimes significant. The findings support adapting persistence-feature weights to the data, while preserving the qualified result that performance is comparable in some cases and better in others.
summary.tldr: WKPI learns how to weight topological features from labeled data, producing competitive and sometimes significantly better graph classification results.

title: Learning metrics for persistence-based summaries and applications for graph classification

abstract: One of the most common mistakes made when performing data analysis is attributing causal meaning to regression coefficients. Formally, a causal effect can only be computed if it is identifiable from a combination of observational data and structural knowledge about the domain under investigation (Pearl, 2000, Ch. 5). Building on the literature of instrumental variables (IVs), a plethora of methods has been developed to identify causal effects in linear systems. Almost invariably, however, the most powerful such methods rely on exponential-time procedures. In this paper, we investigate graphical conditions to allow efficient identification in arbitrary linear structural causal models (SCMs). In particular, we develop a method to efficiently find unconditioned instrumental subsets, which are generalizations of IVs that can be used to tame the complexity of many canonical algorithms found in the literature. Further, we prove that determining whether an effect can be identified with TSID (Weihs et al., 2017), a method more powerful than unconditioned instrumental sets and other efficient identification algorithms, is NP-Complete. Finally, building on the idea of flow constraints, we introduce a new and efficient criterion called Instrumental Cutsets (IC), which is able to solve for parameters missed by all other existing polynomial-time algorithms.

Together, the results expand what efficient causal identification can accomplish while clarifying the complexity of a more powerful alternative. The contribution does not make arbitrary regression coefficients causal: identification still depends on the observational information and the structural assumptions encoded in the model.
summary.tldr: Instrumental Cutsets efficiently identify causal parameters missed by existing polynomial-time methods, while a separate result establishes TSID identification as NP-complete.

title: Efficient Identification in Linear Structural Causal Models with Instrumental Cutsets

abstract: We address a low-rank matrix recovery problem where each column of a rank-r matrix X of size (d1,d2) is compressed beyond the point of recovery to size L with L << d1. Leveraging the joint structure between the columns, we propose a method to recover the matrix to within an epsilon relative error in the Frobenius norm from a total of O(r(d 1 + d 2)\log^6(d 1 + d 2)/\epsilon^2) observations. This guarantee holds uniformly for all incoherent matrices of rank r. In our method, we propose to use a novel matrix norm called the mixed-norm along with the maximum l2 norm of the columns to design a novel convex relaxation for low-rank recovery that is tailored to our observation model. We also show that our proposed mixed-norm, the standard nuclear norm, and the max-norm are particular instances of convex regularization of low-rankness via tensor norms. Finally, we provide a scalable ADMM algorithm for the mixed-norm based method and demonstrate its empirical performance via large-scale simulations.

The useful information lies in the shared structure across columns. The authors develop a method that exploits this joint structure to reconstruct the whole matrix from the compressed observations.

Their recovery guarantee bounds relative error in the Frobenius norm, which measures overall matrix error. For rank r and dimensions d1 and d2, the required observation count is O(r(d1 + d2) log^6(d1 + d2) / epsilon^2). The guarantee applies uniformly to incoherent matrices of rank r, so that stated structural condition is part of the result.

The authors also connect the mixed-norm, nuclear norm, and max-norm through tensor-norm regularization. A scalable ADMM algorithm and large-scale simulations complement the recovery theory with an implementation and empirical assessment.
summary.tldr: A mixed-norm convex method recovers incoherent low-rank matrices by combining information across individually overcompressed columns.

title: Decentralized sketching of low rank matrices

abstract: Interacting with a complex world involves continual learning, in which tasks and data distributions change over time. A continual learning system should demonstrate both plasticity (acquisition of new knowledge) and stability (preservation of old knowledge). Catastrophic forgetting is the failure of stability, in which new experience overwrites previous experience. In the brain, replay of past experience is widely believed to reduce forgetting, yet it has been largely overlooked as a solution to forgetting in deep reinforcement learning. Here, we introduce CLEAR, a replay-based method that greatly reduces catastrophic forgetting in multi-task reinforcement learning. CLEAR leverages off-policy learning and behavioral cloning from replay to enhance stability, as well as on-policy learning to preserve plasticity. We show that CLEAR performs better than state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for mitigating forgetting, despite being significantly less complicated and not requiring any knowledge of the individual tasks being learned.

paragraphs: A continually learning agent needs to acquire new skills without losing old ones as tasks and data distributions change. These requirements are called plasticity and stability. This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting, the failure of stability in which learning from new experience overwrites earlier knowledge, within multi-task reinforcement learning.

The proposed method, CLEAR, combines learning from current experience with replay of past experience. Off-policy learning and behavioral cloning on replayed data support retention of previous behavior. On-policy learning supports adaptation to what the agent is currently experiencing. The method therefore assigns complementary roles to past and present experience within the same learning process.

The authors report that CLEAR greatly reduces forgetting and outperforms the state-of-the-art mitigation techniques considered, while being significantly less complicated. It also does not require knowledge of the individual tasks being learned. This matters because the approach can support retention without depending on an explicit task description. The findings establish replay as an effective component of continual reinforcement learning in the evaluated multi-task setting.
summary.tldr: CLEAR combines replay-based retention with learning from current experience to reduce catastrophic forgetting in multi-task reinforcement learning.

title: Experience Replay for Continual Learning

abstract: We explore the link between deep ensembles and Gaussian processes (GPs) through the lens of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK): a recent development in understanding the training dynamics of wide neural networks (NNs). Previous work has shown that even in the infinite width limit, when NNs become GPs, there is no GP posterior interpretation to a deep ensemble trained with squared error loss. We introduce a simple modification to standard deep ensembles training, through addition of a computationally-tractable, randomised and untrainable function to each ensemble member, that enables a posterior interpretation in the infinite width limit. When ensembled together, our trained NNs give an approximation to a posterior predictive distribution, and we prove that our Bayesian deep ensembles make more conservative predictions than standard deep ensembles in the infinite width limit. Finally, using finite width NNs we demonstrate that our Bayesian deep ensembles faithfully emulate the analytic posterior predictive when available, and outperform standard deep ensembles in various out-of-distribution settings, for both regression and classification tasks.

paragraphs: Deep ensembles combine predictions from several neural networks, but that combination does not automatically have a Bayesian posterior interpretation. The paper examines this distinction using the Neural Tangent Kernel, which describes training dynamics in wide networks. Even at infinite width, standard ensembles trained with squared error lack the Gaussian process posterior interpretation one might expect.

The authors modify each ensemble member by adding a random function that remains fixed during training. This addition is computationally tractable and gives the resulting ensemble a posterior interpretation in the infinite-width limit. The trained networks collectively approximate a posterior predictive distribution. In that same limit, the authors prove that their method makes more conservative predictions than standard deep ensembles.

Experiments then examine finite-width networks, where the limiting theory is not an exact description. These networks closely reproduce the analytic posterior predictive distribution when it is available, and outperform standard ensembles in various out-of-distribution regression and classification settings. The results connect a small training modification to both a precise limiting interpretation and observed improvements when predictions must extend beyond the training distribution.
summary.tldr: Adding a fixed random function to each network gives deep ensembles a Bayesian interpretation at infinite width and improves tested out-of-distribution predictions.

title: Bayesian Deep Ensembles via the Neural Tangent Kernel

abstract: Social media has created new ways for citizens to stay informed on societal matters and participate in political discourse. However, with its algorithmically-curated and virally-propagating content, social media has contributed further to the polarization of opinions by reinforcing users' existing viewpoints. An emerging line of research seeks to understand how content-recommendation algorithms can be re-designed to mitigate societal polarization amplified by social-media interactions. In this paper, we study the problem of allocating seed users to opposing campaigns: by drawing on the equal-time rule of political campaigning on traditional media, our goal is to allocate seed users to campaigners with the aim to maximize the expected number of users who are co-exposed to both campaigns. We show that the problem of maximizing co-exposure is NP-hard and its objective function is neither submodular nor supermodular. However, by exploiting a connection to a submodular function that acts as a lower bound to the objective, we are able to devise a greedy algorithm with provable approximation guarantee. We further provide a scalable instantiation of our approximation algorithm by introducing a novel extension to the notion of random reverse-reachable sets for efficiently estimating the expected co-exposure. We experimentally demonstrate the quality of our proposal on real-world social networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to allocate initial users to two opposing campaigns so that as many people as possible encounter both. Inspired by equal-time rules in traditional political campaigning, it frames this as maximizing expected co-exposure in a social network. The motivation is to address information environments that reinforce existing viewpoints through recommendation and viral sharing.

The authors work around this obstacle by identifying a related submodular function that lower-bounds the desired objective. This connection supports a greedy algorithm with a provable approximation guarantee, providing theoretical support for the resulting seed allocation.

Experiments on real-world social networks demonstrate the quality of the proposed approach. The measured objective is exposure to both campaigns; the work's contribution is a tractable, theoretically supported way to pursue that objective within the broader motivation of mitigating polarization.
summary.tldr: A scalable approximation algorithm chooses campaign seed users to increase the expected number of people exposed to both opposing campaigns.

title: Co-exposure Maximization in Online Social Networks

abstract: Learning object-centric representations of multi-object scenes is a promising approach towards machine intelligence, facilitating high-level reasoning and control from visual sensory data. However, current approaches for \textit{unsupervised object-centric scene representation} are incapable of aggregating information from multiple observations of a scene. As a result, these ``single-view'' methods form their representations of a 3D scene based only on a single 2D observation (view). Naturally, this leads to several inaccuracies, with these methods falling victim to single-view spatial ambiguities. To address this, we propose \textit{The Multi-View and Multi-Object Network (MulMON)}---a method for learning accurate, object-centric representations of multi-object scenes by leveraging multiple views. In order to sidestep the main technical difficulty of the \textit{multi-object-multi-view} scenario---maintaining object correspondences across views---MulMON iteratively updates the latent object representations for a scene over multiple views. To ensure that these iterative updates do indeed aggregate spatial information to form a complete 3D scene understanding, MulMON is asked to predict the appearance of the scene from novel viewpoints during training. Through experiments we show that MulMON better-resolves spatial ambiguities than single-view methods---learning more accurate and disentangled object representations---and also achieves new functionality in predicting object segmentations for novel viewpoints.

paragraphs: Representing a scene as separate objects can support visual reasoning and control. However, a single image leaves spatial ambiguities about the underlying three-dimensional scene. This paper introduces MulMON, a method that learns object-centered representations by combining several views of a scene containing multiple objects.

A central difficulty is keeping track of which object in one view corresponds to which object in another. MulMON addresses this by iteratively updating latent object representations as it processes multiple views. During training, it must also predict how the scene would appear from new viewpoints. That prediction task encourages the updates to accumulate spatial information across observations.

Experiments show that MulMON resolves spatial ambiguities better than the compared single-view methods and learns more accurate, disentangled object representations. It also predicts object segmentations from novel viewpoints. The results suggest that aggregating views can improve both the internal description of individual objects and the ability to describe their appearance from an unseen perspective.
summary.tldr: MulMON combines multiple views into object-centered scene representations, improving spatial disambiguation and enabling segmentation from new viewpoints.

title: Learning Object-Centric Representations of Multi-Object Scenes from Multiple Views

abstract: We study stage-wise conservative linear stochastic bandits: an instance of bandit optimization, which accounts for (unknown) safety constraints that appear in applications such as online advertising and medical trials. At each stage, the learner must choose actions that not only maximize cumulative reward across the entire time horizon, but further satisfy a linear baseline constraint that takes the form of a lower bound on the instantaneous reward. For this problem, we present two novel algorithms, stage-wise conservative linear Thompson Sampling (SCLTS) and stage-wise conservative linear UCB (SCLUCB), that respect the baseline constraints and enjoy probabilistic regret bounds of order $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T} \log^{3/2}T)$ and $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T} \log T)$, respectively. Notably, the proposed algorithms can be adjusted with only minor modifications to tackle different problem variations, such as, constraints with bandit-feedback, or an unknown sequence of baseline rewards. We discuss these and other improvements over the state-of-the art. For instance, compared to existing solutions, we show that SCLTS plays the (non-optimal) baseline action at most $\mathcal{O}(\log{T})$ times (compared to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$). Finally, we make connections to another studied form of safety-constraints that takes the form of an upper bound on the instantaneous reward. While this incurs additional complexity to the learning process as the optimal action is not guaranteed to belong to the safe-set at each round, we show that SCLUCB can properly adjust in this setting via a simple modification.

This paper adds a stage-by-stage requirement: actions must respect a linear baseline constraint imposing a lower bound on instantaneous reward. These results show how conservative exploration can be incorporated into two standard bandit approaches with explicit performance bounds.
summary.tldr: Conservative linear bandit algorithms respect per-stage baseline constraints while achieving probabilistic regret guarantees and limited baseline-action use.

title: Stage-wise Conservative Linear Bandits

abstract: Few-shot image generation seeks to generate more data of a given domain, with only few available training examples. As it is unreasonable to expect to fully infer the distribution from just a few observations (e.g., emojis), we seek to leverage a large, related source domain as pretraining (e.g., human faces). Thus, we wish to preserve the diversity of the source domain, while adapting to the appearance of the target. We adapt a pretrained model, without introducing any additional parameters, to the few examples of the target domain. Crucially, we regularize the changes of the weights during this adaptation, in order to best preserve the information of the source dataset, while fitting the target. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm by generating high-quality results of different target domains, including those with extremely few examples (e.g., 10). We also analyze the performance of our method with respect to some important factors, such as the number of examples and the similarity between the source and target domain.
