paragraphs: Few-shot image generation asks a model to create images in a domain represented by only a handful of training examples. Those examples cannot reasonably reveal the domain's entire distribution. This paper therefore starts with a model pretrained on a larger, related source domain and adapts it to the target domain.

The objective is to combine the source model's diversity with the target examples' appearance. Adaptation changes the existing model without adding parameters. Crucially, the method regularizes weight changes so that fitting the new examples also preserves information acquired from the source dataset. This makes retaining prior knowledge an explicit part of the adaptation process.

The authors demonstrate high-quality generation across different target domains, including cases with only ten examples. They also examine how performance depends on the number of target examples and the similarity between source and target domains. The results support constrained adaptation as a way to use a rich source model when the target data alone provide little information about possible visual variation.
summary.tldr: Regularizing changes to a pretrained image generator enables adaptation from very few target examples while aiming to preserve source-domain diversity.

title: Few-shot Image Generation with Elastic Weight Consolidation

abstract: We introduce Unbalanced Sobolev Descent (USD), a particle descent algorithm for transporting a high dimensional source distribution to a target distribution that does not necessarily have the same mass. We define the Sobolev-Fisher discrepancy between distributions and show that it relates to advection-reaction transport equations and the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric between distributions. USD transports particles along gradient flows of the witness function of the Sobolev-Fisher discrepancy (advection step) and reweighs the mass of particles with respect to this witness function (reaction step). The reaction step can be thought of as a birth-death process of the particles with rate of growth proportional to the witness function. When the Sobolev-Fisher witness function is estimated in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), under mild assumptions we show that USD converges asymptotically (in the limit of infinite particles) to the target distribution in the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) sense. We then give two methods to estimate the Sobolev-Fisher witness with neural networks, resulting in two Neural USD algorithms. The first one implements the reaction step with mirror descent on the weights, while the second implements it through a birth-death process of particles. We show on synthetic examples that USD transports distributions with or without conservation of mass faster than previous particle descent algorithms, and finally demonstrate its use for molecular biology analyses where our method is naturally suited to match developmental stages of populations of differentiating cells based on their single-cell RNA sequencing profile. Code is available at http://github.com/ibm/usd.

paragraphs: Unbalanced Sobolev Descent, or USD, transforms a source distribution toward a target whose total mass may differ. It represents distributions with particles and changes both their positions and their weights. This accommodates situations where matching distributions requires more than moving a fixed amount of mass from one location to another.

The method introduces the Sobolev-Fisher discrepancy and uses its witness function to guide two operations. An advection step moves particles along gradients, while a reaction step adjusts their mass. The latter can also be interpreted as particle birth and death. The paper connects these operations to transport equations and the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric.

With a witness estimated in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, the authors prove asymptotic convergence in maximum mean discrepancy under mild assumptions and in the infinite-particle limit. They also develop two neural versions, using either weight updates or particle birth and death. Synthetic examples show faster transport than previous particle descent methods, and a biological application matches developmental stages of differentiating cell populations using single-cell RNA profiles.
summary.tldr: USD matches distributions by moving particles and changing their mass, with conditional asymptotic guarantees and applications to cell development.

title: Unbalanced Sobolev Descent

abstract: We present a Reverse Reinforcement Learning (Reverse RL) approach for representing retrospective knowledge. General Value Functions (GVFs) have enjoyed great success in representing predictive knowledge, i.e., answering questions about possible future outcomes such as “how much fuel will be consumed in expectation if we drive from A to B?”. GVFs, however, cannot answer questions like “how much fuel do we expect a car to have given it is at B at time t?”. To answer this question, we need to know when that car had a full tank and how that car came to B. Since such questions emphasize the influence of possible past events on the present, we refer to their answers as retrospective knowledge. In this paper, we show how to represent retrospective knowledge with Reverse GVFs, which are trained via Reverse RL. We demonstrate empirically the utility of Reverse GVFs in both representation learning and anomaly detection.

paragraphs: An agent may need to understand how its present situation arose, as well as predict what happens next. Standard General Value Functions represent predictive knowledge, such as expected fuel use on a future trip. They do not answer the retrospective question of how much fuel a car is expected to have when observed at a particular place and time.

That second question depends on possible histories: when the tank was filled and how the car reached its current location. The paper introduces Reverse General Value Functions to represent knowledge about these past influences on the present. It also introduces Reverse Reinforcement Learning as the procedure used to train those representations.

The distinction changes the direction of the question being learned, from consequences of the current situation to historical factors associated with it. The authors demonstrate empirical utility in representation learning and anomaly detection. These findings indicate that retrospective information can be useful for constructing learned descriptions and identifying unusual behavior. The contribution is a framework for representing that information, rather than merely asking an ordinary predictive value function to answer a different question.
summary.tldr: Reverse Reinforcement Learning trains value functions that describe past influences on the present, with demonstrated uses in representation learning and anomaly detection.

title: Learning Retrospective Knowledge with Reverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The idea of slicing divergences has been proven to be successful when comparing two probability measures in various machine learning applications including generative modeling, and consists in computing the expected value of a `base divergence' between \emph{one-dimensional random projections} of the two measures. However, the topological, statistical, and computational consequences of this technique have not yet been well-established. In this paper, we aim at bridging this gap and derive various theoretical properties of sliced probability divergences. First, we show that slicing preserves the metric axioms and the weak continuity of the divergence, implying that the sliced divergence will share similar topological properties. We then precise the results in the case where the base divergence belongs to the class of integral probability metrics. On the other hand, we establish that, under mild conditions, the sample complexity of a sliced divergence does not depend on the problem dimension. We finally apply our general results to several base divergences, and illustrate our theory on both synthetic and real data experiments.

This construction has proved useful in machine learning, including generative modeling. The paper examines which mathematical and statistical properties survive this reduction to one-dimensional comparisons.

The authors show that slicing preserves metric axioms and weak continuity of the divergence, allowing the sliced construction to retain related topological properties. These properties concern whether the comparison behaves like a distance and how it responds when distributions converge. They further specialize the analysis to base divergences belonging to the class of integral probability metrics.

On the statistical side, the paper establishes that sample complexity can be independent of the original problem dimension under mild conditions. This is a conditional result about estimating sliced divergences from data. The authors apply the general theory to several base divergences and illustrate it with synthetic and real-data experiments, providing a mathematical foundation for properties that make slicing useful in practice.
summary.tldr: Slicing preserves key properties of probability divergences and, under mild conditions, yields dimension-independent sample complexity.

title: Statistical and Topological Properties of Sliced Probability Divergences

abstract: Marked temporal point processes (MTPPs) have emerged as a powerful modelingtool for a wide variety of applications which are characterized using discreteevents localized in continuous time. In this context, the events are of two typesendogenous events which occur due to the influence of the previous events andexogenous events which occur due to the effect of the externalities. However, inpractice, the events do not come with endogenous or exogenous labels. To thisend, our goal in this paper is to identify the set of exogenous events from a set ofunlabelled events. To do so, we first formulate the parameter estimation problemin conjunction with exogenous event set selection problem and show that thisproblem is NP hard. Next, we prove that the underlying objective is a monotoneand \alpha-submodular set function, with respect to the candidate set of exogenousevents. Such a characterization subsequently allows us to use a stochastic greedyalgorithm which was originally proposed in~\cite{greedy}for submodular maximization.However, we show that it also admits an approximation guarantee for maximizing\alpha-submodular set function, even when the learning algorithm provides an imperfectestimates of the trained parameters. Finally, our experiments with synthetic andreal data show that our method performs better than the existing approaches builtupon superposition of endogenous and exogenous MTPPs.

paragraphs: A sequence of events can contain both events influenced by earlier events and events driven by outside factors. Marked temporal point processes model discrete events occurring in continuous time, but observed events generally do not arrive labeled by their source. This paper aims to identify the externally driven, or exogenous, events from such unlabeled observations.

The authors combine selection of the exogenous-event set with estimation of the model parameters. They show that the resulting problem is NP-hard, then establish useful structure in its objective: it is monotone and alpha-submodular with respect to the candidate event set. This characterization allows them to apply a stochastic greedy selection algorithm.

The paper proves an approximation guarantee for that algorithm in the alpha-submodular setting, including when parameter learning returns imperfect estimates. The guarantee therefore accommodates estimation error within the analyzed formulation. Experiments on synthetic and real data show better performance than existing approaches based on superposing endogenous and exogenous processes, supporting joint event selection and parameter estimation as a useful alternative.
summary.tldr: The paper jointly selects externally driven events and fits a temporal point-process model, with a greedy approximation guarantee that accommodates imperfect parameter estimates.

title: Learning to Select Exogenous Events for Marked Temporal Point Process

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the question: _Given a small number of datapoints, for example $N = 30$, how tight can PAC-Bayes and test set bounds be made?_ For such small datasets, test set bounds adversely affect generalisation performance by withholding data from the training procedure. In this setting, PAC-Bayes bounds are especially attractive, due to their ability to use all the data to simultaneously learn a posterior and bound its generalisation risk. We focus on the case of i.i.d. data with a bounded loss and consider the generic PAC-Bayes theorem of Germain et al. While their theorem is known to recover many existing PAC-Bayes bounds, it is unclear what the tightest bound derivable from their framework is. For a fixed learning algorithm and dataset, we show that the tightest possible bound coincides with a bound considered by Catoni; and, in the more natural case of distributions over datasets, we establish a lower bound on the best bound achievable in expectation. Interestingly, this lower bound recovers the Chernoff test set bound if the posterior is equal to the prior. Moreover, to illustrate how tight these bounds can be, we study synthetic one-dimensional classification tasks in which it is feasible to meta-learn both the prior and the form of the bound to numerically optimise for the tightest bounds possible. We find that in this simple, controlled scenario, PAC-Bayes bounds are competitive with comparable, commonly used Chernoff test set bounds. However, the sharpest test set bounds still lead to better guarantees on the generalisation error than the PAC-Bayes bounds we consider.

paragraphs: With very small datasets, setting aside test examples removes observations that could help training. PAC-Bayes bounds offer an appealing alternative because the same data can support learning a posterior and bounding its generalization risk. This paper asks how tight those guarantees can become within a particular generic PAC-Bayes framework, assuming independent, identically distributed data and bounded loss.

For a fixed learning algorithm and dataset, the authors show that the tightest bound available in that framework coincides with a Catoni bound. For distributions over datasets, they establish a lower bound on the best expected guarantee. When posterior and prior coincide, that lower bound recovers the Chernoff test-set bound.

The authors also study synthetic one-dimensional classification tasks where they can meta-learn both the prior and the bound's form. In this controlled setting, the resulting PAC-Bayes guarantees compete with commonly used comparable Chernoff bounds. However, the sharpest test-set bounds still provide better generalization guarantees than the PAC-Bayes bounds considered. The findings distinguish advantages in data use from the tightness of the resulting guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes tightness within a PAC-Bayes framework and finds competitive small-data guarantees, though the sharpest tested alternatives remain better.

title: How Tight Can PAC-Bayes be in the Small Data Regime?

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in the task of semi-supervised node classification. However, most existing GNN models require sufficient labeled data for effective network training. Their performance can be seriously degraded when labels are extremely limited. To address this issue, we propose a new framework termed Contrastive Graph Poisson Networks (CGPN) for node classification under extremely limited labeled data. Specifically, our CGPN derives from variational inference; integrates a newly designed Graph Poisson Network (GPN) to effectively propagate the limited labels to the entire graph and a normal GNN, such as Graph Attention Network, that flexibly guides the propagation of GPN; applies a contrastive objective to further exploit the supervision information from the learning process of GPN and GNN models. Essentially, our CGPN can enhance the learning performance of GNNs under extremely limited labels by contrastively propagating the limited labels to the entire graph. We conducted extensive experiments on different types of datasets to demonstrate the superiority of CGPN.

paragraphs: Classifying nodes in a graph becomes difficult when only a tiny number have known labels. Although graph neural networks can use connections among nodes, their training can still deteriorate when direct supervision is extremely scarce. This paper develops Contrastive Graph Poisson Networks, or CGPN, specifically for that setting.

The framework combines a newly designed Graph Poisson Network with a conventional graph neural network, such as a Graph Attention Network. The Poisson component propagates the limited label information throughout the graph, while the conventional network guides that propagation flexibly. The construction is derived from variational inference, giving the combined learning approach a common foundation.

A contrastive objective extracts additional supervision from the learning processes of both components. The central idea is to make scarce labels useful across the graph through guided propagation and contrastive learning. Experiments across different dataset types report superior performance for CGPN. Those results support the proposed combination as a way to improve node classification when the amount of labeled data severely constrains ordinary graph neural network training.
summary.tldr: CGPN combines guided label propagation and contrastive learning to improve graph node classification when labeled examples are extremely scarce.

title: Contrastive Graph Poisson Networks: Semi-Supervised Learning with Extremely Limited Labels

abstract: We present a High-Resolution Transformer (HRFormer) that learns high-resolution representations for dense prediction tasks, in contrast to the original Vision Transformer that produces low-resolution representations and has high memory and computational cost. We take advantage of the multi-resolution parallel design introduced in high-resolution convolutional networks (HRNet [45]), along with local-window self-attention that performs self-attention over small non-overlapping image windows [21], for improving the memory and computation efficiency. In addition, we introduce a convolution into the FFN to exchange information across the disconnected image windows. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the HighResolution Transformer on both human pose estimation and semantic segmentation tasks, e.g., HRFormer outperforms Swin transformer [27] by 1.3 AP on COCO pose estimation with 50% fewer parameters and 30% fewer FLOPs. Code is available at: https://github.com/HRNet/HRFormer

paragraphs: Dense visual prediction requires representations that preserve spatial detail, as in locating human poses or assigning semantic labels across an image. HRFormer is designed to learn high-resolution representations for these tasks. Its motivation is that the original Vision Transformer produces lower-resolution representations while imposing substantial memory and computation costs.

The architecture combines parallel processing at multiple resolutions, drawing on HRNet, with self-attention inside small, non-overlapping image windows. Restricting attention to these windows improves efficiency, but separates their attention computations. To exchange information across the window boundaries, the authors add a convolution to the feed-forward network. The design therefore addresses both local processing cost and communication between windows.

The paper demonstrates effectiveness on human pose estimation and semantic segmentation. In the stated COCO pose comparison, HRFormer exceeds Swin Transformer by 1.3 AP while using 50% fewer parameters and 30% fewer FLOPs. These results support the architecture's ability to combine detailed spatial representations with efficient computation in the evaluated tasks, rather than requiring a larger model to obtain the reported improvement.
summary.tldr: HRFormer combines parallel multi-resolution features, local attention, and cross-window convolution to improve dense prediction with lower reported model and computation costs.

title: HRFormer: High-Resolution Vision Transformer for Dense Predict

abstract: The effectiveness of unsupervised domain adaptation degrades when there is a large discrepancy between the source and target domains. Gradual domain adaption (GDA) is one promising way to mitigate such an issue, by leveraging additional unlabeled data that gradually shift from the source to the target. Through sequentially adapting the model along the "indexed" intermediate domains, GDA substantially improves the overall adaptation performance. In practice, however, the extra unlabeled data may not be separated into intermediate domains and indexed properly, limiting the applicability of GDA. In this paper, we investigate how to discover the sequence of intermediate domains when it is not already available. Concretely, we propose a coarse-to-fine framework, which starts with a coarse domain discovery step via progressive domain discriminator training. This coarse domain sequence then undergoes a fine indexing step via a novel cycle-consistency loss, which encourages the next intermediate domain to preserve sufficient discriminative knowledge of the current intermediate domain. The resulting domain sequence can then be used by a GDA algorithm. On benchmark data sets of GDA, we show that our approach, which we name Intermediate DOmain Labeler (IDOL), can lead to comparable or even better adaptation performance compared to the pre-defined domain sequence, making GDA more applicable and robust to the quality of domain sequences. Codes are available at https://github.com/hongyouc/IDOL.

paragraphs: Adapting a model directly between very different source and target domains can be difficult. Gradual domain adaptation uses additional unlabeled data to provide intermediate steps between them. Its practical complication is that these data may arrive without labels identifying the intermediate domains or the order in which adaptation should proceed.

The proposed Intermediate DOmain Labeler, or IDOL, discovers that ordering through a coarse-to-fine process. It first trains domain discriminators progressively to obtain a rough sequence. It then refines the indexing using a cycle-consistency loss that encourages each next domain to preserve enough of the current domain’s discriminative knowledge. A gradual adaptation algorithm can subsequently use the discovered sequence.

On gradual adaptation benchmarks, the authors report performance comparable to or sometimes better than using predefined domain sequences. This suggests that manually supplied ordering is not always needed to obtain an effective adaptation path. The contribution makes gradual adaptation applicable to less organized unlabeled data and provides an empirical way to improve robustness to the quality of the domain sequence.
summary.tldr: IDOL discovers ordered intermediate domains from unlabeled data, enabling gradual adaptation without a predefined domain sequence.

title: Gradual Domain Adaptation without Indexed Intermediate Domains

abstract: One of the key drivers of complexity in the classical (stochastic) multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem is the difference between mean rewards in the top two arms, also known as the instance gap. The celebrated Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) policy is among the simplest optimism-based MAB algorithms that naturally adapts to this gap: for a horizon of play n, it achieves optimal O(log n) regret in instances with "large" gaps, and a near-optimal O(\sqrt{n log n}) minimax regret when the gap can be arbitrarily "small." This paper provides new results on the arm-sampling behavior of UCB, leading to several important insights. Among these, it is shown that arm-sampling rates under UCB are asymptotically deterministic, regardless of the problem complexity. This discovery facilitates new sharp asymptotics and a novel alternative proof for the O(\sqrt{n log n}) minimax regret of UCB. Furthermore, the paper also provides the first complete process-level characterization of the MAB problem in the conventional diffusion scaling. Among other things, the "small" gap worst-case lens adopted in this paper also reveals profound distinctions between the behavior of UCB and Thompson Sampling, such as an "incomplete learning" phenomenon characteristic of the latter.

paragraphs: In a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses among options with uncertain rewards. A central source of difficulty is the gap between the best two average rewards. Large gaps make the best option easier to distinguish; very small gaps create the challenging cases studied in this paper.

The authors analyze how the Upper Confidence Bound algorithm allocates its choices across arms. They show that its sampling rates become asymptotically deterministic, regardless of problem complexity. This gives a sharper account of long-run sampling behavior and supports a new proof of UCB's near-optimal worst-case regret bound, which grows as the square root of n log n.

The paper also characterizes the evolving bandit process under conventional diffusion scaling, extending the analysis beyond a single final regret quantity. Through this small-gap perspective, it identifies substantial differences between UCB and Thompson Sampling, including an incomplete-learning phenomenon for the latter. These are characterizations of behavior in the studied asymptotic regime, rather than a universal ranking of the two algorithms.
summary.tldr: Analyzing small reward gaps reveals deterministic limiting sampling rates for UCB and distinctive incomplete-learning behavior in Thompson Sampling.

title: A Closer Look at the Worst-case Behavior of Multi-armed Bandit Algorithms

abstract: Offline (or batch) reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms seek to learn an optimal policy from a fixed dataset without active data collection. Based on the composition of the offline dataset, two main methods are used: imitation learning which is suitable for expert datasets, and vanilla offline RL which often requires uniform coverage datasets. From a practical standpoint, datasets often deviate from these two extremes and the exact data composition is usually unknown. To bridge this gap, we present a new offline RL framework that smoothly interpolates between the two extremes of data composition, hence unifying imitation learning and vanilla offline RL. The new framework is centered around a weak version of the concentrability coefficient that measures the deviation of the behavior policy from the expert policy alone. Under this new framework, we ask: can one develop an algorithm that achieves a minimax optimal rate adaptive to unknown data composition? To address this question, we consider a lower confidence bound (LCB) algorithm developed based on pessimism in the face of uncertainty in offline RL. We study finite-sample properties of LCB as well as information-theoretic limits in multi-armed bandits, contextual bandits, and Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our analysis reveals surprising facts about optimality rates. In particular, in both contextual bandits and RL, LCB achieves a faster rate of $1/N$ for nearly-expert datasets compared to the usual rate of $1/\sqrt{N}$ in offline RL, where $N$ is the batch dataset sample size. In contextual bandits with at least two contexts, we prove that LCB is adaptively optimal for the entire data composition range, achieving a smooth transition from imitation learning to offline RL. We further show that LCB is almost adaptively optimal in MDPs.

paragraphs: Learning from a fixed collection of past decisions is easier to characterize when the data either comes from an expert or covers many possible behaviors. Practical datasets often fall between these cases, with their composition unknown. This paper develops a framework that connects imitation learning and offline reinforcement learning across that range.

The framework measures how the data-generating policy differs from an expert policy through a weakened concentrability coefficient. It analyzes a lower confidence bound algorithm, which treats uncertain outcomes pessimistically. The authors examine both its finite-data performance and information-theoretic limits in several decision-making settings.

For nearly expert data, the analysis gives a 1/N rate in contextual bandits and reinforcement learning, faster than the usual 1/√N rate. With at least two contexts, the algorithm is adaptively optimal across the full data-composition range in contextual bandits; in Markov decision processes, it is almost adaptively optimal. These distinctions matter: the framework supports adaptation without knowing the data composition, while the precise optimality claim depends on the setting.
summary.tldr: A pessimistic offline learning framework adapts between expert-like and broadly covering datasets, with setting-dependent optimality guarantees.

title: Bridging Offline Reinforcement Learning and Imitation Learning: A Tale of Pessimism

abstract: The recent explosive interest on transformers has suggested their potential to become powerful ``universal" models for computer vision tasks, such as classification, detection, and segmentation. While those attempts mainly study the discriminative models, we explore transformers on some more notoriously difficult vision tasks, e.g., generative adversarial networks (GANs). Our goal is to conduct the first pilot study in building a GAN \textit{completely free of convolutions}, using only pure transformer-based architectures. Our vanilla GAN architecture, dubbed \textbf{TransGAN}, consists of a memory-friendly transformer-based generator that progressively increases feature resolution, and correspondingly a multi-scale discriminator to capture simultaneously semantic contexts and low-level textures. On top of them, we introduce the new module of grid self-attention for alleviating the memory bottleneck further, in order to scale up TransGAN to high-resolution generation. We also develop a unique training recipe including a series of techniques that can mitigate the training instability issues of TransGAN, such as data augmentation, modified normalization, and relative position encoding. Our best architecture achieves highly competitive performance compared to current state-of-the-art GANs using convolutional backbones. Specifically, TransGAN sets \textbf{new state-of-the-art} inception score of 10.43 and FID of 18.28 on STL-10. It also reaches the inception score of 9.02 and FID of 9.26 on CIFAR-10, and 5.28 FID on CelebA $\mathbf{128} \times \mathbf{128}$, respectively: both on par with the current best results and outperforming StyleGAN-V2. When it comes to higher-resolution (e.g. $\mathbf{256} \times \mathbf{256}$) generation tasks, such as on CelebA-HQ and LSUN-Church, TransGAN continues to produce diverse visual examples with high fidelity and impressive texture details. In addition, we dive deep into the transformer-based generation models to understand how their behaviors differ from convolutional ones, by visualizing training dynamics. The code is available at: https://github.com/VITA-Group/TransGAN.

paragraphs: TransGAN investigates whether a generative adversarial network can generate strong images using transformer architectures throughout, without convolutional layers. The design includes a generator that progressively increases feature resolution and a discriminator that examines multiple scales. These components aim to capture both broad semantic structure and fine image texture.

Scaling this design requires addressing memory demands and unstable training. Visualizations of training dynamics further explore differences from convolutional generators. These findings demonstrate that the proposed transformer-only design can compete strongly in the evaluated image-generation settings.
summary.tldr: TransGAN combines transformer-only generation and discrimination with memory-saving attention and specialized training to achieve competitive image synthesis.

title: TransGAN: Two Pure Transformers Can Make One Strong GAN, and That Can Scale Up

abstract: To measure the difference between two probability distributions, referred to as the source and target, respectively, we exploit both the chain rule and Bayes' theorem to construct conditional transport (CT), which is constituted by both a forward component and a backward one. The forward CT is the expected cost of moving a source data point to a target one, with their joint distribution defined by the product of the source probability density function (PDF) and a source-dependent conditional distribution, which is related to the target PDF via Bayes' theorem. The backward CT is defined by reversing the direction. The CT cost can be approximated by replacing the source and target PDFs with their discrete empirical distributions supported on mini-batches, making it amenable to implicit distributions and stochastic gradient descent-based optimization. When applied to train a generative model, CT is shown to strike a good balance between mode-covering and mode-seeking behaviors and strongly resist mode collapse. On a wide variety of benchmark datasets for generative modeling, substituting the default statistical distance of an existing generative adversarial network with CT is shown to consistently improve the performance. PyTorch code is provided.

The findings support the value of the proposed distribution-comparison objective.
summary.tldr: Conditional transport combines forward and backward distribution comparisons, improving generative modeling and resisting mode collapse in reported experiments.

title: Exploiting Chain Rule and Bayes' Theorem to Compare Probability Distributions

abstract: Stochastic sparse linear bandits offer a practical model for high-dimensional online decision-making problems and have a rich information-regret structure. In this work we explore the use of information-directed sampling (IDS), which naturally balances the information-regret trade-off. We develop a class of information-theoretic Bayesian regret bounds that nearly match existing lower bounds on a variety of problem instances, demonstrating the adaptivity of IDS. To efficiently implement sparse IDS, we propose an empirical Bayesian approach for sparse posterior sampling using a spike-and-slab Gaussian-Laplace prior. Numerical results demonstrate significant regret reductions by sparse IDS relative to several baselines.

paragraphs: Sparse linear bandits model repeated decisions in high-dimensional settings where the underlying reward structure is sparse. Each choice has two consequences: it earns a reward and reveals information that may improve later decisions. This paper studies information-directed sampling as a way to balance the value of learning against the regret incurred while exploring.

The authors develop information-theoretic bounds on Bayesian regret. These bounds nearly match existing lower bounds across a variety of problem instances, providing evidence that the method adapts to different information and reward structures. The result concerns the cumulative cost of decisions under the Bayesian formulation, connecting exploration choices to formal performance guarantees.

For practical implementation, the paper proposes empirical Bayesian posterior sampling with a spike-and-slab Gaussian-Laplace prior. This supplies a sparsity-oriented mechanism for representing uncertainty within the sampling procedure. Numerical experiments report significant regret reductions relative to several baselines. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support information-directed exploration as an effective approach for the sparse linear bandit problems considered.
summary.tldr: Sparse information-directed sampling combines adaptive regret guarantees with a practical Bayesian implementation that reduces regret in numerical experiments.

title: Information Directed Sampling for Sparse Linear Bandits

abstract: Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) neural text generation models, especially the pre-trained ones (e.g., BART and T5), have exhibited compelling performance on various natural language generation tasks. However, the black-box nature of these models limits their application in tasks where specific rules (e.g., controllable constraints, prior knowledge) need to be executed. Previous works either design specific model structures (e.g., Copy Mechanism corresponding to the rule "the generated output should include certain words in the source input'') or implement specialized inference algorithms (e.g., Constrained Beam Search) to execute particular rules through the text generation. These methods require the careful design case-by-case and are difficult to support multiple rules concurrently. In this paper, we propose a novel module named Neural Rule-Execution Tracking Machine (NRETM) that can be equipped into various transformer-based generators to leverage multiple rules simultaneously to guide the neural generation model for superior generation performance in an unified and scalable way. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks verify the effectiveness of our proposed model in both controllable and general text generation tasks.

Earlier approaches often handle a particular rule through a specially designed model component or a specialized decoding procedure.

The paper proposes the Neural Rule-Execution Tracking Machine, or NRETM, as a module that can be added to different transformer-based generators. It uses multiple rules simultaneously to guide generation within a unified framework. This addresses the difficulty of building separate mechanisms case by case and then making several of them work together.

Experiments on several benchmarks support the module’s effectiveness in both controllable generation and general text generation. The reported benefit therefore extends beyond the narrow setting of producing text under explicit constraints. The contribution is a reusable way to incorporate rule execution into transformer generation, with empirical improvements across the examined tasks. The abstract presents this as effective guidance rather than a formal guarantee that every generated output satisfies every possible rule.
summary.tldr: NRETM adds a reusable module to transformer generators so multiple rules can guide text generation together.

title: Neural Rule-Execution Tracking Machine For Transformer-Based Text Generation

abstract: Gaussian Processes (GPs) define distributions over functions and their generalization capabilities depend heavily on the choice of kernels. In this paper, we propose a novel structure-aware random Fourier (SRF) kernel for GPs that brings several benefits when modeling graph-structured data. First, SRF kernel is defined with a spectral distribution based on the Fourier duality given by the Bochner's theorem, transforming the kernel learning problem to a distribution inference problem. Second, SRF kernel admits a random Fourier feature formulation that makes the kernel scalable for optimization. Third, SRF kernel enables to leverage geometric structures by taking subgraphs as inputs. To effectively optimize GPs with SRF kernel, we develop a variational EM algorithm, which alternates between an inference procedure (E-step) and a learning procedure (M-step). Experimental results on five real-world datasets show that our model can achieve state-of-the-art performance in two typical graph learning tasks, i.e., object classification and link prediction.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes describe distributions over functions, and their ability to generalize depends strongly on the kernel that expresses relationships between inputs. For graph data, those relationships should reflect structure. This paper introduces a structure-aware random Fourier kernel that accepts subgraphs as inputs, allowing geometric information to enter the model.

The kernel is defined through a spectral distribution using the Fourier relationship supplied by Bochner's theorem. That construction turns learning a kernel into inferring a distribution. A random Fourier feature representation makes optimization scalable, connecting the distribution-based formulation with a computationally manageable way to fit the model.

The authors develop a variational expectation-maximization algorithm that alternates between inference and learning. Experiments on five real-world datasets show that the model can achieve leading performance on object classification and link prediction. The contribution brings together three pieces: subgraphs that expose structure, a learned spectral distribution that defines similarity, and a feature representation that supports efficient optimization.
summary.tldr: A structure-aware Fourier kernel combines subgraph inputs, spectral-distribution inference, and scalable features for Gaussian-process learning on graphs.

title: Structure-Aware Random Fourier Kernel for Graphs

abstract: Self-supervised learning has been shown to be very effective in learning useful representations, and yet much of the success is achieved in data types such as images, audio, and text. The success is mainly enabled by taking advantage of spatial, temporal, or semantic structure in the data through augmentation. However, such structure may not exist in tabular datasets commonly used in fields such as healthcare, making it difficult to design an effective augmentation method, and hindering a similar progress in tabular data setting. In this paper, we introduce a new framework, Subsetting features of Tabular data (SubTab), that turns the task of learning from tabular data into a multi-view representation learning problem by dividing the input features to multiple subsets. We argue that reconstructing the data from the subset of its features rather than its corrupted version in an autoencoder setting can better capture its underlying latent representation. In this framework, the joint representation can be expressed as the aggregate of latent variables of the subsets at test time, which we refer to as collaborative inference. Our experiments show that the SubTab achieves the state of the art (SOTA) performance of 98.31% on MNIST in tabular setting, on par with CNN-based SOTA models, and surpasses existing baselines on three other real-world datasets by a significant margin.

SubTab approaches this problem by treating different subsets of a table’s features as multiple views of the same example.

The authors argue that this can capture underlying latent structure better than reconstructing from a corrupted input in an autoencoder. summary.tldr: SubTab learns tabular representations from feature subsets and combines their latent representations, achieving strong results on four evaluated datasets.

title: SubTab: Subsetting Features of Tabular Data for Self-Supervised Representation Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of tensor estimation from noisy observations with possibly missing entries. A nonparametric approach to tensor completion is developed based on a new model which we coin as sign representable tensors. The model represents the signal tensor of interest using a series of structured sign tensors. Unlike earlier methods, the sign series representation effectively addresses both low- and high-rank signals, while encompassing many existing tensor models---including CP models, Tucker models, single index models, structured tensors with repeating entries---as special cases. We provably reduce the tensor estimation problem to a series of structured classification tasks, and we develop a learning reduction machinery to empower existing low-rank tensor algorithms for more challenging high-rank estimation. Excess risk bounds, estimation errors, and sample complexities are established. We demonstrate the outperformance of our approach over previous methods on two datasets, one on human brain connectivity networks and the other on topic data mining.

This provides a nonparametric approach to completion that can address both low-rank and high-rank signals, expanding the range of tensors the method can estimate.

The authors prove that estimating the tensor can be reduced to solving a sequence of structured classification problems. Their reduction lets existing low-rank tensor algorithms contribute to the more challenging task of estimating high-rank signals.

These establish quantitative support for the reduction rather than relying only on a new representation. Experiments on human brain connectivity and topic-mining datasets show improvements over previous methods. The findings suggest that useful structure can reside in a tensor’s sign-series representation even when low rank alone is insufficient.
summary.tldr: Structured sign series turn noisy tensor completion into classification tasks that can handle both low-rank and high-rank signals.

title: Beyond the Signs: Nonparametric Tensor Completion via Sign Series

abstract: Tabular datasets are the last "unconquered castle" for deep learning, with traditional ML methods like Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees still performing strongly even against recent specialized neural architectures. In this paper, we hypothesize that the key to boosting the performance of neural networks lies in rethinking the joint and simultaneous application of a large set of modern regularization techniques. As a result, we propose regularizing plain Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) networks by searching for the optimal combination/cocktail of 13 regularization techniques for each dataset using a joint optimization over the decision on which regularizers to apply and their subsidiary hyperparameters. We empirically assess the impact of these regularization cocktails for MLPs in a large-scale empirical study comprising 40 tabular datasets and demonstrate that (i) well-regularized plain MLPs significantly outperform recent state-of-the-art specialized neural network architectures, and (ii) they even outperform strong traditional ML methods, such as XGBoost.

paragraphs: Tabular prediction remains a setting where traditional methods such as gradient-boosted trees compete strongly with specialized neural networks. This paper asks whether plain multilayer perceptrons can perform better through a more careful combination of regularization methods. The central hypothesis is that jointly selecting those methods is an important part of neural-network performance.

For each dataset, the approach searches over a collection of 13 regularization techniques. It jointly decides which techniques to apply and how to set their associated hyperparameters. The resulting combination is dataset-specific, so the method treats regularization choices as interacting parts of a single optimization problem rather than independent fixed additions.

An empirical study across 40 tabular datasets finds that the resulting well-regularized multilayer perceptrons significantly outperform recent specialized neural architectures and also outperform strong traditional methods such as XGBoost. These findings establish the strength of the tested tuning approach on that collection of datasets. They also show why a simple network’s architecture alone is an incomplete description of its competitiveness: the jointly chosen training regularization can substantially affect the comparison.
summary.tldr: Jointly tuning combinations of regularizers makes plain multilayer perceptrons outperform specialized neural models and strong tree methods in a 40-dataset study.

title: Well-tuned Simple Nets Excel on Tabular Datasets

abstract: Sliced mutual information (SMI) is defined as an average of mutual information (MI) terms between one-dimensional random projections of the random variables. It serves as a surrogate measure of dependence to classic MI that preserves many of its properties but is more scalable to high dimensions. However, a quantitative characterization of how SMI itself and estimation rates thereof depend on the ambient dimension, which is crucial to the understanding of scalability, remain obscure. This work provides a multifaceted account of the dependence of SMI on dimension, under a broader framework termed $k$-SMI, which considers projections to $k$-dimensional subspaces. Using a new result on the continuity of differential entropy in the 2-Wasserstein metric, we derive sharp bounds on the error of Monte Carlo (MC)-based estimates of $k$-SMI, with explicit dependence on $k$ and the ambient dimension, revealing their interplay with the number of samples. We then combine the MC integrator with the neural estimation framework to provide an end-to-end $k$-SMI estimator, for which optimal convergence rates are established. We also explore asymptotics of the population $k$-SMI as dimension grows, providing Gaussian approximation results with a residual that decays under appropriate moment bounds. All our results trivially apply to SMI by setting $k=1$. Our theory is validated with numerical experiments and is applied to sliced InfoGAN, which altogether provide a comprehensive quantitative account of the scalability question of $k$-SMI, including SMI as a special case when $k=1$.

title: $k$-Sliced Mutual Information: A Quantitative Study of Scalability with Dimension

abstract: Modern neural recording techniques allow neuroscientists to observe the spiking activity of many neurons simultaneously. Although previous work has illustrated how activity within and between known populations of neurons can be summarized by low-dimensional latent vectors, in many cases what determines a unique population may be unclear. Neurons differ in their anatomical location, but also, in their cell types and response properties. Moreover, multiple distinct populations may not be well described by a single low-dimensional, linear representation.To tackle these challenges, we develop a clustering method based on a mixture of dynamic Poisson factor analyzers (DPFA) model, with the number of clusters treated as an unknown parameter. To do the analysis of DPFA model, we propose a novel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to efficiently sample its posterior distribution. Validating our proposed MCMC algorithm with simulations, we find that it can accurately recover the true clustering and latent states and is insensitive to the initial cluster assignments. We then apply the proposed mixture of DPFA model to multi-region experimental recordings, where we find that the proposed method can identify novel, reliable clusters of neurons based on their activity, and may, thus, be a useful tool for neural data analysis.

paragraphs: Recording many neurons at once creates a grouping problem: neurons can differ in location, cell type, and response properties, so useful populations may not be obvious in advance. A single low-dimensional linear description may also fail to capture several distinct populations. This paper develops a method that discovers groups from their spiking activity.

The model combines multiple dynamic Poisson factor analyzers, allowing different clusters to have their own low-dimensional descriptions of changing activity. The number of clusters is itself an unknown parameter. The authors also develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to sample the model’s posterior distribution, supporting inference about both the grouping and the underlying latent states.

In simulations, the inference method accurately recovers the true clusters and latent states and is insensitive to its initial cluster assignments. Applied to experimental recordings spanning multiple regions, it identifies novel, reliable activity-based groups. These results suggest a way to organize neural recordings when population membership is uncertain, while retaining a compact description of how each population behaves over time.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian mixture model discovers neuron populations and their evolving latent activity while treating the number of populations as unknown.

title: Bayesian Clustering of Neural Spiking Activity Using a Mixture of Dynamic Poisson Factor Analyzers

abstract: During initial iterations of training in most Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms, agents perform a significant number of random exploratory steps. In the real world, this can limit the practicality of these algorithms as it can lead to potentially dangerous behavior. Hence safe exploration is a critical issue in applying RL algorithms in the real world. This problem has been recently well studied under the Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) Framework, where in addition to single-stage rewards, an agent receives single-stage costs or penalties as well depending on the state transitions. The prescribed cost functions are responsible for mapping undesirable behavior at any given time-step to a scalar value. The goal then is to find a feasible policy that maximizes reward returns while constraining the cost returns to be below a prescribed threshold during training as well as deployment.We propose an On-policy Model-based Safe Deep RL algorithm in which we learn the transition dynamics of the environment in an online manner as well as find a feasible optimal policy using the Lagrangian Relaxation-based Proximal Policy Optimization. We use an ensemble of neural networks with different initializations to tackle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty issues faced during environment model learning. We compare our approach with relevant model-free and model-based approaches in Constrained RL using the challenging Safe Reinforcement Learning benchmark - the Open AI Safety Gym. We demonstrate that our algorithm is more sample efficient and results in lower cumulative hazard violations as compared to constrained model-free approaches. Further, our approach shows better reward performance than other constrained model-based approaches in the literature.

paragraphs: Random exploration during reinforcement learning can produce dangerous behavior before an agent learns a useful policy. This paper works within constrained Markov decision processes, where transitions produce costs as well as rewards. The objective is to maximize accumulated reward while keeping accumulated cost below a prescribed threshold during training and deployment.

The proposed on-policy algorithm learns an environment transition model online and combines it with a constrained version of proximal policy optimization using Lagrangian relaxation. An ensemble of neural networks with different initializations addresses uncertainty in environment modeling, including uncertainty associated with limited knowledge and variability in outcomes. The learned model and policy optimization jointly support the search for a feasible, rewarding policy.

Evaluation takes place in OpenAI Safety Gym against constrained model-free and model-based approaches. The method uses samples more efficiently and accumulates fewer hazard violations than the compared constrained model-free methods. It also achieves better rewards than the compared constrained model-based methods. These reported improvements support safer and more efficient learning in the benchmark; the stated empirical result is reduced violations, not elimination of all unsafe behavior.
summary.tldr: An online environment model paired with constrained PPO improves sample efficiency and reduces hazard violations in the reported safe reinforcement learning evaluations.

title: Model-based Safe Deep Reinforcement Learning via a Constrained Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithm

abstract: Recent advances in coreset methods have shown that a selection of representative datapoints can replace massive volumes of data for Bayesian inference, preserving the relevant statistical information and significantly accelerating subsequent downstream tasks. Existing variational coreset constructions rely on either selecting subsets of the observed datapoints, or jointly performing approximate inference and optimizing pseudodata in the observed space akin to inducing points methods in Gaussian Processes. So far, both approaches are limited by complexities in evaluating their objectives for general purpose models, and require generating samples from a typically intractable posterior over the coreset throughout inference and testing. In this work, we present a black-box variational inference framework for coresets that overcomes these constraints and enables principled application of variational coresets to intractable models, such as Bayesian neural networks. We apply our techniques to supervised learning problems, and compare them with existing approaches in the literature for data summarization and inference.

Existing variational coreset constructions rely on either selecting subsets of the observed datapoints, or jointly performing approximate inference and optimizing pseudodata in the observed space akin to inducing points methods in Gaussian Processes. So far, both approaches are limited by complexities in evaluating their objectives for general purpose models, and require generating samples from a typically intractable posterior over the coreset throughout inference and testing. In this work, we present a black-box variational inference framework for coresets that overcomes these constraints and enables principled application of variational coresets to intractable models, such as Bayesian neural networks. We apply our techniques to supervised learning problems, and compare them with existing approaches in the literature for data summarization and inference.

paragraphs: A coreset is a compact collection of representative data used in place of a much larger dataset. For Bayesian inference, the aim is to preserve statistically relevant information while making subsequent computation faster. Existing variational approaches either choose observed examples or optimize artificial examples that summarize the original data.

The paper identifies obstacles that make these methods difficult to apply broadly. Their optimization objectives can be complicated to evaluate, and they require samples from a posterior distribution over the coreset that is usually intractable. Those requirements can undermine the usefulness of data compression when the underlying probabilistic model is itself difficult to analyze.

The authors introduce a black-box variational inference framework designed to overcome these constraints and extend principled coreset methods to models such as Bayesian neural networks. They apply it to supervised learning and compare it with existing summarization and inference approaches. The central contribution is broader applicability of variational coresets, allowing compact data summaries to support inference in settings where earlier constructions were computationally awkward.
summary.tldr: A black-box variational framework makes Bayesian coreset construction applicable to difficult models such as Bayesian neural networks.

title: Black-box coreset variational inference

abstract: In this study, we investigate the task of data pre-selection, which aims to select instances for labeling from an unlabeled dataset through a single pass, thereby optimizing performance for undefined downstream tasks with a limited annotation budget. Previous approaches to data pre-selection relied solely on visual features extracted from foundation models, such as CLIP and BLIP-2, but largely ignored the powerfulness of text features. In this work, we argue that, with proper design, the joint feature space of both vision and text can yield a better representation for data pre-selection. To this end, we introduce UP-DP, a simple yet effective unsupervised prompt learning approach that adapts vision-language models, like BLIP-2, for data pre-selection. Specifically, with the BLIP-2 parameters frozen, we train text prompts to extract the joint features with improved representation, ensuring a diverse cluster structure that covers the entire dataset. We extensively compare our method with the state-of-the-art using seven benchmark datasets in different settings, achieving up to a performance gain of 20\%. Interestingly, the prompts learned from one dataset demonstrate significant generalizability and can be applied directly to enhance the feature extraction of BLIP-2 from other datasets. To the best of our knowledge, UP-DP is the first work to incorporate unsupervised prompt learning in a vision-language model for data pre-selection.

These findings support unsupervised prompt learning as a way to adapt the representation used for data selection while keeping the underlying vision-language model fixed.

title: UP-DP: Unsupervised Prompt Learning for Data Pre-Selection with Vision-Language Models

abstract: Contrastive Learning (CL) has achieved impressive performance in self-supervised learning tasks, showing superior generalization ability. Inspired by the success, adopting CL into collaborative filtering (CF) is prevailing in semi-supervised topK recommendations. The basic idea is to routinely conduct heuristic-based data augmentation and apply contrastive losses (e.g., InfoNCE) on the augmented views. Yet, some CF-tailored challenges make this adoption suboptimal, such as the issue of out-of-distribution, the risk of false negatives, and the nature of top-K evaluation. They necessitate the CL-based CF scheme to focus more on mining hard negatives and distinguishing false negatives from the vast unlabeled user-item interactions, for informative contrast signals. Worse still, there is limited understanding of contrastive loss in CF methods, especially w.r.t. its generalization ability. To bridge the gap, we delve into the reasons underpinning the success of contrastive loss in CF, and propose a principled Adversarial InfoNCE loss (AdvInfoNCE), which is a variant of InfoNCE, specially tailored for CF methods. AdvInfoNCE adaptively explores and assigns hardness to each negative instance in an adversarial fashion and further utilizes a fine-grained hardness-aware ranking criterion to empower the recommender’s generalization ability. Training CF models with AdvInfoNCE, we validate the effectiveness of AdvInfoNCE on both synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets, thus showing its generalization ability to mitigate out-of-distribution problems. Given the theoretical guarantees and empirical superiority of AdvInfoNCE over most contrastive loss functions, we advocate its adoption as a standard loss in recommender systems, particularly for the out-of-distribution tasks. Codes are available at https://github.com/LehengTHU/AdvInfoNCE.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning has become a common ingredient in collaborative filtering, where systems recommend items from patterns of user interaction. However, conventional augmentation and contrastive losses do not fully address recommendation-specific issues. The paper introduces Adversarial InfoNCE, a version of the InfoNCE loss designed for collaborative filtering. It adaptively assigns a level of difficulty to each negative instance through an adversarial procedure. A detailed ranking criterion then uses those difficulty assignments to shape training, connecting the treatment of negative examples to the recommender’s ability to generalize.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees and evaluate the loss on synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets. They report empirical advantages over most compared contrastive losses and evidence that the method mitigates out-of-distribution problems. The contribution places the selection and weighting of informative negative signals at the center of contrastive recommendation training.
summary.tldr: Adversarial InfoNCE adapts the difficulty assigned to negative interactions to improve collaborative-filtering generalization, including under distribution shift.

title: Empowering Collaborative Filtering with Principled Adversarial Contrastive Loss

abstract: Many of the most commonly explored natural language processing (NLP) information extraction tasks can be thought of as evaluations of declarative knowledge, or fact-based information extraction. Procedural knowledge extraction, i.e., breaking down a described process into a series of steps, has received much less attention, perhaps in part due to the lack of structured datasets that capture the knowledge extraction process from end-to-end. To address this unmet need, we present FlaMBé (Flow annotations for Multiverse Biological entities), a collection of expert-curated datasets across a series of complementary tasks that capture procedural knowledge in biomedical texts. This dataset is inspired by the observation that one ubiquitous source of procedural knowledge that is described as unstructured text is within academic papers describing their methodology. The workflows annotated in FlaMBé are from texts in the burgeoning field of single cell research, a research area that has become notorious for the number of software tools and complexity of workflows used. Additionally, FlaMBé provides, to our knowledge, the largest manually curated named entity recognition (NER) and disambiguation (NED) datasets for tissue/cell type, a fundamental biological entity that is critical for knowledge extraction in the biomedical research domain. Beyond providing a valuable dataset to enable further development of NLP models for procedural knowledge extraction, automating the process of workflow mining also has important implications for advancing reproducibility in biomedical research.

This paper addresses the relative shortage of structured resources for procedural knowledge extraction, focusing on single-cell research, where numerous software tools and complex workflows make methods especially challenging to organize.

The authors introduce FlaMBé, a collection of expert-curated datasets spanning complementary tasks involved in extracting procedural knowledge from biomedical text. The authors describe the tissue and cell-type resources as the largest manually curated datasets of their kind to their knowledge. The contribution supplies training and evaluation material for developing workflow-extraction systems across the process. Automated workflow mining could also support biomedical reproducibility by making described procedures easier to recover and inspect; the abstract presents this as an important implication of the work.
summary.tldr: FlaMBé provides expert-curated datasets for extracting biomedical workflows and identifying tissue and cell-type entities in single-cell research.

title: Into the Single Cell Multiverse: an End-to-End Dataset for Procedural Knowledge Extraction in Biomedical Texts

abstract: Current auxiliary learning methods mainly adopt the methodology of reweighing losses for the manually collected auxiliary data and tasks. However, these methods heavily rely on domain knowledge during data collection, which may be hardly available in reality. Therefore, current methods will become less effective and even do harm to the primary task when unhelpful auxiliary data and tasks are employed. To tackle the problem, we propose a joint data-task generation framework for auxiliary learning (DTG-AuxL), which can bring benefits to the primary task by generating the new auxiliary data and task in a joint manner. The proposed DTG-AuxL framework contains a joint generator and a bi-level optimization strategy. Specifically, the joint generator contains a feature generator and a label generator, which are designed to be applicable and expressive for various auxiliary learning scenarios. The bi-level optimization strategy optimizes the joint generator and the task learning model, where the joint generator is effectively optimized in the upper level via the implicit gradient from the primary loss and the explicit gradient of our proposed instance regularization, while the task learning model is optimized in the lower level by the generated data and task. Extensive experiments show that our proposed DTG-AuxL framework consistently outperforms existing methods in various auxiliary learning scenarios, particularly when the manually collected auxiliary data and tasks are unhelpful.

paragraphs: Auxiliary learning uses additional tasks and data to help a primary task. Choosing useful auxiliary material often requires domain knowledge, and poorly chosen material can hurt the main objective. This paper proposes DTG-AuxL, which jointly generates auxiliary data and tasks rather than relying solely on reweighting manually collected ones.

The framework contains a feature generator and a label generator, allowing it to construct both inputs and their associated learning targets. A bi-level optimization procedure connects this generation process to the primary task. At the lower level, the task model learns from generated data and tasks. At the upper level, the generator receives an implicit gradient from the primary loss and an explicit gradient from an instance regularization term.

This arrangement makes the primary learning objective a source of guidance for auxiliary generation. Experiments across multiple auxiliary learning scenarios show consistent improvements over the compared methods, with particularly strong benefits when manually supplied auxiliary data and tasks are unhelpful. The findings support jointly designing what auxiliary examples contain and what the model is asked to learn from them.
summary.tldr: DTG-AuxL jointly generates auxiliary features and labels, using the primary task’s loss to guide their usefulness.

title: Joint Data-Task Generation for Auxiliary Learning

abstract: When machine learning is outsourced to a rational agent, conflicts of interest might arise and severely impact predictive performance. In this work, we propose a theoretical framework for incentive-aware delegation of machine learning tasks. We model delegation as a principal-agent game, in which accurate learning can be incentivized by the principal using performance-based contracts. Adapting the economic theory of contract design to this setting, we define budget-optimal contracts and prove they take a simple threshold form under reasonable assumptions. In the binary-action case, the optimality of such contracts is shown to be equivalent to the classic Neyman-Pearson lemma, establishing a formal connection between contract design and statistical hypothesis testing. Empirically, we demonstrate that budget-optimal contracts can be constructed using small-scale data, leveraging recent advances in the study of learning curves and scaling laws. Performance and economic outcomes are evaluated using synthetic and real-world classification tasks.

paragraphs: Outsourcing a classification task creates an incentive problem when the party doing the learning has interests that differ from the party requesting it. Predictive performance can suffer even when both parties act rationally. This paper develops a theoretical framework for designing payments that encourage accurate learning under such delegation.

The framework models the relationship as a principal-agent game and uses performance-based contracts. The authors define contracts that are optimal in budget terms and prove that, under their assumptions, these contracts have a simple threshold structure. In the case with two possible agent actions, the optimality result is equivalent to the Neyman-Pearson lemma, connecting incentive design with statistical hypothesis testing.

The empirical work examines whether such contracts can be constructed from small-scale data using learning curves and scaling laws. Results demonstrate that this construction is possible in the studied settings, with both predictive and economic outcomes evaluated on synthetic and real classification tasks. The work thus combines a conditional mathematical characterization of contract structure with evidence about how those contracts can be estimated.
summary.tldr: A principal-agent framework identifies simple performance-based contracts that can incentivize accurate outsourced classification.

title: Delegated Classification

abstract: The Tanimoto coefficient is commonly used to measure the similarity between molecules represented as discrete fingerprints,either as a distance metric or a positive definite kernel. While many kernel methods can be accelerated using random feature approximations, at present there is a lack of such approximations for the Tanimoto kernel. In this paper we propose two kinds of novel random features to allow this kernel to scale to large datasets, and in the process discover a novel extension of the kernel to real-valued vectors. We theoretically characterize these random features, and provide error bounds on the spectral norm of the Gram matrix. Experimentally, we show that these random features are effective at approximating the Tanimoto coefficient of real-world datasetsand are useful for molecular property prediction and optimization tasks. Future updates to this work will be available at http://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14809.

This paper develops two kinds of random features to fill that gap.

The construction also yields a new extension of the kernel to real-valued vectors. The authors characterize the proposed features theoretically and bound the spectral-norm error of the Gram matrix, the matrix of pairwise kernel similarities. The contribution connects a familiar molecular similarity measure with a computational approach suited to larger datasets. It also broadens the representation beyond discrete fingerprints through the real-valued extension developed alongside the approximations.
summary.tldr: Two random-feature constructions make Tanimoto kernel methods more scalable and introduce an extension to real-valued vectors.

title: Tanimoto Random Features for Scalable Molecular Machine Learning

abstract: Offline safe reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms promise to learn policies that satisfy safety constraints directly in offline datasets without interacting with the environment. This arrangement is particularly important in scenarios with high sampling costs and potential dangers, such as autonomous driving and robotics. However, the influence of safety constraints and out-of-distribution (OOD) actions have made it challenging for previous methods to achieve high reward returns while ensuring safety. In this work, we propose a Variational Optimization with Conservative Eestimation algorithm (VOCE) to solve the problem of optimizing safety policies in the offline dataset. Concretely, we reframe the problem of offline safe RL using probabilistic inference, which introduces variational distributions to make the optimization of policies more flexible. Subsequently, we utilize pessimistic estimation methods to estimate the Q-value of cost and reward, which mitigates the extrapolation errors induced by OOD actions. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate that the VOCE algorithm achieves competitive performance across multiple experimental tasks, particularly outperforming state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of safety.

paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning seeks policies that earn rewards while satisfying safety constraints using only previously collected data. This matters when further interaction would be costly or dangerous. A major challenge is evaluating actions poorly represented in that data: errors in estimating their rewards and safety costs can undermine policy optimization.

VOCE reformulates the problem as probabilistic inference and introduces variational distributions to make policy optimization more flexible. It then uses pessimistic estimates for both reward and cost Q-values, which summarize the consequences of taking actions. These conservative estimates are intended to reduce extrapolation errors associated with actions outside the dataset’s distribution.

Across multiple experimental tasks, VOCE achieves competitive performance and particularly strong safety results relative to state-of-the-art algorithms. The findings support combining flexible probabilistic optimization with conservative evaluation of unfamiliar actions. The safety improvement is an empirical result of the reported experiments, showing how this combination can help manage the tension between pursuing reward and respecting safety constraints in offline learning.
summary.tldr: VOCE combines variational policy optimization with conservative reward and cost estimates to improve safety in offline reinforcement-learning experiments.

title: VOCE: Variational Optimization with Conservative Estimation for Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Indoor rooms are among the most common use cases in 3D scene understanding. Current state-of-the-art methods for this task are driven by large annotated datasets. Room layouts are especially important, consisting of structural elements in 3D, such as wall, floor, and ceiling. However, they are difficult to annotate, especially on pure RGB video. We propose a novel method to produce generic 3D room layouts just from 2D segmentation masks, which are easy to annotate for humans. Based on these 2D annotations, we automatically reconstruct 3D plane equations for the structural elements and their spatial extent in the scene, and connect adjacent elements at the appropriate contact edges. We annotate and publicly release 2246 3D room layouts on the RealEstate10k dataset, containing YouTube videos. We demonstrate the high quality of these 3D layouts annotations with extensive experiments.
