In the studied games, preferences are represented using a friendship graph and an enemy graph. These relationships translate naturally into clustering, where similar data points act like friends and dissimilar points act like enemies.

The authors investigate two ways to judge a grouping, called local stability and local popularity. Both concern changes involving a single agent, giving the analysis a concrete scale at which to assess a partition. They develop efficient mechanisms for finding partitions satisfying these notions and examine the computational complexity of the associated problems.

Simulations demonstrate applications to clustering and community detection. The contribution is both algorithmic and conceptual: it connects methods for forming groups according to individual preferences with methods for organizing data according to similarity. The resulting guarantees concern the specified local notions, while the simulations show how those ideas can support practical grouping tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper develops clustering algorithms through coalition games, using friendship and enmity graphs to find locally stable or locally popular groupings.

title: Clustering via Hedonic Games: New Concepts and Algorithms

abstract: Recently, long-thought reasoning models achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, but often incur substantial inference overhead, making efficiency a critical concern. Our empirical analysis reveals that the benefit of using Long-CoT varies across problems: while some problems require elaborate reasoning, others show no improvement—or even degraded accuracy. This motivates adaptive reasoning strategies that tailor reasoning depth to the input. However, prior work primarily reduces redundancy within long reasoning paths, limiting exploration of more efficient strategies beyond the Long-CoT paradigm. To address this, we propose a novel two-stage framework for adaptive and efficient reasoning. First, we construct a hybrid reasoning model by merging long and short CoT models to enable diverse reasoning styles. Second, we apply bi-level preference training to guide the model to select suitable reasoning styles (group-level), and prefer concise and correct reasoning within each style group (instance-level). Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly reduces inference costs compared to other baseline approaches, while maintaining performance. Notably, on five mathematical datasets, the average length of reasoning is reduced by more than 50\%, highlighting the potential of adaptive strategies to optimize reasoning efficiency in large language models.

summary.tldr: Ada-R1 learns when to use long or short reasoning, cutting average reasoning length by over 50% on five mathematics datasets while maintaining performance.

title: Ada-R1: Hybrid-CoT via Bi-Level Adaptive Reasoning Optimization

abstract: Diffusion models have recently gained prominence in offline reinforcement learning due to their ability to effectively learn high-performing, generalizable policies from static datasets. Diffusion-based planners facilitate long-horizon decision-making by generating high-quality trajectories through iterative denoising, guided by return-maximizing objectives. However, existing guided sampling strategies such as Classifier Guidance, Classifier-Free Guidance, and Monte Carlo Sample Selection either produce suboptimal multi-modal actions, struggle with distributional drift, or incur prohibitive inference-time costs. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{\textit{Prior Guidance}} (PG), a novel guided sampling framework that replaces the standard Gaussian prior of a behavior-cloned diffusion model with a learnable distribution, optimized via a behavior-regularized objective. PG directly generates high-value trajectories without costly reward optimization of the diffusion model itself, and eliminates the need to sample multiple candidates at inference for sample selection. We present an efficient training strategy that applies behavior regularization in latent space, and empirically demonstrate that PG outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion policies and planners across diverse long-horizon offline RL benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ku-dmlab/PG.

paragraphs: Prior Guidance improves diffusion-based planning in offline reinforcement learning, where policies are learned from a fixed dataset. These planners create trajectories through iterative denoising. Existing ways of steering generation toward high returns can struggle with multiple action modes, drift from the data distribution, or require expensive inference-time searches.

The proposed method changes the distribution from which generation begins. It replaces the standard Gaussian prior of a behavior-cloned diffusion model with a learned distribution, optimized using an objective that includes behavior regularization. This directs generation toward valuable trajectories without costly reward optimization of the diffusion model itself. It also removes the need to generate multiple candidates solely to select among them at inference time.

The authors provide an efficient training strategy that applies behavior regularization in latent space. Across varied long-horizon offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks, Prior Guidance outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion policies and planners. The contribution is to move guidance into the learned starting distribution, combining return-oriented trajectory generation with a training mechanism that accounts for the behavior represented in the dataset.
summary.tldr: Prior Guidance learns the starting distribution for diffusion planning, improving benchmark performance without inference-time selection among multiple candidate trajectories.

title: Prior-Guided Diffusion Planning for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Visual captioning benchmarks have become outdated with the emergence of modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as the brief ground-truth sentences and traditional metrics fail to assess detailed captions effectively. While recent benchmarks attempt to address this by focusing on keyword extraction or object-centric evaluation, they remain limited to vague-view or object-view analyses and incomplete visual element coverage. In this paper, we introduce CAPability, a comprehensive multi-view benchmark for evaluating visual captioning across 12 dimensions spanning six critical views. We curate nearly 11K human-annotated images and videos with visual element annotations to evaluate the generated captions. CAPability stably assesses both the correctness and thoroughness of captions with \textit{precision} and \textit{hit} metrics. By converting annotations to QA pairs, we further introduce a heuristic metric, \textit{know but cannot tell} ($K\bar{T}$), indicating a significant performance gap between QA and caption capabilities. Our work provides a holistic analysis of MLLMs' captioning abilities, as we identify their strengths and weaknesses across various dimensions, guiding future research to enhance specific aspects of their capabilities.

paragraphs: Detailed image and video captions need evaluation that captures both accurate statements and omitted information. The paper argues that older benchmarks, with short reference captions and traditional metrics, do not adequately assess modern multimodal models. More recent evaluations also leave gaps by concentrating on keywords, objects, or incomplete sets of visual elements.

CAPability evaluates captions across twelve dimensions organized into six views. It contains nearly eleven thousand human-annotated images and videos, with annotations describing visual elements. Its precision and hit metrics separately assess correctness and thoroughness. This separation matters because a caption can accurately describe a small part of the content while still leaving much of the visual information unmentioned.

The authors also convert annotations into question-answer pairs and introduce a heuristic called 'know but cannot tell.' It indicates a substantial gap between what models can answer when questioned and what they express in captions. Together, these evaluations identify strengths and weaknesses across dimensions, making it possible to target specific captioning capabilities for improvement.
summary.tldr: CAPability evaluates caption accuracy and coverage across multiple dimensions and exposes gaps between answering visual questions and generating captions.

title: CAPability: A Comprehensive Visual Caption Benchmark for Evaluating Both Correctness and Thoroughness

abstract: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) are used to test practical privacy of machine learning models. MIAs complement formal guarantees from differential privacy (DP) under a more realistic adversary model. We analyse MIA vulnerability of fine-tuned neural networks both empirically and theoretically, the latter using a simplified model of fine-tuning. We show that the vulnerability of non-DP models when measured as the attacker advantage at a fixed false positive rate reduces according to a simple power law as the number of examples per class increases. A similar power-law applies even for the most vulnerable points, but the dataset size needed for adequate protection of the most vulnerable points is very large.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether an attacker can identify examples that were used to train a model. This paper studies that privacy vulnerability in fine-tuned neural networks, focusing on how it changes with the number of training examples per class. It combines empirical analysis with theoretical analysis based on a simplified model of fine-tuning.

For models trained without differential privacy, the authors find that vulnerability decreases according to a simple power law as examples per class increase. Vulnerability is measured as attacker advantage at a fixed false-positive rate. Keeping that error rate fixed makes the reported relationship specifically about attack effectiveness under a consistent constraint on false accusations of membership.

A similar power-law relationship applies to the most vulnerable examples, but protecting those examples adequately requires a very large dataset. Thus, the relationship between dataset size and privacy does not imply that modest data growth protects everyone well. The study positions practical attack measurements as complementary to formal differential-privacy guarantees, while revealing how class-level data availability shapes exposure.
summary.tldr: Membership-inference vulnerability falls with examples per class according to a power law, but the most exposed examples require very large datasets for adequate protection.

title: Impact of Dataset Properties on Membership Inference Vulnerability of Deep Transfer Learning

abstract: The imperative of user privacy protection and regulatory compliance necessitates sensitive data removal in model training, yet this process often induces distributional shifts that undermine model performance-particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. We propose a novel data removal approach that enhances deep predictive models through factor decorrelation and loss perturbation. Our approach introduces: (1) a discriminative-preserving factor decorrelation module employing dynamic adaptive weight adjustment and iterative representation updating to reduce feature redundancy and minimize inter-feature correlations. (2) a smoothed data removal mechanism with loss perturbation that creates information-theoretic safeguards against data leakage during removal operations. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets show that our approach outperforms other baselines and consistently achieves high predictive accuracy and robustness even under significant distribution shifts. The results highlight its superior efficiency and adaptability in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios.

paragraphs: Removing sensitive training data can disrupt a predictive model's performance, especially when it later encounters inputs that differ from its training distribution. This paper approaches removal as a joint problem of protecting information and maintaining useful representations. Its method combines changes to the model's features with a smoothed removal mechanism.

The feature component reduces redundancy and correlations between learned factors while seeking to preserve information that distinguishes prediction targets. It uses dynamically adjusted weights and repeatedly updates the representation. The removal component perturbs the loss and introduces information-theoretic safeguards against leakage during removal operations. These components address different pressures: retaining predictive structure and limiting exposure of information associated with the removed data.

Experiments on five benchmark datasets report better results than the compared baselines, with high predictive accuracy and robustness even under substantial distribution shifts. The authors also report efficiency and adaptability in both familiar and out-of-distribution settings. The stated contribution is a removal procedure that couples privacy-oriented safeguards with representation changes designed to sustain prediction quality.
summary.tldr: The method combines feature decorrelation and loss perturbation to protect information during data removal while preserving predictive performance.

title: Factor Decorrelation Enhanced Data Removal from Deep Predictive Models

abstract: Accurate video forecasting enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate hazards, robotics and surveillance systems to predict human intent, and environmental models to issue timely warnings for extreme weather events. However, existing methods remain limited: transformers rely on global attention with quadratic complexity, making them impractical for high-resolution, long-horizon video prediction, while convolutional and recurrent networks suffer from short-range receptive fields and vanishing gradients, losing key information over extended sequences. To overcome these challenges, we introduce VideoTitans, the first architecture to adapt the gradient-driven Titans memory—originally designed for language modelling to video prediction. VideoTitans integrates three core ideas: (i) a sliding-window attention core that scales linearly with sequence length and spatial resolution, (ii) an episodic memory that dynamically retains only informative tokens based on a gradient-based surprise signal, and (iii) a small set of persistent tokens encoding task-specific priors that stabilize training and enhance generalization. Extensive experiments on Moving-MNIST, Human3.6M, TrafficBJ and WeatherBench benchmarks show that VideoTitans consistently reduces computation (FLOPs) and achieves competitive visual fidelity compared to state-of-the-art recurrent, convolutional, and efficient-transformer methods. Comprehensive ablations confirm that each proposed component contributes significantly.

paragraphs: Video prediction requires tracking nearby changes while retaining information from earlier frames. Global attention becomes expensive for large, long sequences, while convolutional and recurrent approaches can lose long-range information. VideoTitans adapts gradient-driven Titans memory from language modeling to video prediction, combining a limited attention window with mechanisms for retaining longer-term information.

Its attention core uses a sliding window and scales linearly with sequence length and spatial resolution. An episodic memory retains informative tokens using a gradient-based surprise signal. A small collection of persistent tokens encodes task-specific prior information to stabilize training and improve generalization. These components provide distinct ways to use recent observations, selected past information, and learned task knowledge.

Experiments on Moving-MNIST, Human3.6M, TrafficBJ, and WeatherBench report consistently fewer floating-point operations and competitive visual fidelity against recurrent, convolutional, and efficient-transformer methods. Ablations find significant contributions from each component. The results support this combination of attention and memory as an efficient video-prediction architecture, with competitive rather than universally superior visual quality.
summary.tldr: VideoTitans combines local attention, surprise-driven memory, and persistent task tokens to reduce video-prediction computation while maintaining competitive visual fidelity.

title: VideoTitans: Scalable Video Prediction with Integrated Short- and Long-term Memory

abstract: Shadow characteristics are of great importance for scene understanding. Existing works mainly consider shadow regions as binary masks, often leading to imprecise detection results and suboptimal performance for scene understanding. We demonstrate that such an assumption oversimplifies light-object interactions in the scene, as the scene details under either hard or soft shadows remain visible to a certain degree. Based on this insight, we aim to reformulate the shadow detection paradigm from the opacity perspective, and introduce a new fine-grained shadow detection method. In particular, given an input image, we first propose a shadow opacity augmentation module to generate realistic images with varied shadow opacities. We then introduce a shadow feature separation module to learn the shadow position and opacity representations separately, followed by an opacity mask prediction module that fuses these representations and predicts fine-grained shadow detection results. In addition, we construct a new dataset with opacity-annotated shadow masks across varied scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms the baselines qualitatively and quantitatively, enhancing a wide range of applications, including shadow removal, shadow editing, and 3D reconstruction.

paragraphs: A binary shadow mask records whether a location is shadowed but cannot express how strongly the shadow obscures the scene. This paper argues that this simplifies the interaction between light and objects too much. Details remain visible to varying degrees under both hard and soft shadows, motivating detection that also represents opacity.

The method first generates realistic training images with varied shadow opacity through an augmentation module. It then learns separate representations for shadow position and opacity. A prediction module combines these representations into a fine-grained opacity mask, making both where the shadow falls and how opaque it is part of the output.

The authors also construct a dataset with opacity-annotated shadow masks across varied scenarios. Experiments show qualitative and quantitative improvements over baselines, along with benefits for shadow removal, shadow editing, and three-dimensional reconstruction. The contribution changes the information supplied by shadow detection: downstream applications receive a graded description of the shadow, better reflecting the visible scene details that remain underneath it.
summary.tldr: The paper predicts shadow opacity as well as location, improving fine-grained detection and downstream image and reconstruction tasks.

title: Under the Shadow: Exploiting Opacity Variation for Fine-grained Shadow Detection

abstract: Model merging is a technique that combines multiple large pretrained models into a single model, enhancing performance and broadening task adaptability without original data or additional training. However, most existing model merging methods focus primarily on exploring the parameter space, merging models with identical architectures. Despite its potential, merging in the architecture space remains in its early stages due to the vast search space and challenges related to layer compatibility. This paper designs a hierarchical model merging framework named HM3, formulating a bilevel multi-objective model merging problem across both parameter and architecture spaces. At the parameter level, HM3 integrates existing merging methods to quickly identify optimal parameters. Based on these, an actor-critic strategy with efficient policy discretization is employed at the architecture level to explore inference paths with Markov property in the layer-granularity search space for reconstructing these optimal models. By training reusable policy and value networks, HM3 learns Pareto optimal models to provide customized solutions for various tasks. Experimental results on language and vision tasks demonstrate that HM3 outperforms methods focusing solely on the parameter or architecture space.

paragraphs: Model merging combines pretrained models to broaden their capabilities. Most methods concentrate on combining parameter values within matching architectures. This paper also explores how layers can be assembled into inference paths, a harder search problem because the number of possible arrangements is large and layer compatibility must be considered.

HM3 organizes the problem into two levels with multiple objectives. At the parameter level, it incorporates existing merging methods to identify useful parameter combinations. At the architecture level, an actor-critic strategy searches paths through layers, using efficient policy discretization and paths with the Markov property. The two levels connect parameter choices with architectural reconstruction.

Reusable policy and value networks are trained to find Pareto-optimal models: solutions representing different tradeoffs among objectives. This supports customized choices for different tasks rather than requiring one universal compromise. Experiments on language and vision tasks report better performance than methods searching only parameters or only architectures. The results support coordinating the two search spaces, while making clear that HM3 itself trains networks to guide that search.
summary.tldr: HM3 jointly searches parameter combinations and layer-level inference paths to produce merged models with different task tradeoffs.

title: HM3: Hierarchical Multi-Objective Model Merging for Pretrained Models

abstract: A common and effective strategy for humans to improve an unsatisfactory outcome in daily life is to find a cause of this outcome and correct the cause. In this paper, we investigate whether this human improvement strategy can be applied to improving reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for alignment of language models (LMs). In particular, it is observed in the literature that LMs tuned by RLHF can still output unsatisfactory responses. This paper proposes a method to improve the unsatisfactory responses by correcting their causes. Our method has two parts. The first part proposes a post-hoc explanation method to explain why an unsatisfactory response is generated to a prompt by identifying the training data that lead to this response. We formulate this problem as a constrained combinatorial optimization problem where the objective is to find a set of training data closest to this prompt-response pair in a feature representation space, and the constraint is that the prompt-response pair can be decomposed as a convex combination of this set of training data in the feature space. We propose an efficient iterative data selection algorithm to solve this problem. The second part proposes an unlearning method that improves unsatisfactory responses to some prompts by unlearning the training data that lead to these unsatisfactory responses and, meanwhile, does not significantly degrade satisfactory responses to other prompts. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm can improve RLHF.

paragraphs: Language models can still produce unsatisfactory responses after reinforcement learning from human feedback. This paper investigates a targeted repair strategy: identify training examples associated with an unwanted response, then unlearn those examples. It connects an explanation of a particular failure with an intervention intended to improve the model's behavior.

The explanation stage searches for training examples close to the problematic prompt-response pair in a feature representation. It imposes an additional requirement: the pair must be expressible as a convex combination of the selected examples in that space, meaning a weighted mixture with nonnegative weights summing to one. An iterative selection algorithm addresses this constrained optimization problem.

The second stage unlearns the identified data. The authors report improvement on unsatisfactory responses to some prompts without significantly degrading satisfactory responses to others, and their experiments demonstrate that the algorithm can improve RLHF. The result supports targeted data-based repair in the evaluated setting, with the feature-space explanation supplying the examples on which that repair operates.
summary.tldr: The paper links unwanted RLHF responses to selected training examples and unlearns those examples to improve some responses while largely preserving satisfactory behavior.

title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback to Improve Alignment

abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have advanced photorealistic novel view synthesis, but their reliance on photometric reconstruction introduces artifacts, commonly known as "floaters". These artifacts degrade novel view quality, particularly in unseen regions where NeRF optimization is unconstrained. We propose a fast, post-hoc NeRF cleanup method that eliminates such artifacts by enforcing a Free Space Prior, ensuring that unseen regions remain empty while preserving the structure of observed areas. Unlike existing approaches that rely on Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation or complex, data-driven priors, our method adopts a Maximum-a-Posteriori (MAP) approach with a simple yet effective global prior. This enables our method to clean artifacts in both seen and unseen areas, significantly improving novel view quality even in challenging scene regions. Our approach generalizes across diverse NeRF architectures and datasets while requiring no additional memory beyond the original NeRF. Compared to state-of-the-art cleanup methods, our method is 2.5x faster in inference and completes cleanup training in under 30 seconds. Our code will be made publicly available.

This paper proposes a cleanup procedure applied after the initial NeRF training to remove such artifacts and improve views from new positions.

Its central ingredient is a Free Space Prior that favors keeping unseen regions empty while preserving observed scene structure. The method uses maximum-a-posteriori estimation, combining reconstruction with this global prior. The prior supplies guidance where photographic evidence is weak, allowing the cleanup to address artifacts in both observed and unobserved regions.

These findings position the approach as a lightweight way to refine an existing reconstruction.
summary.tldr: A simple empty-space prior removes NeRF artifacts through fast post-training cleanup while preserving observed scene structure.

title: Optimize the Unseen - Fast NeRF Cleanup with Free Space Prior

abstract: Effective conversational agents must personalize their interactions to adapt to user preferences, personalities, and attributes across diverse domains like education and healthcare. Current methods like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), often prioritize helpfulness and safety but fall short in fostering truly empathetic, adaptive, and personalized dialogues. Existing personalization approaches typically rely on extensive user history, limiting their effectiveness for new or context-limited users. To address these limitations, we propose leveraging a user model to incorporate a curiosity-based intrinsic reward into multi-turn RLHF. This novel reward mechanism encourages the agent to actively infer user traits by optimizing conversations to improve its user model's accuracy. Consequently, the agent delivers more personalized interactions by learning more about the user. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness in two distinct domains: significantly improving personalization performance in a conversational recommendation task, and personalizing conversations for different learning styles in an educational setting with improved generalization capabilities compared to traditional multi-turn RLHF, all while maintaining conversation quality. Our method offers a promising solution for creating more personalized, adaptive, and engaging conversational agents.

To address these limitations, we propose leveraging a user model to incorporate a curiosity-based intrinsic reward into multi-turn RLHF. This novel reward mechanism encourages the agent to actively infer user traits by optimizing conversations to improve its user model's accuracy. Consequently, the agent delivers more personalized interactions by learning more about the user. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness in two distinct domains: significantly improving personalization performance in a conversational recommendation task, and personalizing conversations for different learning styles in an educational setting with improved generalization capabilities compared to traditional multi-turn RLHF, all while maintaining conversation quality. Our method offers a promising solution for creating more personalized, adaptive, and engaging conversational agents.

paragraphs: Personalizing a conversation is difficult when an agent has little history about its user. Standard reinforcement learning from human feedback emphasizes qualities such as helpfulness and safety, but those objectives do not directly encourage learning about individual preferences. This paper makes that learning process an explicit part of conversational training.

The method introduces a user model and a curiosity-based intrinsic reward into multi-turn reinforcement learning. The agent receives an incentive to conduct conversations that improve the accuracy of its user model. As it infers more about a person’s traits, it can use that understanding to adapt later interactions, connecting information gathering with personalization across turns.

The authors demonstrate the approach in conversational recommendation and education. They report significantly better personalization in recommendation and conversations adapted to different learning styles, with improved generalization relative to traditional multi-turn reinforcement learning from human feedback. Conversation quality is maintained in the reported evaluations. The findings support rewarding progress in understanding the user as a useful training objective alongside producing good responses.
summary.tldr: A curiosity reward encourages conversational agents to learn user traits during dialogue and use that knowledge for better personalization.

title: Enhancing Personalized Multi-Turn Dialogue with Curiosity Reward

abstract: We study the distributed multi-agent multi-armed bandit problem with heterogeneous rewards over random communication graphs. Uniquely, at each time step $t$ agents communicate over a time-varying random graph $\mathcal{G}\_t$ generated by applying the Erdős–Rényi model to a fixed connected base graph $\mathcal{G}$ (for classical Erdos-Rényi graphs, $\mathcal{G}$ is a complete graph), where each potential edge in $\mathcal{G}$ is randomly and independently present with the link probability $p$. Notably, the resulting random graph is not necessarily connected at each time step. Each agent's arm rewards follow time-invariant distributions, and the reward distribution for the same arm may differ across agents. The goal is to minimize the cumulative expected regret relative to the global mean reward of each arm, defined as the average of that arm’s mean rewards across all agents. To this end, we propose a fully distributed algorithm that integrates the arm elimination strategy with the random gossip algorithm. We theoretically show that the regret upper bound is of order $\log T$ and is highly interpretable, where $T$ is the time horizon. It includes the optimal centralized regret $\mathcal O\left(\sum_{k: \Delta_k>0} \frac{\log T}{\Delta_k}\right)$ and an additional term $\mathcal O\left(\frac{N^2 \log T}{p \lambda_{N-1}(\operatorname{Lap}(\mathcal{G}))} + \frac{KN^2 \log T}{p}\right)$ where $N$ and $K$ denote the total number of agents and arms, respectively. This term reflects the impact of $\mathcal G$'s algebraic connectivity $\lambda_{N-1}(\operatorname{Lap}(\mathcal{G}))$ and the link probability $p$, and thus highlights a fundamental trade-off between communication efficiency and regret. As a by-product, we show a nearly optimal regret lower bound. Finally, our numerical experiments not only show the superiority of our algorithm over existing benchmarks, but also validate the theoretical regret scaling with problem complexity.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a group of agents can learn which choices give the best average reward when communication links appear randomly. The same choice can have different reward distributions for different agents, so each agent's local experience tells only part of the story. The objective is to perform well against rewards averaged across the entire group.

The proposed algorithm combines arm elimination, which discards choices judged unpromising, with random gossip, which spreads information between agents. Communication follows a fixed connected base network, but each possible link is independently available with probability p. Consequently, the network need not be connected at every step. Reward distributions remain fixed over time.

The theoretical regret bound grows logarithmically with the time horizon. It separates a centralized learning term from an additional communication term involving group size, the number of choices, link availability, and base-network connectivity. This makes the cost of unreliable communication explicit. A nearly optimal lower bound and numerical experiments further support the analysis and its predicted scaling.
summary.tldr: A distributed bandit algorithm achieves logarithmic regret while explicitly accounting for random communication failures and differing rewards across agents.

title: Distributed Multi-Agent Bandits Over Erdős-Rényi Random Networks

abstract: We study offline reinforcement learning in average-reward MDPs, which presents increased challenges from the perspectives of distribution shift and non-uniform coverage, and has been relatively underexamined from a theoretical perspective. While previous work obtains performance guarantees under single-policy data coverage assumptions, such guarantees utilize additional complexity measures which are uniform over all policies, such as the uniform mixing time. We develop sharp guarantees depending only on the target policy, specifically the bias span and a novel policy hitting radius, yielding the first fully single-policy sample complexity bound for average-reward offline RL. We are also the first to handle general weakly communicating MDPs, contrasting restrictive structural assumptions made in prior work. To achieve this, we introduce an algorithm based on pessimistic discounted value iteration enhanced by a novel quantile clipping technique, which enables the use of a sharper empirical-span-based penalty function. Our algorithm also does not require any prior parameter knowledge for its implementation. Remarkably, we show via hard examples that learning under our conditions requires coverage assumptions beyond the stationary distribution of the target policy, distinguishing single-policy complexity measures from previously examined cases. We also develop lower bounds nearly matching our main result.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from existing data, making coverage of relevant behavior especially important. For average-reward problems, earlier guarantees assumed coverage of one target policy but still relied on complexity measures spanning all policies. This paper develops sample-complexity guarantees whose complexity terms depend only on the target policy, using its bias span and a new policy hitting radius.

The analysis handles general weakly communicating Markov decision processes. Its algorithm combines pessimistic discounted value iteration with quantile clipping, which enables a sharper penalty based on an empirically measured span. The implementation also avoids requiring prior knowledge of the problem parameters. These elements support the paper's first fully single-policy bound for this setting.

Hard examples reveal an important coverage requirement: observing the target policy's stationary distribution alone is insufficient under the paper's conditions. Coverage must also reach beyond that long-run distribution. Nearly matching lower bounds support the sharpness of the main guarantee. Thus, the work both refines which policy complexity matters and clarifies what data coverage learning requires.
summary.tldr: The paper derives target-policy-specific offline RL guarantees and shows that coverage beyond the policy's stationary distribution is required.

title: Optimal Single-Policy Sample Complexity and Transient Coverage for Average-Reward Offline RL

abstract: We consider the problem of adaptive stratified sampling for Monte Carlo integration of a function, given a finite number of function evaluations perturbed by noise. Here we address the problem of adapting simultaneously the number of samples into each stratum and the stratification itself. We show a tradeoff in the size of the partitioning. On the one hand it is important to refine the partition in areas where the observation noise or the function are heterogeneous in order to reduce this variability. But on the other hand, a too refined stratification makes it harder to assign the samples according to a near-optimal (oracle) allocation strategy. In this paper we provide an algorithm \em Monte-Carlo Upper-Lower Confidence Bound that selects online, among a large class of partitions, the partition that provides a near-optimal trade-off, and allocates the samples almost optimally on this partition.

paragraphs: Stratified Monte Carlo integration divides a domain into regions and samples within each region to estimate an integral. This paper considers a finite budget of noisy function evaluations. It addresses two decisions together: how to partition the domain and how many samples to assign to each resulting region.

Those decisions create a tradeoff. Finer partitions can reduce variability where the function or observation noise is heterogeneous. But dividing too finely makes it harder to allocate the available samples close to an oracle strategy. A useful partition must therefore balance the benefit of finer distinctions against the difficulty of distributing limited observations effectively.

The proposed Monte-Carlo Upper-Lower Confidence Bound algorithm chooses a partition online from a large class of candidates. It selects one with a near-optimal tradeoff and allocates samples almost optimally within it. The contribution is joint adaptation of the sampling regions and their budgets, recognizing that neither choice can be judged independently of the other.
summary.tldr: An adaptive Monte Carlo algorithm jointly selects a near-optimal partition and an almost-optimal sample allocation under a finite noisy-evaluation budget.

title: Toward Optimal Stratification for Stratified Monte-Carlo Integration

abstract: Point process data are commonly observed in fields like healthcare and social science. Designing predictive models for such event streams is an under-explored problem, due to often scarce training data. In this work we propose a multitask point process model, leveraging information from all tasks via a hierarchical Gaussian process (GP). Nonparametric learning functions implemented by a GP, which map from past events to future rates, allow analysis of flexible arrival patterns. To facilitate efficient inference, we propose a sparse construction for this hierarchical model, and derive a variational Bayes method for learning and inference. Experimental results are shown on both synthetic data and an application on real electronic health records.

paragraphs: Event streams record occurrences over time, such as events found in healthcare or social science data. Predicting these streams can be difficult when each prediction task has little training data. This paper addresses that shortage with a multitask point process model, allowing related tasks to contribute information to a shared predictive framework.

The model uses a hierarchical Gaussian process to share information across tasks. Its learned functions connect past events to future event rates: how frequently events are expected to occur. Because these functions are nonparametric, the approach can represent flexible arrival patterns without restricting every task to a simple fixed functional form.

To make learning and inference efficient, the authors introduce a sparse construction for the hierarchy and derive a variational Bayes method. They report experiments on synthetic data and real electronic health records. The central contribution is therefore a combination of information sharing, flexible temporal prediction, and an inference strategy designed to make that combination practical.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Gaussian process shares information across event-prediction tasks while learning flexible relationships between past events and future rates.

title: A Multitask Point Process Predictive Model

abstract: We introduce structured prediction energy networks (SPENs), a flexible framework for structured prediction. A deep architecture is used to define an energy function of candidate labels, and then predictions are produced by using back-propagation to iteratively optimize the energy with respect to the labels. This deep architecture captures dependencies between labels that would lead to intractable graphical models, and performs structure learning by automatically learning discriminative features of the structured output. One natural application of our technique is multi-label classification, which traditionally has required strict prior assumptions about the interactions between labels to ensure tractable learning and prediction. We are able to apply SPENs to multi-label problems with substantially larger label sets than previous applications of structured prediction, while modeling high-order interactions using minimal structural assumptions. Overall, deep learning provides remarkable tools for learning features of the inputs to a prediction problem, and this work extends these techniques to learning features of structured outputs. Our experiments provide impressive performance on a variety of benchmark multi-label classification tasks, demonstrate that our technique can be used to provide interpretable structure learning, and illuminate fundamental trade-offs between feed-forward and iterative structured prediction.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves outputs whose components depend on one another, such as multiple labels assigned to the same input. This paper introduces structured prediction energy networks, or SPENs. A deep network defines an energy function over candidate labels, and prediction proceeds by iteratively optimizing that energy with respect to the labels using back-propagation.

The architecture learns features of structured outputs, extending deep learning’s feature-learning role beyond the inputs. It can capture label dependencies that would make corresponding graphical models intractable. For multilabel classification, this enables modeling high-order interactions with minimal structural assumptions and handling substantially larger label sets than earlier structured-prediction applications considered by the authors.

Experiments report strong performance across benchmark multilabel tasks and show that the learned structure can be interpretable. They also examine trade-offs between feed-forward prediction and iterative structured prediction. The contribution is therefore both a flexible way to learn output relationships and an inference procedure that searches over candidate outputs, with empirical evidence about the benefits and trade-offs of that combination.
summary.tldr: SPENs learn deep energy functions over structured outputs and predict by iteratively optimizing candidate labels.

title: Structured Prediction Energy Networks

abstract: We introduce Group equivariant Convolutional Neural Networks (G-CNNs), a natural generalization of convolutional neural networks that reduces sample complexity by exploiting symmetries. G-CNNs use G-convolutions, a new type of layer that enjoys a substantially higher degree of weight sharing than regular convolution layers. G-convolutions increase the expressive capacity of the network without increasing the number of parameters. Group convolution layers are easy to use and can be implemented with negligible computational overhead for discrete groups generated by translations, reflections and rotations. G-CNNs achieve state of the art results on CIFAR10 and rotated MNIST.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes convolutional neural networks by building more symmetries into their layers. The proposed Group equivariant Convolutional Neural Networks, or G-CNNs, exploit relationships associated with transformations such as translations, reflections, and rotations. The stated benefit is reduced sample complexity: using symmetry helps the model learn from fewer examples.

The core building block is the G-convolution. It shares weights more extensively than an ordinary convolutional layer, allowing related transformations to use common learned parameters. The authors state that this construction increases expressive capacity without increasing the parameter count. Greater sharing therefore provides a way to strengthen the model's structure without simply making its parameter set larger.

For discrete groups generated by translations, reflections, and rotations, the layers can be implemented with negligible computational overhead. The paper reports state-of-the-art results on CIFAR10 and rotated MNIST. Together, the construction and experiments support explicitly encoding relevant symmetries as a useful architectural choice, with the computational-overhead claim specifically tied to the stated classes of discrete transformations.
summary.tldr: G-CNNs exploit symmetry through expanded weight sharing, increasing expressive capacity without adding parameters.

title: Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks

abstract: We propose a new way of deriving policy gradient updates for reinforcement learning. Our technique, based on Fourier analysis, recasts integrals that arise with expected policy gradients as convolutions and turns them into multiplications. The obtained analytical solutions allow us to capture the low variance benefits of EPG in a broad range of settings. For the critic, we treat trigonometric and radial basis functions, two function families with the universal approximation property. The choice of policy can be almost arbitrary, including mixtures or hybrid continuous-discrete probability distributions. Moreover, we derive a general family of sample-based estimators for stochastic policy gradients, which unifies existing results on sample-based approximation. We believe that this technique has the potential to shape the next generation of policy gradient approaches, powered by analytical results.

paragraphs: Expected policy gradients involve integrals that can be difficult to evaluate across different policy and critic choices. This paper develops a Fourier-analysis approach to deriving those updates. It rewrites the relevant integrals as convolutions and then turns the convolutions into multiplications, providing a route to analytical solutions.

The resulting solutions extend the low-variance benefits of expected policy gradients to a broad range of settings. The analysis covers trigonometric and radial basis critics, two families with universal approximation properties. Policy choices can be almost arbitrary, including mixtures and distributions that combine continuous and discrete components, making the framework applicable beyond a narrow pairing of policy and critic.

The paper also derives a general family of sample-based stochastic policy-gradient estimators that unifies existing approximation results. Its contribution joins analytical integration and sampling within one mathematical approach. The authors suggest that this could influence future policy-gradient methods; that prospective impact is presented as a possibility, while the analytical derivations are the established contribution.
summary.tldr: Fourier analysis yields analytical expected policy gradients for broad policy and critic families and unifies sample-based estimators.

title: Fourier Policy Gradients

abstract: We analyze two novel randomized variants of the Frank-Wolfe (FW) or conditional gradient algorithm. While classical FW algorithms require solving a linear minimization problem over the domain at each iteration, the proposed method only requires to solve a linear minimization problem over a small subset of the original domain. The first algorithm that we propose is a randomized variant of the original FW algorithm and achieves a $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ sublinear convergence rate as in the deterministic counterpart. The second algorithm is a randomized variant of the Away-step FW algorithm, and again as its deterministic counterpart, reaches linear (i.e., exponential) convergence rate making it the first provably convergent randomized variant of Away-step FW. In both cases, while subsampling reduces the convergence rate by a constant factor, the linear minimization step can be a fraction of the cost of that of the deterministic versions, especially when the data is streamed. We illustrate computational gains of both algorithms on regression problems, involving both $\ell_1$ and latent group lasso penalties.

paragraphs: Frank–Wolfe optimization requires solving a linear minimization problem over the feasible domain at each iteration. This paper reduces the work involved in that step by considering only a small sampled subset of the domain. It develops randomized versions of both the original Frank–Wolfe algorithm and its away-step variant.

The randomized original method retains a sublinear convergence rate proportional to one divided by the iteration count. The randomized away-step method retains linear, or exponential, convergence, and the authors identify it as the first randomized away-step variant with a convergence proof. Subsampling slows the rates by a constant factor while preserving these respective forms of convergence.

The practical trade-off is that a cheaper iteration can offset slower progress per iteration. The linear minimization step may cost only a fraction of its deterministic counterpart, especially with streamed data. Regression experiments involving l1 and latent group lasso penalties illustrate computational gains for both algorithms, connecting the convergence analysis to actual optimization savings.
summary.tldr: Subsampling makes Frank–Wolfe steps cheaper while preserving the convergence-rate forms of the original and away-step algorithms.

title: Frank-Wolfe with Subsampling Oracle

abstract: We propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) scheme to perform state inference in non-linear non-Gaussian state-space models. Current state-of-the-art methods to address this problem rely on particle MCMC techniques and its variants, such as the iterated conditional Sequential Monte Carlo (cSMC) scheme, which uses a Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) type proposal within MCMC. A deficiency of standard SMC proposals is that they only use observations up to time $t$ to propose states at time $t$ when an entire observation sequence is available. More sophisticated SMC based on lookahead techniques could be used but they can be difficult to put in practice. We propose here replica cSMC where we build SMC proposals for one replica using information from the entire observation sequence by conditioning on the states of the other replicas. This approach is easily parallelizable and we demonstrate its excellent empirical performance when compared to the standard iterated cSMC scheme at fixed computational complexity.

Current state-of-the-art methods to address this problem rely on particle MCMC techniques and its variants, such as the iterated conditional Sequential Monte Carlo (cSMC) scheme, which uses a Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) type proposal within MCMC. A deficiency of standard SMC proposals is that they only use observations up to time $t$ to propose states at time $t$ when an entire observation sequence is available. More sophisticated SMC based on lookahead techniques could be used but they can be difficult to put in practice. We propose here replica cSMC where we build SMC proposals for one replica using information from the entire observation sequence by conditioning on the states of the other replicas. This approach is easily parallelizable and we demonstrate its excellent empirical performance when compared to the standard iterated cSMC scheme at fixed computational complexity.

paragraphs: This paper concerns recovering hidden states from observations in nonlinear, non-Gaussian state-space models. Particle MCMC methods address this problem using sequential proposals inside a Markov chain Monte Carlo procedure. A weakness of standard sequential proposals is that a state at a given time is proposed using observations only up to that time, even when later observations are already available.

Replica conditional Sequential Monte Carlo introduces multiple replicas and constructs proposals for one replica by conditioning on the states of the others. Through those states, the proposal can use information from the entire observation sequence. This offers a way to incorporate later evidence into state proposals without relying on the more sophisticated lookahead procedures that the abstract describes as difficult to implement.

The approach is readily parallelizable, so its replica structure also supports concurrent computation. The authors report strong empirical performance relative to standard iterated conditional Sequential Monte Carlo at fixed computational complexity. That comparison evaluates the benefit of using the available observation sequence more fully while controlling the stated computational budget.
summary.tldr: Replica cSMC uses other replicas’ states to incorporate full-sequence information into proposals and improves empirical state inference at matched computational complexity.

title: Replica Conditional Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: When machine learning models are deployed on a test distribution different from the training distribution, they can perform poorly, but overestimate their performance. In this work, we aim to better estimate a model’s performance under distribution shift, without supervision. To do so, we use a set of domain-invariant predictors as a proxy for the unknown, true target labels. Since the error of the resulting risk estimate depends on the target risk of the proxy model, we study generalization of domain-invariant representations and show that the complexity of the latent representation has a significant influence on the target risk. Empirically, our approach (1) enables self-tuning of domain adaptation models, and (2) accurately estimates the target error of given models under distribution shift. Other applications include model selection, deciding early stopping and error detection.

In this work, we aim to better estimate a model’s performance under distribution shift, without supervision. To do so, we use a set of domain-invariant predictors as a proxy for the unknown, true target labels. Since the error of the resulting risk estimate depends on the target risk of the proxy model, we study generalization of domain-invariant representations and show that the complexity of the latent representation has a significant influence on the target risk. Empirically, our approach (1) enables self-tuning of domain adaptation models, and (2) accurately estimates the target error of given models under distribution shift. paragraphs: A model can lose accuracy when deployed on data that differ from its training distribution, while still appearing overly confident about its performance. This paper studies how to estimate that performance without labeled target data. The practical objective is to assess a deployed model when its actual test errors cannot be measured directly.

The method uses a collection of domain-invariant predictors as substitutes for the unavailable target labels. These proxy predictions provide a way to estimate risk, but the estimate's error depends on how well the proxy model itself performs on the target distribution. The authors therefore analyze domain-invariant representations and show that the complexity of the latent representation substantially influences target risk.

Empirically, the approach accurately estimates target error in the evaluated distribution shifts and enables domain adaptation models to tune themselves. The authors also identify model selection, early stopping, and error detection as applications. The proxy dependence explains why representation quality matters both for prediction and for evaluating other models.
summary.tldr: Domain-invariant proxy predictors estimate performance without target labels, with estimation quality depending on the proxies' own target performance.

title: Estimating Generalization under Distribution Shifts via Domain-Invariant Representations

abstract: Trustworthy AI is a critical issue in machine learning where, in addition to training a model that is accurate, one must consider both fair and robust training in the presence of data bias and poisoning. However, the existing model fairness techniques mistakenly view poisoned data as an additional bias to be fixed, resulting in severe performance degradation. To address this problem, we propose FR-Train, which holistically performs fair and robust model training. We provide a mutual information-based interpretation of an existing adversarial training-based fairness-only method, and apply this idea to architect an additional discriminator that can identify poisoned data using a clean validation set and reduce its influence. In our experiments, FR-Train shows almost no decrease in fairness and accuracy in the presence of data poisoning by both mitigating the bias and defending against poisoning. We also demonstrate how to construct clean validation sets using crowdsourcing, and release new benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Training data can contain both social bias and deliberately poisoned examples. The paper argues that existing fairness methods may treat poisoning as another bias to correct, causing substantial performance degradation. FR-Train addresses fairness and resistance to poisoning together, so efforts to mitigate bias also account for the reliability of the training data.

The authors first interpret an existing adversarial fairness-training method through mutual information. They use that interpretation to design an additional discriminator that identifies poisoned data with help from a clean validation set. Reducing the influence of these examples allows the training process to pursue fairness while defending against corrupted supervision.

In the reported experiments, FR-Train experiences almost no loss of fairness or accuracy under data poisoning. The clean validation set is an explicit part of the approach, and the authors demonstrate how crowdsourcing can construct such sets. They also release benchmark datasets. The findings support treating fairness and robustness as interacting training objectives rather than addressing data bias without considering poisoning.
summary.tldr: FR-Train uses a clean validation set and an additional discriminator to jointly mitigate bias and reduce poisoned data's influence.

title: FR-Train: A Mutual Information-Based Approach to Fair and Robust Training

abstract: Many important real-world problems have action spaces that are high-dimensional, continuous or both, making full enumeration of all possible actions infeasible. Instead, only small subsets of actions can be sampled for the purpose of policy evaluation and improvement. In this paper, we propose a general framework to reason in a principled way about policy evaluation and improvement over such sampled action subsets. This sample-based policy iteration framework can in principle be applied to any reinforcement learning algorithm based upon policy iteration. Concretely, we propose Sampled MuZero, an extension of the MuZero algorithm that is able to learn in domains with arbitrarily complex action spaces by planning over sampled actions. We demonstrate this approach on the classical board game of Go and on two continuous control benchmark domains: DeepMind Control Suite and Real-World RL Suite.

paragraphs: Planning becomes difficult when an agent has too many possible actions to enumerate. The problem is especially apparent when actions are continuous, high-dimensional, or both. In these settings, policy evaluation and improvement must work with small sampled subsets of actions, raising the question of how to make those updates principled.

The paper develops a sample-based policy iteration framework for reasoning about this restricted view of the action space. Its scope is broad: in principle, the framework can be applied to any reinforcement learning algorithm based on policy iteration. The central contribution is a way to organize evaluation and improvement when only some actions are available for consideration.

The authors instantiate the framework as Sampled MuZero, an extension that plans over sampled actions and is designed to learn in domains with arbitrarily complex action spaces. They demonstrate it on Go and on the DeepMind Control Suite and Real-World RL Suite. These examples establish applications across board-game decisions and continuous control without requiring exhaustive enumeration of possible actions.
summary.tldr: Sampled MuZero applies a general sample-based policy iteration framework to planning in action spaces too large or continuous to enumerate.

title: Learning and Planning in Complex Action Spaces

abstract: The posterior over Bayesian neural network (BNN) parameters is extremely high-dimensional and non-convex. For computational reasons, researchers approximate this posterior using inexpensive mini-batch methods such as mean-field variational inference or stochastic-gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo (SGMCMC). To investigate foundational questions in Bayesian deep learning, we instead use full batch Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) on modern architectures. We show that (1) BNNs can achieve significant performance gains over standard training and deep ensembles; (2) a single long HMC chain can provide a comparable representation of the posterior to multiple shorter chains; (3) in contrast to recent studies, we find posterior tempering is not needed for near-optimal performance, with little evidence for a “cold posterior” effect, which we show is largely an artifact of data augmentation; (4) BMA performance is robust to the choice of prior scale, and relatively similar for diagonal Gaussian, mixture of Gaussian, and logistic priors; (5) Bayesian neural networks show surprisingly poor generalization under domain shift; (6) while cheaper alternatives such as deep ensembles and SGMCMC can provide good generalization, their predictive distributions are distinct from HMC. Notably, deep ensemble predictive distributions are similarly close to HMC as standard SGLD, and closer than standard variational inference.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty through a distribution over network parameters, but that distribution is difficult to explore. The paper uses full-batch Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on modern architectures to investigate its properties, moving beyond the inexpensive approximations commonly used for computational reasons. This provides a basis for examining both predictive performance and approximation behavior.

The experiments show that Bayesian networks can substantially outperform standard training and deep ensembles. One long sampling chain can represent the posterior comparably to multiple shorter chains. The authors find little evidence that artificially cooling the posterior is needed for near-optimal performance, attributing the cold-posterior effect largely to data augmentation. Bayesian model averaging is also robust to prior scale and relatively similar across the tested prior families.

The findings include unexpectedly poor generalization under domain shift. Cheaper methods can generalize well while producing predictive distributions distinct from Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Deep ensembles are about as close to its predictions as standard SGLD and closer than standard variational inference, showing that predictive success and agreement with this posterior-sampling approach are separate considerations.
summary.tldr: Full-batch Hamiltonian Monte Carlo reveals strong Bayesian prediction results alongside domain-shift weaknesses and differences from cheaper posterior approximations.

title: What Are Bayesian Neural Network Posteriors Really Like?

abstract: Datacenter vision systems widely use small, specialized convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on specific tasks for high-throughput inference. These settings employ accelerators with massive computational capacity, but which specialized CNNs underutilize due to having low arithmetic intensity. This results in suboptimal application-level throughput and poor returns on accelerator investment. Increasing batch size is the only known way to increase both application-level throughput and accelerator utilization for inference, but yields diminishing returns; specialized CNNs poorly utilize accelerators even with large batch size. We propose FoldedCNNs, a new approach to CNN design that increases inference throughput and utilization beyond large batch size. FoldedCNNs rethink the structure of inputs and layers of specialized CNNs to boost arithmetic intensity: in FoldedCNNs, f images with C channels each are concatenated into a single input with fC channels and jointly classified by a wider CNN. Increased arithmetic intensity in FoldedCNNs increases the throughput and GPU utilization of specialized CNN inference by up to 2.5x and 2.8x, with accuracy close to the original CNN in most cases.

paragraphs: Small convolutional networks specialized for particular vision tasks can leave much of a datacenter accelerator’s capacity unused. Their low arithmetic intensity means their workload does not make effective use of the available computation. Increasing batch size helps, but the authors identify diminishing returns: even large batches can leave these specialized networks using accelerators poorly.

FoldedCNNs changes the network’s input and layer structure to address this problem. It combines f images, each with C channels, into one input with fC channels. A wider convolutional network then classifies those images jointly. This changes how computation is organized inside the model, raising arithmetic intensity beyond what increasing the ordinary batch size achieves.

The reported evaluations show throughput improvements of up to 2.5 times and GPU-utilization improvements of up to 2.8 times. Accuracy remains close to that of the original network in most cases. These qualified results suggest that redesigning specialized networks around accelerator use can improve inference efficiency, while making accuracy preservation an empirical consideration rather than an automatic guarantee.
summary.tldr: FoldedCNNs jointly processes images through a wider network, improving throughput and GPU utilization while retaining similar accuracy in most tested cases.

title: Boosting the Throughput and Accelerator Utilization of Specialized CNN Inference Beyond Increasing Batch Size

abstract: When training an implicit generative model, ideally one would like the generator to reproduce all the different modes and subtleties of the target distribution. Naturally, when comparing two empirical distributions, the larger the sample population, the more these statistical nuances can be captured. However, existing objective functions are computationally constrained in the amount of samples they can consider by the memory required to process a batch of samples. In this paper, we build upon recent progress in sliced Wasserstein distances, a family of differentiable metrics for distribution discrepancy based on the Optimal Transport paradigm. We introduce a procedure to train these distances with virtually any batch size, allowing the discrepancy measure to capture richer statistics and better approximating the distance between the underlying continuous distributions. As an example, we demonstrate the matching of the distribution of Inception features with batches of tens of thousands of samples, achieving FID scores that outperform state-of-the-art implicit generative models.

paragraphs: A generative model should reproduce the different modes and fine details of its target distribution. Comparing larger collections of generated and target samples can expose more of that structure. In practice, the memory needed to process a training batch limits how many samples a distribution-matching objective can consider together.

This paper develops a training procedure based on sliced Wasserstein distances, differentiable measures of distribution discrepancy derived from optimal transport. The procedure supports virtually any batch size, loosening the memory-related restriction on the number of samples used in the comparison. Larger sample populations allow the discrepancy measure to capture richer statistics and better approximate the distance between the underlying continuous distributions.

As a demonstration, the authors match distributions of Inception features using batches containing tens of thousands of samples. They report FID scores outperforming state-of-the-art implicit generative models. The stated result shows how expanding the statistical view available to a distribution-matching objective can translate into improved generative performance in the demonstrated setting.
summary.tldr: A sliced Wasserstein training procedure enables very large sample comparisons and yields improved reported FID scores for implicit generative models.

title: Run-Sort-ReRun: Escaping Batch Size Limitations in Sliced Wasserstein Generative Models

abstract: Collaborative learning allows participants to jointly train a model without data sharing. To update the model parameters, the central server broadcasts model parameters to the clients, and the clients send updating directions such as gradients to the server. While data do not leave a client device, the communicated gradients and parameters will leak a client’s privacy. Attacks that infer clients’ privacy from gradients and parameters have been developed by prior work. Simple defenses such as dropout and differential privacy either fail to defend the attacks or seriously hurt test accuracy. We propose a practical defense which we call Double-Blind Collaborative Learning (DBCL). The high-level idea is to apply random matrix sketching to the parameters (aka weights) and re-generate random sketching after each iteration. DBCL prevents clients from conducting gradient-based privacy inferences which are the most effective attacks. DBCL works because from the attacker’s perspective, sketching is effectively random noise that outweighs the signal. Notably, DBCL does not much increase computation and communication costs and does not hurt test accuracy at all.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning keeps training data on client devices, but clients still exchange model parameters and update directions such as gradients with a server. Those messages can reveal private information. This paper addresses attacks that infer client information from the learning process even though the original data never leaves the device.

Double-Blind Collaborative Learning, or DBCL, applies random matrix sketching to model weights and generates a fresh sketch at every iteration. From an attacker’s perspective, the sketching acts as random noise strong enough to overwhelm the informative signal. The paper states that this prevents clients from performing gradient-based privacy inference.

The practical aim is to protect these communications without undermining collaborative training. The authors report that DBCL adds little computation or communication cost and does not reduce test accuracy. This addresses the tradeoff they identify in simple defenses, which can fail against attacks or substantially harm accuracy. The stated protection concerns client-side gradient-based inference, keeping the claim tied to the attack mechanism examined.
summary.tldr: DBCL refreshes random sketches of model weights to block client gradient-based privacy inference while reporting little overhead and no accuracy loss.

title: Matrix Sketching for Secure Collaborative Machine Learning

abstract: Meta reinforcement learning (meta-RL) extracts knowledge from previous tasks and achieves fast adaptation to new tasks. Despite recent progress, efficient exploration in meta-RL remains a key challenge in sparse-reward tasks, as it requires quickly finding informative task-relevant experiences in both meta-training and adaptation. To address this challenge, we explicitly model an exploration policy learning problem for meta-RL, which is separated from exploitation policy learning, and introduce a novel empowerment-driven exploration objective, which aims to maximize information gain for task identification. We derive a corresponding intrinsic reward and develop a new off-policy meta-RL framework, which efficiently learns separate context-aware exploration and exploitation policies by sharing the knowledge of task inference. Experimental evaluation shows that our meta-RL method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on various sparse-reward MuJoCo locomotion tasks and more complex sparse-reward Meta-World tasks.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning uses experience from previous tasks to adapt quickly to new ones. Sparse rewards make this difficult because an agent must first find experiences that reveal what task it faces. The paper treats this search for informative experience as a learning problem in its own right during both meta-training and adaptation.

MetaCURE separates the exploration policy from the exploitation policy. Its empowerment-driven exploration objective seeks information gain for identifying the task, and the authors derive an intrinsic reward corresponding to that objective. A new off-policy framework learns both policies while allowing them to share knowledge about task inference.

This separation gives exploration a specific purpose: collect information that helps identify the current task, while the exploitation policy learns how to act using that knowledge. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on sparse-reward MuJoCo locomotion tasks and more complex sparse-reward Meta-World tasks. The results support explicitly training task-informative exploration as part of rapid adaptation.
summary.tldr: MetaCURE learns separate exploration and exploitation policies, rewarding exploration that reveals task identity to improve sparse-reward adaptation.

title: MetaCURE: Meta Reinforcement Learning with Empowerment-Driven Exploration

abstract: In a Markov decision process (MDP), an agent interacts with the environment via perceptions and actions. During this process, the agent aims to maximize its own gain. Hence, appropriate regulations are often required, if we hope to take the external costs/benefits of its actions into consideration. In this paper, we study how to regulate such an agent by redesigning model parameters that can affect the rewards and/or the transition kernels. We formulate this problem as a bilevel program, in which the lower-level MDP is regulated by the upper-level model designer. To solve the resulting problem, we develop a scheme that allows the designer to iteratively predict the agent’s reaction by solving the MDP and then adaptively update model parameters based on the predicted reaction. The algorithm is first theoretically analyzed and then empirically tested on several MDP models arising in economics and robotics.

In this paper, we study how to regulate such an agent by redesigning model parameters that can affect the rewards and/or the transition kernels. We formulate this problem as a bilevel program, in which the lower-level MDP is regulated by the upper-level model designer. The algorithm is first theoretically analyzed and then empirically tested on several MDP models arising in economics and robotics.

paragraphs: An agent in a Markov decision process chooses actions to improve its own rewards. Those choices can also impose costs or create benefits outside the agent’s objective. This paper studies how a designer can account for those external effects by changing parameters that influence rewards, environmental transitions, or both.

The authors express this interaction as a two-level optimization problem. At the lower level, the agent solves its decision problem under the current model. At the upper level, the designer chooses how that model should change. This structure makes the agent’s response part of the design problem: changing incentives or dynamics can change which behavior the agent prefers.

Their algorithm repeatedly solves the agent’s decision problem to predict its reaction, then updates the model parameters using that prediction. The paper provides a theoretical analysis and empirical tests on models from economics and robotics. Its contribution is a concrete framework for adapting an environment’s rules while explicitly accounting for the behavior those rules induce.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a two-level optimization method for redesigning rewards and dynamics around an agent’s predicted response.

title: Adaptive Model Design for Markov Decision Process

abstract: We propose a new representation of visual data that disentangles object position from appearance. Our method, termed Deep Latent Particles (DLP), decomposes the visual input into low-dimensional latent “particles”, where each particle is described by its spatial location and features of its surrounding region. To drive learning of such representations, we follow a VAE-based based approach and introduce a prior for particle positions based on a spatial-Softmax architecture, and a modification of the evidence lower bound loss inspired by the Chamfer distance between particles. We demonstrate that our DLP representations are useful for downstream tasks such as unsupervised keypoint (KP) detection, image manipulation, and video prediction for scenes composed of multiple dynamic objects. In addition, we show that our probabilistic interpretation of the problem naturally provides uncertainty estimates for particle locations, which can be used for model selection, among other tasks.
