paragraphs: Deep Latent Particles represents an image through a collection of compact latent particles. Each particle carries a spatial location and features describing its surrounding region. This separates where visual content is located from what that content looks like, giving the representation an explicit spatial organization.

The method learns these representations through a variational autoencoder approach. It introduces a prior over particle positions based on a spatial-Softmax architecture and modifies the training objective using an idea inspired by Chamfer distance between particles. These choices shape how particle locations and local appearance information are learned together from visual inputs.

The authors demonstrate uses in unsupervised keypoint detection, image manipulation, and video prediction for scenes containing multiple moving objects. The probabilistic formulation also provides uncertainty estimates for particle locations, which can support model selection. The findings show that the particle representation can serve several downstream tasks while expressing uncertainty about where its visual components are located.
summary.tldr: Deep Latent Particles learns spatially organized image representations that separate position from appearance and estimate location uncertainty.

title: Unsupervised Image Representation Learning with Deep Latent Particles

abstract: The AutoAttack (AA) has been the most reliable method to evaluate adversarial robustness when considerable computational resources are available. However, the high computational cost (e.g., 100 times more than that of the project gradient descent attack) makes AA infeasible for practitioners with limited computational resources, and also hinders applications of AA in the adversarial training (AT). In this paper, we propose a novel method, minimum-margin (MM) attack, to fast and reliably evaluate adversarial robustness. Compared with AA, our method achieves comparable performance but only costs 3% of the computational time in extensive experiments. The reliability of our method lies in that we evaluate the quality of adversarial examples using the margin between two targets that can precisely identify the most adversarial example. The computational efficiency of our method lies in an effective Sequential TArget Ranking Selection (STARS) method, ensuring that the cost of the MM attack is independent of the number of classes. The MM attack opens a new way for evaluating adversarial robustness and provides a feasible and reliable way to generate high-quality adversarial examples in AT.

paragraphs: Evaluating adversarial robustness requires attacks that can reliably expose a model’s weaknesses. The paper identifies computational cost as a major obstacle to using AutoAttack, particularly when resources are limited or adversarial examples must be generated during training. It proposes the minimum-margin attack as a faster way to perform this evaluation.

The method evaluates candidate adversarial examples through the margin between two targets. The authors use this quantity to identify the most adversarial candidate. A second component, Sequential TArget Ranking Selection, makes target selection efficient and keeps the attack’s cost independent of the number of classes. These components address the quality of the selected examples and the expense of finding them.

Across extensive experiments, the minimum-margin attack achieves performance comparable to AutoAttack while requiring only 3% of its computational time. This is an empirical comparison from the reported evaluations. The result supports using the method both to assess robustness with fewer resources and to generate high-quality adversarial examples within adversarial training.
summary.tldr: The minimum-margin attack matches AutoAttack’s reported evaluation performance using 3% of its computational time in the paper’s experiments.

title: Fast and Reliable Evaluation of Adversarial Robustness with Minimum-Margin Attack

abstract: Data distortion is commonly applied in vision models during both training (e.g methods like MixUp and CutMix) and evaluation (e.g. shape-texture bias and robustness). This data modification can introduce artificial information. It is often assumed that the resulting artefacts are detrimental to training, whilst being negligible when analysing models. We investigate these assumptions and conclude that in some cases they are unfounded and lead to incorrect results. Specifically, we show current shape bias identification methods and occlusion robustness measures are biased and propose a fairer alternative for the latter. Subsequently, through a series of experiments we seek to correct and strengthen the community’s perception of how augmenting affects learning of vision models. Based on our empirical results we argue that the impact of the artefacts must be understood and exploited rather than eliminated.

paragraphs: Vision models frequently encounter deliberately modified images during training and evaluation. These modifications can introduce artificial information alongside the changes they are intended to create. The paper examines two common assumptions: that such artifacts harm training, and that they are negligible when modified images are used to analyze a model.

The authors find that these assumptions fail in some cases and can lead to incorrect conclusions. They show bias in existing methods for identifying shape preference and in measures of robustness to occlusion. For occlusion robustness, they propose a fairer alternative. This matters because an evaluation intended to reveal model behavior can also reflect information introduced by the evaluation procedure.

Further experiments investigate how augmentation affects learning in vision models. Based on their empirical results, the authors argue for understanding and exploiting artifacts rather than automatically eliminating them. The claim is contextual: artificial information can affect both learning and measurement, and its role needs examination. The paper thus challenges assumptions about modification artifacts through evidence about training and evaluation.
summary.tldr: Artificial image modifications can bias evaluations and influence learning in useful ways, challenging common assumptions about their artifacts.

title: On the Effects of Artificial Data Modification

abstract: It is well known that accurate probabilistic predictors can be trained through empirical risk minimisation with proper scoring rules as loss functions. While such learners capture so-called aleatoric uncertainty of predictions, various machine learning methods have recently been developed with the goal to let the learner also represent its epistemic uncertainty, i.e., the uncertainty caused by a lack of knowledge and data. An emerging branch of the literature proposes the use of a second-order learner that provides predictions in terms of distributions on probability distributions. However, recent work has revealed serious theoretical shortcomings for second-order predictors based on loss minimisation. In this paper, we generalise these findings and prove a more fundamental result: There seems to be no loss function that provides an incentive for a second-order learner to faithfully represent its epistemic uncertainty in the same manner as proper scoring rules do for standard (first-order) learners. As a main mathematical tool to prove this result, we introduce the generalised notion of second-order scoring rules.

While such learners capture so-called aleatoric uncertainty of predictions, various machine learning methods have recently been developed with the goal to let the learner also represent its epistemic uncertainty, i.e., the uncertainty caused by a lack of knowledge and data. An emerging branch of the literature proposes the use of a second-order learner that provides predictions in terms of distributions on probability distributions. However, recent work has revealed serious theoretical shortcomings for second-order predictors based on loss minimisation. In this paper, we generalise these findings and prove a more fundamental result: There seems to be no loss function that provides an incentive for a second-order learner to faithfully represent its epistemic uncertainty in the same manner as proper scoring rules do for standard (first-order) learners. As a main mathematical tool to prove this result, we introduce the generalised notion of second-order scoring rules.

paragraphs: A probabilistic predictor describes uncertainty about an outcome. Proper scoring rules provide losses that encourage such predictors to report probabilities faithfully. This paper asks whether an analogous training principle can support epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty arising from limited knowledge and data, beyond the aleatoric uncertainty captured by ordinary probabilistic predictions.

The setting is second-order prediction, where a learner returns a distribution over probability distributions. This richer output is intended to express uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Earlier work identified theoretical problems with training these predictors through loss minimization. The authors generalize those findings by introducing a broader mathematical notion of second-order scoring rules.

Their result challenges the prospect of finding a loss that incentivizes faithful epistemic uncertainty in the same way proper scoring rules support ordinary predictions. The abstract phrases the conclusion as there seeming to be no such loss. Its significance concerns the connection between an expressive output format and the training incentive needed to make that output meaningful; representing distributions over distributions does not itself establish the desired analogue of proper scoring.
summary.tldr: The paper develops second-order scoring rules and finds a fundamental obstacle to incentivizing faithful epistemic uncertainty through loss minimization.

title: On Second-Order Scoring Rules for Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of establishing the accountability and fairness of transparent machine learning models through monotonicity. Although there have been numerous studies on individual monotonicity, pairwise monotonicity is often overlooked in the existing literature. This paper studies transparent neural networks in the presence of three types of monotonicity: individual monotonicity, weak pairwise monotonicity, and strong pairwise monotonicity. As a means of achieving monotonicity while maintaining transparency, we propose the monotonic groves of neural additive models. As a result of empirical examples, we demonstrate that monotonicity is often violated in practice and that monotonic groves of neural additive models are transparent, accountable, and fair.

Although there have been numerous studies on individual monotonicity, pairwise monotonicity is often overlooked in the existing literature. This paper studies transparent neural networks in the presence of three types of monotonicity: individual monotonicity, weak pairwise monotonicity, and strong pairwise monotonicity. As a means of achieving monotonicity while maintaining transparency, we propose the monotonic groves of neural additive models. As a result of empirical examples, we demonstrate that monotonicity is often violated in practice and that monotonic groves of neural additive models are transparent, accountable, and fair.

paragraphs: A transparent model can expose how it makes predictions while still behaving inconsistently with desired monotonic relationships. Monotonicity concerns whether model outputs respect specified directional relationships. This paper studies those requirements as a route to accountability and fairness in transparent machine learning models.

The authors distinguish three forms: individual monotonicity, weak pairwise monotonicity, and strong pairwise monotonicity. Their emphasis on pairwise requirements broadens the analysis beyond the individual monotonicity studied more commonly in earlier work. This matters because checking only one category of directional behavior does not address every category considered by the paper.

To combine these requirements with transparency, the authors propose monotonic groves of neural additive models. Their empirical examples show that monotonicity violations occur in practice and demonstrate transparent, accountable, and fair behavior for the proposed models. The findings position monotonicity as a concrete property to examine and enforce when managing model risk. The fairness conclusion is presented through those empirical examples and the paper's monotonicity-based approach.
summary.tldr: Monotonic groves of neural additive models address individual and pairwise monotonicity while preserving transparency.

title: How to address monotonicity for model risk management?

abstract: In this paper, we consider federated Q-learning, which aims to learn an optimal Q-function by periodically aggregating local Q-estimates trained on local data alone. Focusing on infinite-horizon tabular Markov decision processes, we provide sample complexity guarantees for both the synchronous and asynchronous variants of federated Q-learning. In both cases, our bounds exhibit a linear speedup with respect to the number of agents and sharper dependencies on other salient problem parameters. Moreover, existing approaches to federated Q-learning adopt an equally-weighted averaging of local Q-estimates, which can be highly sub-optimal in the asynchronous setting since the local trajectories can be highly heterogeneous due to different local behavior policies. Existing sample complexity scales inverse proportionally to the minimum entry of the stationary state-action occupancy distributions over all agents, requiring that every agent covers the entire state-action space. Instead, we propose a novel importance averaging algorithm, giving larger weights to more frequently visited state-action pairs. The improved sample complexity scales inverse proportionally to the minimum entry of the average stationary state-action occupancy distribution of all agents, thus only requiring the agents collectively cover the entire state-action space, unveiling the blessing of heterogeneity.

paragraphs: Federated Q-learning combines value estimates learned independently by multiple agents through periodic aggregation. This paper studies infinite-horizon tabular Markov decision processes and provides sample-complexity guarantees for synchronous and asynchronous variants. In both settings, its bounds show a linear speedup with the number of agents and sharper dependence on other problem parameters.

Equally averaging their estimates can then be highly suboptimal. Earlier complexity guarantees depend on the least-visited pair across all agents, requiring every individual agent to cover the entire state-action space.

Heterogeneity can consequently become useful through complementary exploration.
summary.tldr: Importance-weighted aggregation lets federated Q-learning benefit from collective state-action coverage while retaining linear speedup guarantees.

title: The Blessing of Heterogeneity in Federated Q-Learning: Linear Speedup and Beyond

abstract: Image super-resolution (SR) with generative adversarial networks (GAN) has achieved great success in restoring realistic details. However, it is notorious that GAN-based SR models will inevitably produce unpleasant and undesirable artifacts, especially in practical scenarios. Previous works typically suppress artifacts with an extra loss penalty in the training phase. They only work for in-distribution artifact types generated during training. When applied in real-world scenarios, we observe that those improved methods still generate obviously annoying artifacts during inference. In this paper, we analyze the cause and characteristics of the GAN artifacts produced in unseen test data without ground-truths. We then develop a novel method, namely, DeSRA, to Detect and then “Delete” those SR Artifacts in practice. Specifically, we propose to measure a relative local variance distance from MSE-SR results and GAN-SR results, and locate the problematic areas based on the above distance and semantic-aware thresholds. After detecting the artifact regions, we develop a finetune procedure to improve GAN-based SR models with a few samples, so that they can deal with similar types of artifacts in more unseen real data. Equipped with our DeSRA, we can successfully eliminate artifacts from inference and improve the ability of SR models to be applied in real-world scenarios. The code will be available at https://github.com/TencentARC/DeSRA.

The paper focuses on artifacts that appear in previously unseen real images, where ground-truth high-resolution versions are unavailable. It argues that training-time artifact penalties remain tied to the artifact types encountered during training, leaving problems when models are used in practice.

DeSRA first detects suspicious regions by comparing outputs from an MSE-based super-resolution model and a GAN-based model. Its signal is a relative distance between their local variances, combined with thresholds that account for semantic content. This comparison provides a way to locate problematic areas without requiring a correct reference image for the new input.

After detection, DeSRA uses a few samples in a fine-tuning procedure that improves the GAN-based model’s handling of similar artifacts in further unseen data. The authors report successful artifact removal and improved practical applicability. The central contribution is a correction process informed by failures observed during actual use, connecting artifact localization with model adaptation rather than relying entirely on the original training penalty.
summary.tldr: DeSRA detects super-resolution artifacts without ground-truth images and uses a few examples to fine-tune the model against similar failures.

title: DeSRA: Detect and Delete the Artifacts of GAN-based Real-World Super-Resolution Models

abstract: Recent works have shown that tackling offline reinforcement learning (RL) with a conditional policy produces promising results. The Decision Transformer (DT) combines the conditional policy approach and a transformer architecture, showing competitive performance against several benchmarks. However, DT lacks stitching ability – one of the critical abilities for offline RL to learn the optimal policy from sub-optimal trajectories. This issue becomes particularly significant when the offline dataset only contains sub-optimal trajectories. On the other hand, the conventional RL approaches based on Dynamic Programming (such as Q-learning) do not have the same limitation; however, they suffer from unstable learning behaviours, especially when they rely on function approximation in an off-policy learning setting. In this paper, we propose the Q-learning Decision Transformer (QDT) to address the shortcomings of DT by leveraging the benefits of Dynamic Programming (Q-learning). It utilises the Dynamic Programming results to relabel the return-to-go in the training data to then train the DT with the relabelled data. Our approach efficiently exploits the benefits of these two approaches and compensates for each other’s shortcomings to achieve better performance.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing collection of trajectories. Decision Transformers approach this through conditional sequence modeling, but lack stitching ability: combining useful portions of suboptimal trajectories into a better policy. This weakness becomes especially consequential when the dataset contains only trajectories that are themselves suboptimal.

Q-learning offers dynamic-programming machinery that does not share this limitation, although off-policy learning with function approximation can be unstable. The proposed Q-learning Decision Transformer combines the approaches through the training data. It uses dynamic-programming results to relabel return-to-go values, then trains a Decision Transformer using those revised labels.

Return-to-go labels describe the future return associated with positions in a trajectory, so changing them changes the performance information supplied during conditional training. The authors report that this combination improves performance by exploiting complementary strengths and compensating for weaknesses. The contribution is a concrete connection between value-based learning and sequence modeling, using improved return labels to address the original transformer's stitching limitation.
summary.tldr: QDT uses dynamic programming to relabel trajectory returns before training a Decision Transformer, improving learning from suboptimal offline data.

title: Q-learning Decision Transformer: Leveraging Dynamic Programming for Conditional Sequence Modelling in Offline RL

abstract: Motivated by the efficiency and rapid convergence of pre-trained models for solving downstream tasks, this paper extensively studies the impact of Continual Learning (CL) models as pre-trainers. We find that, in both supervised and unsupervised CL, the transfer quality of representations does not show a noticeable degradation of fine-tuning performance but rather increases gradually. This is because CL models can learn improved task-general features when easily forgetting task-specific knowledge. Based on this observation, we suggest a new unsupervised CL framework with masked modeling, which aims to capture fluent task-generic representation during training. Furthermore, we propose a new fine-tuning scheme, GLobal Attention Discretization (GLAD), that preserves rich task-generic representation during solving downstream tasks. The model fine-tuned with GLAD achieves competitive performance and can also be used as a good pre-trained model itself. We believe this paper breaks the barriers between pre-training and fine-tuning steps and leads to a sustainable learning framework in which the continual learner incrementally improves model generalization, yielding better transfer to unseen tasks.

Its evaluation asks how well the models support subsequent fine-tuning as they keep learning. In both supervised and unsupervised settings, the authors observe that transfer quality gradually improves rather than showing a noticeable decline.

They explain this pattern through a distinction between task-specific knowledge and features useful across tasks. A model may forget details of earlier tasks while developing representations that transfer better. Building on this observation, the paper proposes an unsupervised continual-learning framework based on masked modeling, intended to capture representations that remain useful across changing tasks.

The authors also introduce GLobal Attention Discretization, or GLAD, a fine-tuning scheme designed to preserve these general representations while adapting to a downstream task. Models fine-tuned with GLAD achieve competitive performance and remain useful as pretrained models themselves. The findings motivate a sustainable sequence of learning and adaptation, although the broader vision of continual improvement is presented as the authors’ interpretation rather than a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: Continual learners can improve transferable representations even while forgetting task-specific knowledge, motivating methods that preserve general features.

title: Continual Learners are Incremental Model Generalizers

abstract: Understanding the generalization properties of heavy-tailed stochastic optimization algorithms has attracted increasing attention over the past years. While illuminating interesting aspects of stochastic optimizers by using heavy-tailed stochastic differential equations as proxies, prior works either provided expected generalization bounds, or introduced non-computable information theoretic terms. Addressing these drawbacks, in this work, we prove high-probability generalization bounds for heavy-tailed SDEs which do not contain any nontrivial information theoretic terms. To achieve this goal, we develop new proof techniques based on estimating the entropy flows associated with the so-called fractional Fokker-Planck equation (a partial differential equation that governs the evolution of the distribution of the corresponding heavy-tailed SDE). In addition to obtaining high-probability bounds, we show that our bounds have a better dependence on the dimension of parameters as compared to prior art. Our results further identify a phase transition phenomenon, which suggests that heavy tails can be either beneficial or harmful depending on the problem structure. We support our theory with experiments conducted in a variety of settings.

To achieve this goal, we develop new proof techniques based on estimating the entropy flows associated with the so-called fractional Fokker-Planck equation (a partial differential equation that governs the evolution of the distribution of the corresponding heavy-tailed SDE). In addition to obtaining high-probability bounds, we show that our bounds have a better dependence on the dimension of parameters as compared to prior art. paragraphs: Heavy-tailed stochastic differential equations serve as mathematical proxies for stochastic optimization algorithms. This paper studies what these models imply about generalization: how performance on training data relates to performance beyond it. Earlier analyses supplied either bounds in expectation or bounds containing information-theoretic quantities that could not be computed.

The authors prove high-probability generalization bounds without nontrivial information-theoretic terms. Their proof technique estimates entropy flows associated with the fractional Fokker-Planck equation, which describes how the probability distribution of the heavy-tailed process evolves. This connects distributional dynamics to guarantees that hold with high probability, rather than describing only an average across outcomes.

The resulting bounds also improve the dependence on parameter dimension relative to prior work. A further finding is a phase transition suggesting that heavy tails may help or hurt depending on the problem's structure. Experiments across several settings support the theory. The analysis therefore offers a more qualified account of heavy-tailed behavior than a blanket claim that it always improves generalization.
summary.tldr: New high-probability bounds clarify how heavy-tailed optimization proxies generalize and suggest that heavy tails can help or hurt depending on problem structure.

title: Generalization Bounds for Heavy-Tailed SDEs through the Fractional Fokker-Planck Equation

abstract: The multi-plane representation has been highlighted for its fast training and inference across static and dynamic neural radiance fields. This approach constructs relevant features via projection onto learnable grids and interpolating adjacent vertices. However, it has limitations in capturing low-frequency details and tends to overuse parameters for low-frequency features due to its bias toward fine details, despite its multi-resolution concept. This phenomenon leads to instability and inefficiency when training poses are sparse. In this work, we propose a method that synergistically integrates multi-plane representation with a coordinate-based MLP network known for strong bias toward low-frequency signals. The coordinate-based network is responsible for capturing low-frequency details, while the multi-plane representation focuses on capturing fine-grained details. We demonstrate that using residual connections between them seamlessly preserves their own inherent properties. Additionally, the proposed progressive training scheme accelerates the disentanglement of these two features. We demonstrate empirically that our proposed method not only outperforms baseline models for both static and dynamic NeRFs with sparse inputs, but also achieves comparable results with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Multi-plane representations make neural radiance fields fast to train and query by projecting onto learned grids and interpolating features. However, the paper finds that their preference for fine detail can make broad, low-frequency structure inefficient to represent. With sparse training poses, this can lead to unstable learning and wasted parameters.

The proposed method pairs the multi-plane representation with a coordinate-based multilayer perceptron, whose bias favors low-frequency signals. The coordinate network captures broad structure, while the grid representation focuses on finer detail. Residual connections preserve the characteristic behavior of each component, and a progressive training scheme accelerates the separation of their roles.

Experiments on both static and dynamic neural radiance fields with sparse inputs show improvements over baseline models. The method also achieves comparable results with fewer parameters. These findings support allocating different kinds of scene structure to representations suited to learning them, rather than asking the multi-plane component to spend substantial capacity on both broad patterns and fine details.
summary.tldr: Combining a coordinate network for broad structure with multi-plane features for fine detail improves sparse-input neural radiance fields.

title: Synergistic Integration of Coordinate Network and Tensorial Feature for Improving Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse Inputs

abstract: Efficiently serving large language models (LLMs) requires batching many requests together to reduce the cost per request. Yet, the key-value (KV) cache, which stores attention keys and values to avoid re-computations, significantly increases memory demands and becomes the new bottleneck in speed and memory usage. This memory demand increases with larger batch sizes and longer context lengths. Additionally, the inference speed is limited by the size of KV cache, as the GPU’s SRAM must load the entire KV cache from the main GPU memory for each token generated, causing the computational core to be idle during this process. A straightforward and effective solution to reduce KV cache size is quantization, which decreases the total bytes taken by KV cache. However, there is a lack of in-depth studies that explore the element distribution of KV cache to understand the hardness and limitation of KV cache quantization. To fill the gap, we conducted a comprehensive study on the element distribution in KV cache of popular LLMs. Our findings indicate that the key cache should be quantized per-channel, i.e., group elements along the channel dimension and quantize them together. In contrast, the value cache should be quantized per-token. From this analysis, we developed a tuning-free 2bit KV cache quantization algorithm, named KIVI. With the hardware-friendly implementation, KIVI can enable Llama (Llama-2), Falcon, and Mistral models to maintain almost the same quality while using 2.6$\times$ less peak memory usage (including the model weight). This reduction in memory usage enables up to 4x larger batch size, bringing $2.35 \times \sim 3.47 \times$ throughput on real LLM inference workload.

This cache grows with context length and batch size, increasing memory use and data movement. KIVI addresses this serving bottleneck by reducing the numerical precision of cached values, allowing the cache to occupy fewer bytes.

KIVI turns that distinction into a tuning-free, two-bit quantization algorithm with a hardware-friendly implementation. Treating the two cache components differently is the design choice motivated by the distribution study.

The reduced memory requirement permits up to four times larger batches and delivers 2.35–3.47 times throughput on real inference workloads. These results connect cache-aware quantization directly to practical serving capacity.
summary.tldr: KIVI quantizes attention keys and values differently at two bits, reducing memory and increasing serving throughput while largely preserving quality.

title: KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache

abstract: We study interactive learning in a setting where the agent has to generate a response (e.g., an action or trajectory) given a context and an instruction. In contrast, to typical approaches that train the system using reward or expert supervision on response, we study learning with hindsight labeling where a teacher provides an instruction that is most suitable for the agent’s generated response. This hindsight labeling of instruction is often easier to provide than providing expert supervision of the optimal response which may require expert knowledge or can be impractical to elicit. We initiate the theoretical analysis of interactive learning with hindsight labeling. We first provide a lower bound showing that in general, the regret of any algorithm must scale with the size of the agent’s response space. Next, we study a specialized setting where the underlying instruction-response distribution can be decomposed as a low-rank matrix. We introduce an algorithm called LORIL for this setting and show that it is a no-regret algorithm with the regret scaling with $\sqrt{T}$ and depends on the intrinsic rank but does not depend on the agent’s response space. We provide experiments showing the performance of LORIL in practice for 2 domains.

paragraphs: The paper studies an interactive learner that receives a context and an instruction, then produces an action or trajectory. Its teacher responds by supplying an instruction that would fit what the agent actually did. This hindsight labeling can be easier to obtain than an expert demonstration of the optimal response.

The authors first establish a general difficulty: any algorithm’s regret must scale with the size of the response space. They then examine a structured setting in which the distribution connecting instructions and responses can be represented by a low-rank matrix. This assumption supplies a way to describe those relationships using a smaller intrinsic dimension.

For that setting, the proposed LORIL algorithm has regret growing with the square root of the number of interactions and depending on intrinsic rank rather than response-space size. This yields a no-regret result under the low-rank structure. Experiments in two domains illustrate practical performance. The theoretical contrast explains how structural assumptions can make hindsight feedback useful even when the agent has many possible responses.
summary.tldr: Under a low-rank instruction–response model, LORIL learns from hindsight instructions with regret depending on intrinsic rank rather than response-space size.

title: Provable Interactive Learning with Hindsight Instruction Feedback

abstract: Algorithmic predictions are increasingly used to inform the allocations of goods and interventions in the public sphere. In these domains, predictions serve as a means to an end. They provide stakeholders with insights into likelihood of future events as a means to improve decision making quality, and enhance social welfare. However, if maximizing welfare is the ultimate goal, prediction is only a small piece of the puzzle. There are various other policy levers a social planner might pursue in order to improve bottom-line outcomes, such as expanding access to available goods, or increasing the effect sizes of interventions. Given this broad range of design decisions, a basic question to ask is: What is the relative value of prediction in algorithmic decision making? How do the improvements in welfare arising from better predictions compare to those of other policy levers? The goal of our work is to initiate the formal study of these questions. Our main results are theoretical in nature. We identify simple, sharp conditions determining the relative value of prediction vis-à-vis expanding access, within several statistical models that are popular amongst quantitative social scientists. Furthermore, we illustrate how these theoretical insights can guide the design of algorithmic decision making systems in practice.

A social planner may also improve welfare by expanding access or making an intervention more effective. This paper asks how gains from better prediction compare with gains available through other policy choices.

Its main contribution is a theoretical comparison between improving predictions and expanding access. Within several statistical models commonly used in quantitative social science, the authors derive simple, sharp conditions determining their relative value. This frames predictive improvement as one option in a broader allocation problem, with its usefulness assessed through welfare.

The paper also illustrates how the theoretical insights can inform the design of algorithmic decision systems in practice. The findings do not establish a universal preference for better prediction or broader access; their comparisons depend on the conditions in the analyzed models. Their value is to make the choice explicit and mathematically assessable when the ultimate objective is improving social outcomes.
summary.tldr: The paper derives conditions for when better predictions improve welfare more or less than expanding access to goods or interventions.

title: The Relative Value of Prediction in Algorithmic Decision Making

abstract: The Balanced-Pairwise-Affinities (BPA) feature transform is designed to upgrade the features of a set of input items to facilitate downstream matching or grouping related tasks. The transformed set encodes a rich representation of high order relations between the input features. A particular min-cost-max-flow fractional matching problem, whose entropy regularized version can be approximated by an optimal transport (OT) optimization, leads to a transform which is efficient, differentiable, equivariant, parameterless and probabilistically interpretable. While the Sinkhorn OT solver has been adapted extensively in many contexts, we use it differently by minimizing the cost between a set of features to itself and using the transport plan’s rows as the new representation.Empirically, the transform is highly effective and flexible in its use and consistently improves networks it is inserted into, in a variety of tasks and training schemes. We demonstrate state-of-the-art results in few-shot classification, unsupervised image clustering and person re-identification. Code is available at github.com/DanielShalam/BPA .

paragraphs: The Balanced-Pairwise-Affinities transform changes a set of input features into representations that capture richer relationships among the items. Its goal is to help downstream tasks that match or group related examples. The transformed representation encodes higher-order relationships, making the structure of the feature set part of how each item is represented.

The construction starts from a fractional matching problem whose entropy-regularized version can be approximated using optimal transport. Its distinctive step is to match the feature set to itself and use rows of the resulting transport plan as the new features. The transform is efficient, differentiable, equivariant, parameterless, and has a probabilistic interpretation.

The authors report consistent improvements when inserting the transform into networks across varied tasks and training schemes. They demonstrate state-of-the-art results in few-shot classification, unsupervised image clustering, and person re-identification. These findings support the value of representing items through balanced relationships within the set, using a transform that can participate in learning without adding its own trainable parameters.
summary.tldr: BPA turns self-matching optimal-transport relationships into parameterless features that improve several matching and grouping tasks.

title: The Balanced-Pairwise-Affinities Feature Transform

abstract: We study a model of machine teaching where the teacher mapping is constructed from a size function on both concepts and examples. The main question in machine teaching is the minimum number of examples needed for any concept, the so-called teaching dimension. A recent paper (Ferri et al., 2024) conjectured that the worst case for this model, as a function of the size of the concept class, occurs when the consistency matrix contains the binary representations of numbers from zero and up. In this paper we prove their conjecture. The result can be seen as a generalization of a theorem resolving the edge isoperimetry problem for hypercubes (Hart, 1976), and our proof is based on a lemma of (Graham, 1970).

This paper studies a particular model in which a size function on concepts and examples determines the teacher mapping. The quantity of interest is the teaching dimension: the minimum example requirement needed to handle any concept in the class.

That worst case occurs when the consistency matrix contains the binary representations of consecutive numbers starting at zero. The result gives a specific combinatorial arrangement that attains the hardest teaching requirement within the model.

The proof connects this teaching question to the geometry of hypercubes. The authors describe their theorem as a generalization of a result resolving the hypercube edge-isoperimetry problem and base their argument on an existing combinatorial lemma. The contribution is an exact theoretical characterization of the worst case for this teaching model, giving the previously conjectured binary arrangement a proven extremal role.
summary.tldr: The paper proves which binary consistency-matrix arrangement gives the worst teaching dimension in a size-based machine-teaching model.

title: On a Combinatorial Problem Arising in Machine Teaching

abstract: We present Self-Play Preference Optimization (SPO), an algorithm for reinforcement learning from human feedback. Our approach is minimalist in that it does not require training a reward model nor unstable adversarial training and is therefore rather simple to implement. Our approach is maximalist in that it provably handles non-Markovian, intransitive, and stochastic preferences while being robust to the compounding errors that plague offline approaches to sequential prediction. To achieve the preceding qualities, we build upon the concept of a Minimax Winner (MW), a notion of preference aggregation from the social choice theory literature that frames learning from preferences as a zero-sum game between two policies. By leveraging the symmetry of this game, we prove that rather than using the traditional technique of dueling two policies to compute the MW, we can simply have a single agent play against itself while maintaining strong convergence guarantees. Practically, this corresponds to sampling multiple trajectories from a policy, asking a preference or teacher model to compare them, and then using the proportion of wins as the reward for a particular trajectory. We demonstrate that on a suite of continuous control tasks, we are able to learn significantly more efficiently than reward-model based approaches while maintaining robustness to the intransitive and stochastic preferences that frequently occur in practice when aggregating human judgments.

A preference or teacher model judges these trajectories, and each trajectory receives a reward based on the fraction of comparisons it wins. This avoids training a separate reward model and gives preference feedback a direct role in policy improvement.

The theoretical foundation is the Minimax Winner, a way of combining preferences through a zero-sum game between policies. The authors use the game's symmetry to show that one agent playing against itself can replace a duel between separately maintained policies while retaining strong convergence guarantees. Their analysis covers preferences that depend on history, contain cycles, or involve randomness.

On continuous control tasks, SPO learns significantly more efficiently than the evaluated reward-model approaches while remaining robust to cyclic and stochastic preferences. The contribution therefore joins a relatively simple training procedure with support for complicated preference patterns. Its guarantees also address the accumulation of errors associated with offline approaches to sequential prediction.
summary.tldr: SPO uses self-comparisons to train policies without a separate reward model, with guarantees covering complex preferences and encouraging continuous-control results.

title: A Minimaximalist Approach to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong generalization capabilities to novel tasks when prompted with language instructions and in-context demos. Since this ability sensitively depends on the quality of prompts, various methods have been explored to automate the instruction design. While these methods demonstrated promising results, they also restricted the searched prompt to one instruction. Such simplification significantly limits their capacity, as a single demo-free instruction might not be able to cover the entire complex problem space of the targeted task. To alleviate this issue, we adopt the Mixture-of-Expert paradigm and divide the problem space into a set of sub-regions; Each sub-region is governed by a specialized expert, equipped with both an instruction and a set of demos. A two-phase process is developed to construct the specialized expert for each region: (1) demo assignment: Inspired by the theoretical connection between in-context learning and kernel regression, we group demos into experts based on their semantic similarity; (2) instruction assignment: A region-based joint search of an instruction per expert complements the demos assigned to it, yielding a synergistic effect. The resulting method, codenamed Mixture-of-Prompts (MoP), achieves an average win rate of 81% against prior arts across several major benchmarks.

paragraphs: Automated prompt design often searches for one instruction to handle an entire task. This paper argues that a single instruction without demonstrations may not cover a complex task's full problem space. Mixture-of-Prompts instead divides that space into regions, each handled by an expert prompt containing both an instruction and demonstrations.

Construction proceeds in two phases. First, demonstrations are grouped into experts according to semantic similarity, motivated by a theoretical connection between in-context learning and kernel regression. Second, a region-based joint search chooses an instruction for each expert that complements its assigned demonstrations. The two components are designed together so that instructions and examples support the same specialized region.

Across several major benchmarks, the authors report an average win rate of 81% against prior approaches. This is a comparative win-rate result, rather than an assertion that the method answers 81% of all questions correctly. The findings support expanding prompt optimization beyond one universal instruction and using coordinated instruction-and-demonstration combinations to address variation within a task.
summary.tldr: Mixture-of-Prompts automatically builds specialized instruction-and-demonstration experts, achieving an average 81% win rate against prior approaches on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: One Prompt is not Enough: Automated Construction of a Mixture-of-Expert Prompts

abstract: We introduce a new framework for studying meta-learning methods using PAC-Bayesian theory. Its main advantage over previous work is that it allows for more flexibility in how the transfer of knowledge between tasks is realized. For previous approaches, this could only happen indirectly, by means of learning prior distributions over models. In contrast, the new generalization bounds that we prove express the process of meta-learning much more directly as learning the learning algorithm that should be used for future tasks. The flexibility of our framework makes it suitable to analyze a wide range of meta-learning mechanisms and even design new mechanisms. Other than our theoretical contributions we also show empirically that our framework improves the prediction quality in practical meta-learning mechanisms.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across tasks to improve learning on future tasks. A theoretical framework must therefore describe what gets transferred and how that transfer affects generalization. Previous PAC-Bayesian approaches represented this transfer indirectly by learning prior distributions over models, limiting the mechanisms that could be expressed within their analyses.

This paper develops new generalization bounds that describe meta-learning more directly as learning the learning algorithm itself. The object carried forward to future tasks can therefore be the procedure used to learn from them. This expands the framework’s flexibility beyond representing shared knowledge only through a learned model prior.

The authors argue that the framework can analyze a wide range of existing meta-learning mechanisms and help design new ones. They also report empirical improvements in prediction quality for practical meta-learning mechanisms. The theoretical and experimental contributions address complementary questions: how to reason about more varied forms of knowledge transfer, and whether mechanisms developed within that broader view can improve predictions in practice.
summary.tldr: New PAC-Bayesian bounds frame meta-learning as learning a learning algorithm, allowing more flexible knowledge transfer across tasks.

title: More Flexible PAC-Bayesian Meta-Learning by Learning Learning Algorithms

abstract: We study the problem of learning in zero-sum matrix games with repeated play and bandit feedback. Specifically, we focus on developing uncoupled algorithms that guarantee, without communication between players, convergence of the last-iterate to a Nash equilibrium. Although the non-bandit case has been studied extensively, this setting has only been explored recently, with a bound of $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/8})$ on the exploitability gap. We show that, for uncoupled algorithms, guaranteeing convergence of the policy profiles to a Nash equilibrium is detrimental to the performances, with the best attainable rate being $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/4})$ in contrast to the usual $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ rate for convergence of the average iterates. We then propose two algorithms that achieve this optimal rate. The first algorithm leverages a straightforward tradeoff between exploration and exploitation, while the second employs a regularization technique based on a two-step mirror descent approach.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated play in zero-sum matrix games when players receive bandit feedback and learn without communicating. The goal is for their latest policies to converge to a Nash equilibrium. That requirement differs from convergence of an average over past policies: it asks the current state of play itself to approach equilibrium.

The authors establish that this last-iterate requirement carries a convergence-rate cost for uncoupled algorithms. They identify O(T^(-1/4)) as the best attainable rate in the studied setting, compared with the usual O(T^(-1/2)) rate for average iterates. This also improves on the previously available O(T^(-1/8)) bound on the exploitability gap described in the abstract.

Two proposed algorithms attain the optimal last-iterate rate. One uses a direct exploration–exploitation trade-off, while the other applies regularization through a two-step mirror-descent approach. Together, the lower-bound result and matching algorithms characterize the difficulty of the problem. They show both the cost of requiring convergence of current policies and how to meet that requirement at the optimal rate.
summary.tldr: For uncoupled zero-sum learning with bandit feedback, the paper establishes an optimal last-iterate rate of O(T^(-1/4)) and gives two matching algorithms.

title: The Harder Path: Last Iterate Convergence for Uncoupled Learning in Zero-Sum Games with Bandit Feedback

abstract: It is difficult to anticipate the myriad challenges that a predictive model will encounter once deployed. Common practice entails a reactive, cyclical approach: model deployment, data mining, and retraining. We instead develop a proactive longtail discovery process by imagining additional data during training. In particular, we develop general model-based longtail signals, including a differentiable, single forward pass formulation of epistemic uncertainty that does not impact model parameters or predictive performance but can flag rare or hard inputs. We leverage these signals as guidance to generate additional training data from a latent diffusion model in a process we call Longtail Guidance (LTG). Crucially, we can perform LTG without retraining the diffusion model or the predictive model, and we do not need to expose the predictive model to intermediate diffusion states. Data generated by LTG exhibit semantically meaningful variation, yield significant generalization improvements on numerous image classification benchmarks, and can be analyzed by a VLM to proactively discover, textually explain, and address conceptual gaps in a deployed predictive model.

paragraphs: Predictive models often reveal their weaknesses only after deployment, leading to repeated cycles of collecting difficult examples and retraining. This paper proposes discovering such weaknesses proactively by generating additional training examples. Its Longtail Guidance method steers a latent diffusion model toward inputs that signals from the predictive model identify as rare or difficult.

The authors develop general signals for this purpose, including a differentiable measure of epistemic uncertainty computed in one forward pass. They state that this formulation leaves model parameters and predictive performance unaffected. The guidance process requires no retraining of either the diffusion model or predictive model, and the predictor does not need to process intermediate diffusion states.

Generated examples show meaningful semantic variation and produce significant generalization improvements across multiple image-classification benchmarks. A vision-language model can also analyze them to explain conceptual gaps in words. This connects data generation with diagnosis: the same process can supply useful training examples and help reveal which concepts a deployed predictor handles poorly.
summary.tldr: Longtail Guidance steers diffusion generation toward a predictor’s difficult cases to improve generalization and expose conceptual gaps.

title: Generative Data Mining with Longtail-Guided Diffusion

abstract: We develop a semi-amortized, policy-based, approach to Bayesian experimental design (BED) called Stepwise Deep Adaptive Design (Step-DAD). Like existing, fully amortized, policy-based BED approaches, Step-DAD trains a design policy upfront before the experiment. However, rather than keeping this policy fixed, Step-DAD periodically updates it as data is gathered, refining it to the particular experimental instance. This test-time adaptation improves both the flexibility and the robustness of the design strategy compared with existing approaches. Empirically, Step-DAD consistently demonstrates superior decision-making and robustness compared with current state-of-the-art BED methods.

paragraphs: Bayesian experimental design concerns choosing experiments as information becomes available. Policy-based approaches can train a design policy before the experiment begins, preparing it to make subsequent choices. This paper asks how that preparation can be combined with further learning during the particular experiment being carried out.

Stepwise Deep Adaptive Design, or Step-DAD, starts with an upfront trained policy, as existing fully amortized approaches do. It then periodically updates that policy using newly gathered data. This is the meaning of its semi-amortized design: the method combines advance training with additional adaptation rather than keeping the learned policy fixed throughout the experiment.

The updates refine the policy to the specific experimental instance, improving the strategy's flexibility and robustness. Empirically, Step-DAD consistently achieves better decision-making and robustness than current state-of-the-art Bayesian experimental design methods in the reported comparisons. The contribution is a way to make experimental design responsive at the policy-learning level, so observations can improve the strategy itself as well as inform the next experimental choice.
summary.tldr: Step-DAD periodically updates a pretrained experimental-design policy as data arrives, improving reported decision-making and robustness.

title: Step-DAD: Semi-Amortized Policy-Based Bayesian Experimental Design

abstract: Markov processes serve as universal models for many real-world random processes. This paper presents a data-driven approach to learning these models through the spectral decomposition of the infinitesimal generator (IG) of the Markov semigroup. Its unbounded nature complicates traditional methods such as vector-valued regression and Hilbert-Schmidt operator analysis. Existing techniques, including physics-informed kernel regression, are computationally expensive and limited in scope, with no recovery guarantees for transfer operator methods when the time-lag is small. We propose a novel method leveraging the IG’s resolvent, characterized by the Laplace transform of transfer operators. This approach is robust to time-lag variations, ensuring accurate eigenvalue learning even for small time-lags. Our statistical analysis applies to a broader class of Markov processes than current methods while reducing computational complexity from quadratic to linear in the state dimension. Finally, we demonstrate our theoretical findings in several experiments.

Existing approaches can also be expensive or lack recovery guarantees when observations have small time lags.

This changes the object being learned while retaining access to the generator's spectral information. The authors report robustness to variations in time lag, including accurate eigenvalue learning when that lag is small.

Their statistical analysis applies to a broader class of Markov processes than current methods, and the approach reduces computational complexity from quadratic to linear in state dimension. Experiments demonstrate the theoretical findings. The combined contribution addresses both the mathematical difficulty of learning the generator and the computational burden associated with high-dimensional states, while improving the treatment of closely spaced observations.
summary.tldr: Learning a Markov generator through its resolvent supports small-time-lag eigenvalue recovery while reducing computational complexity to linear in state dimension.

title: Laplace Transform Based Low-Complexity Learning of Continuous Markov Semigroups

abstract: Contrastive learning operates on a simple yet effective principle: Embeddings of positive pairs are pulled together, while those of negative pairs are pushed apart. In this paper, we propose a unified framework for understanding contrastive learning through the lens of cosine similarity, and present two key theoretical insights derived from this framework. First, in full-batch settings, we show that perfect alignment of positive pairs is unattainable when negative-pair similarities fall below a threshold, and this misalignment can be mitigated by incorporating within-view negative pairs into the objective. Second, in mini-batch settings, smaller batch sizes induce stronger separation among negative pairs in the embedding space, i.e., higher variance in their similarities, which in turn degrades the quality of learned representations compared to full-batch settings. To address this, we propose an auxiliary loss that reduces the variance of negative-pair similarities in mini-batch settings. Empirical results show that incorporating the proposed loss improves performance in small-batch settings.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning encourages matching examples to have similar embeddings and nonmatching examples to be separated. This paper studies the interaction between those goals through a unified framework based on cosine similarity. It shows that the geometry of negative pairs can influence both positive-pair alignment and the quality of the learned representation.

In full-batch training, the authors prove that perfect alignment of positive pairs is unattainable when negative-pair similarities fall below a threshold. Adding within-view negative pairs to the objective can mitigate this misalignment. The result is conditional on the stated similarity regime and identifies a tension within the training objective.

For mini-batch training, the analysis finds that smaller batches produce greater variance in negative-pair similarities and worse representations compared with full-batch training. The authors therefore introduce an auxiliary loss that reduces that variance. Experiments show improvements in small-batch settings, connecting a theoretical account of embedding geometry to a practical modification of the objective. The approach targets how negative-pair similarities are distributed, beyond merely pushing those pairs apart.
summary.tldr: An analysis of embedding similarities motivates a variance-reducing loss that improves contrastive learning with small batches.

title: On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning

abstract: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? In this work, we provide evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating—a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. We integrate the model-agnostic theory of optimal prediction with mechanistic interpretability to analyze transformers trained on a tractable family of hidden Markov models that generate rich geometric patterns in neural activations. Our primary analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, revealing how the first attention layer implements these constrained updates, with extensions to multi-layer architectures demonstrating how subsequent layers refine these representations. We find that attention carries out an algorithm with a natural interpretation in the probability simplex, and create representations with distinctive geometric structure. We show how both the algorithmic behavior and the underlying geometry of these representations can be theoretically predicted in detail—including the attention pattern, OV-vectors, and embedding vectors—by modifying the equations for optimal future token predictions to account for the architectural constraints of attention. Our approach provides a principled lens on how architectural constraints shape the implementation of optimal prediction, revealing why transformers develop specific intermediate geometric structures.

paragraphs: This paper examines why transformers develop particular geometric patterns in their internal representations. The authors study models trained to predict the next token in sequences generated by a tractable family of hidden Markov models. This setting lets them connect a mathematical account of optimal prediction with detailed analysis of the computations learned inside a transformer.

The model performs a parallelized, partial form of inference shaped by what the architecture can implement. The main analysis concerns single-layer transformers, where the first attention layer produces structured representations of beliefs. Extensions to deeper models show how later layers refine those representations.

Their predictions cover attention patterns, embedding vectors, and OV-vectors, which participate in attention’s output computation. This links visible activation geometry to a proposed inference algorithm, providing an explanation grounded in the studied tasks and architectures rather than treating those shapes as unexplained patterns.
summary.tldr: Experiments and theory on hidden Markov model tasks connect transformer representation geometry to Bayesian belief updates constrained by attention.

title: Constrained Belief Updates Explain Geometric Structures in Transformer Representations

abstract: Computer Vision (CV) has yet to fully achieve the zero-shot task generalization observed in Natural Language Processing (NLP), despite following many of the milestones established in NLP, such as large transformer models, extensive pre-training, and the auto-regression paradigm, among others. In this paper, we rethink the reality that CV adopts discrete and terminological task definitions (e.g., "image segmentation"), and conjecture it is a key barrier that hampers zero-shot task generalization. Our hypothesis is that without truly understanding previously-seen tasks—due to these terminological definitions—deep models struggle to generalize to novel tasks. To verify this, we introduce Explanatory Instructions, which provide an intuitive way to define CV task objectives through detailed linguistic transformations from input images to outputs. We create a large-scale dataset comprising 12 million "image input $\to$ explanatory instruction $\to$ output" triplets, and train an auto-regressive-based vision-language model (AR-based VLM) that takes both images and explanatory instructions as input. By learning to follow these instructions, the AR-based VLM achieves instruction-level zero-shot capabilities for previously-seen tasks and demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization for unseen CV tasks. Code and dataset will be open-sourced.

paragraphs: Computer vision models still struggle to generalize to new tasks from instructions alone. This paper investigates whether conventional task names, such as image segmentation, provide too little explanation of what a model should do. The authors hypothesize that these compact labels hinder understanding of familiar tasks and consequently make unfamiliar tasks harder to interpret.

They replace such definitions with Explanatory Instructions: detailed language describing the transformation from an input image to the desired output. To train this behavior, they build a dataset containing 12 million image, instruction, and output triplets. An autoregressive vision-language model learns to produce outputs from both the image and the explanatory text.

The resulting model handles new instructions for previously encountered tasks and shows strong zero-shot generalization to unseen vision tasks. These are distinct forms of generalization: interpreting fresh descriptions of familiar objectives and following descriptions of new objectives. The findings support the proposed role of explanatory task language, while the claim that terminology is a key barrier remains the hypothesis motivating the study.
summary.tldr: Detailed descriptions of image-to-output transformations help a vision-language model generalize to new instructions and unseen vision tasks.

title: Explanatory Instructions: Towards Unified Vision Tasks Understanding and Zero-shot Generalization

abstract: We study the incorporation of equivariances into vector-valued GPs and more general classes of random field models. While kernels guaranteeing equivariances have been investigated previously, their evaluation is often computationally prohibitive due to required integrations over the involved groups. In this work, we provide a kernel characterization of stochastic equivariance for centred second-order vector-valued random fields and we construct integration-free equivariant kernels based on the notion of fundamental regions of group actions. We establish data-efficient and computationally lightweight GP models for velocity fields and molecular electric dipole moments and demonstrate that proposed integration-free kernels may also be leveraged to extract equivariant components from data.
originalAbstract: We study the incorporation of equivariances into vector-valued GPs and more general classes of random field models. While kernels guaranteeing equivariances have been investigated previously, their evaluation is often computationally prohibitive due to required integrations over the involved groups. In this work, we provide a kernel characterization of stochastic equivariance for centred second-order vector-valued random fields and we construct integration-free equivariant kernels based on the notion of fundamental regions of group actions. We establish data-efficient and computationally lightweight GP models for velocity fields and molecular electric dipole moments and demonstrate that proposed integration-free kernels may also be leveraged to extract equivariant components from data.

paragraphs: Equivariance describes how a model's outputs should change consistently when its inputs undergo a relevant transformation. Incorporating such structure into vector-valued Gaussian processes can require kernels whose evaluation integrates over transformation groups. Those integrations can be computationally expensive, making a mathematically appropriate model difficult to use in practice.

The paper develops a kernel characterization of stochastic equivariance for centered, second-order vector-valued random fields. It then constructs equivariant kernels that avoid the integrations, using fundamental regions of group actions. The result connects a theoretical description of the required symmetry with a construction intended to make kernel evaluation computationally lighter.

The authors establish data-efficient, lightweight Gaussian process models for velocity fields and molecular electric dipole moments. They also demonstrate that the kernels may be used to extract equivariant components from data. The contribution therefore supports both prediction with known transformation structure and analysis of data for components that follow that structure, extending beyond a single application of Gaussian process modeling.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs equivariant kernels without costly group integrations, enabling lightweight Gaussian process models for structured vector-valued data.

title: Integration-free Kernels for Equivariant Gaussian Process Modelling

abstract: Weakly supervised video anomaly detection (WS-VAD) is tasked with pinpointing temporal intervals containing anomalous events within untrimmed videos, utilizing only video-level annotations. However, a significant challenge arises due to the absence of dense frame-level annotations, often leading to incomplete localization in existing WS-VAD methods. To address this issue, we present a novel LEC-VAD, Learning Event Completeness for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection, which features a dual structure designed to encode both category-aware and category-agnostic semantics between vision and language. Within LEC-VAD, we devise semantic regularities that leverage an anomaly-aware Gaussian mixture to learn precise event boundaries, thereby yielding more complete event instances. Besides, we develop a novel memory bank-based prototype learning mechanism to enrich concise text descriptions associated with anomaly-event categories. This innovation bolsters the text’s expressiveness, which is crucial for advancing WS-VAD. Our LEC-VAD demonstrates remarkable advancements over the current state-of-the-art methods on two benchmark datasets XD-Violence and UCF-Crime.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised video anomaly detection must locate anomalous events in time using labels that describe an entire video. Without annotations for individual frames, a detector may identify only part of an event. LEC-VAD focuses on recovering more complete event intervals, making the start and end of an anomaly central to the learning problem.

The method uses a dual structure to connect vision and language through both category-aware and category-agnostic semantics. This allows it to represent information tied to particular anomaly types alongside information that is not category-specific. Semantic regularities built around an anomaly-aware Gaussian mixture guide the learning of event boundaries and more complete event instances.

A second component uses a memory bank and prototype learning to enrich the short text descriptions associated with anomaly categories. More expressive descriptions strengthen the language information available to the detector. Evaluations on XD-Violence and UCF-Crime report substantial advances over current state-of-the-art methods. The findings support jointly improving temporal boundary learning and the semantic descriptions used to recognize anomalous events.
summary.tldr: LEC-VAD combines vision-language semantics, boundary learning, and enriched category descriptions to locate more complete anomalous events from video-level labels.

title: Learning Event Completeness for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection

abstract: We examine the interplay between ordinal, preference-based solution concepts in games and the long-run behavior of game dynamics, asking in particular to what extent the combinatorial data of a game—its preference graph—determine the outcomes of no-regret learning dynamics—such as follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In one direction, we show that the skeleton of every dynamically stable set (i.e. the set of pure profiles it contains) must also be preferentially stable, that is, it must be closed under profitable deviations. We then ask the converse question: when do preferences determine the long-run behavior of the players’ learning dynamics? We begin by showing that preferences characterize asymptotic stability in the case of subgames—i.e. subsets of pure profiles obtained by restricting players’ action sets. Beyond this case however, the equivalence between dynamic and preferential stability collapses: concretely, we construct a three-player game with a preferentially stable set whose span is dynamically unstable, showing in this way that preferences do not suffice as a criterion of dynamic stability. We then bridge this gap via the notion of resilience under aggregate deviations, an easy-to-check payoff-based condition that guarantees asymptotic stability of arbitrary spans of pure strategies.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether knowing which outcomes players prefer is enough to predict where learning in a game will settle. It studies preference graphs alongside no-regret learning dynamics such as follow-the-regularized-leader. The distinction matters because preferences record the direction of improvement without recording how large each payoff improvement is.

The authors show that the pure strategy profiles within any dynamically stable set must be closed under profitable deviations: an improving move cannot lead outside that collection. For subgames formed by restricting each player’s available actions, preferences also characterize asymptotic stability. In this structured case, preference information provides the desired connection to long-run behavior.

The equivalence fails more generally. A constructed three-player game has a preferentially stable set whose span is dynamically unstable. To bridge the gap, the paper introduces resilience under aggregate deviations, an easily checked condition that uses payoff information and guarantees asymptotic stability for arbitrary spans. Preference ordering thus provides useful constraints but is not always sufficient.
summary.tldr: Preference graphs characterize learning stability in subgames, but more general stability requires additional payoff information.

title: What Preferences Can—and Cannot—Predict in Multi-Agent Online Learning

abstract: Recently, it has received growing attention in building AI Scientist agents with Large Language Models (LLMs). Since scientific discovery fundamentally relies on uncovering causal relationships from observations, the capability of causal thinking that distinguish causation from correlation and hidden biases, is essential to LLM agents. Despite a number of existing benchmarks for AI scientists, they do not explicitly incorporate challenges from hidden confounders, selection bias, and noisy measurements that widely exist in real-world scientific discovery. To this end, we present CausalGame, a benchmark that evaluates the causal thinking capabilities of LLM agents through interactive games. More specifically, we ask LLM agents to actively design experimental protocols, collect observation data and derive a final solution with an explanation report. To emulate realistic scientific discovery challenges, we design 14 game settings with the incorporation of selection bias, noisy measurements, and hidden confounders. The results with 29 frontier LLM agents show that they consistently fail to reason about and recover the underlying causal relationships required to solve the games. CausalGame provides a controlled testbed for evaluating causal thinking of AI Scientist agents. The project is available at causalgame.github.io .

paragraphs: CausalGame evaluates whether language-model agents can discover what causes an outcome through interactive experiments. This capability matters for automated science because observed associations can be misleading. A hidden influence, biased selection of observations, or measurement noise can make a plausible explanation differ from the actual causal relationship.

The benchmark contains 14 game settings that incorporate these obstacles. Agents must design experimental protocols, gather observations, and produce a solution accompanied by an explanation report. This setup evaluates a connected discovery process: the agent must decide what evidence to obtain and then reason from that evidence, rather than merely answer a question about an already prepared dataset.

Tests involving 29 frontier language-model agents find that they consistently fail to recover the causal relationships needed to solve the games. The result identifies a weakness in the evaluated agents’ scientific reasoning under these controlled challenges. CausalGame provides a way to examine that weakness explicitly, including situations where correlation, hidden confounding, and biased observations complicate discovery.
summary.tldr: CausalGame tests experimental causal reasoning in interactive games and finds persistent failures among 29 evaluated language-model agents.

title: CausalGame: Benchmarking Causal Thinking of LLM Agents in Games

abstract: Domain Incremental Learning is a critical scenario that requires models to continuously adapt to new data domains without retraining. However, domain shifts often cause severe performance degradation. To address this, we propose Hybrid Energy-Distance Prompt, a domain-incremental framework inspired by Helmholtz free energy. HEDP introduces an energy regularization loss to enhance the separability of domain representations and a hybrid energy-distance weighted mechanism that fuses energy-based and distance-based cues to improve domain selection and generalization. Experiments on multiple benchmarks, including CORe50, show that HEDP achieves superior performance on unseen domains with a 2.57% accuracy gain, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting and enhancing open-world adaptability. Our code is available at https://github.com/dannis97500/HEDP.
