paragraphs: Domain incremental learning asks a model to adapt as new data domains arrive without retraining from scratch. Changes between domains can sharply reduce performance and interfere with previously learned behavior. HEDP addresses this setting with a prompt-based framework that combines two kinds of evidence when selecting a domain.

Inspired by Helmholtz free energy, the method adds an energy regularization loss that encourages domain representations to be easier to distinguish. It then combines energy-based information with distance-based information through a weighted mechanism. The two components serve related purposes: learning more separable representations and using both cues to improve domain selection and generalization.

Experiments on multiple benchmarks, including CORe50, report stronger performance on unseen domains and a 2.57% accuracy improvement. The results also support reduced catastrophic forgetting and better adaptability to new domains. The significance is that distinguishing known domain representations can be paired with a more informative selection mechanism to support continued adaptation. The reported outcome is mitigation of forgetting, rather than a claim that earlier knowledge is always preserved completely.
summary.tldr: HEDP combines energy and distance cues in a prompt-based framework to improve domain adaptation and reduce forgetting.

title: HEDP: A Hybrid Energy-Distance Prompt-based Framework for Domain Incremental Learning

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are bottlenecked by sparse, irregular memory access. Popular frameworks such as DGL and PyTorch Geometric support general message passing, but complex layers often materialize edge-wise intermediates, increasing memory traffic and limiting scalability on large graphs. We take an I/O- and arithmetic-intensity–centric view and show that widely used layers fall into three kernel families: SpMM-based convolutions, reduction-based aggregations, and attention-based layers (GATv2/Graph Transformer). For each family, we develop GPU kernels that reduce data movement, improve locality, and remain robust across realistic graphs. We also study graph reordering and find that its impact depends on the kernel mapping: it benefits neighbor-parallel (gather-dominated) kernels more consistently than feature-parallel designs. Empirically, our fused attention kernels reach up to 3.9$\times$ speedup for Graph Transformer (median 1.6$\times$), with Tensor Core (block-sparse) variants up to 7.3$\times$ on locally dense graphs; for GATv2 we reach up to 8.5$\times$ speedup (median 2.0$\times$) while reducing peak memory by up to 76$\times$ (median 6$\times$). Our degree-aware reduction kernels achieve up to 10$\times$ speedup (median 2.6$\times$). For SpMM-based layers, properly cached cuSPARSE achieves up to 8$\times$ speedup over DGL and outperforms evaluated custom baselines in the majority of evaluations. We release our implementations as drop-in replacements in our GitHub repository to support reproducible, hardware-aware GNN acceleration.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often spend substantial resources moving data through irregular memory accesses. Complex layers can also create intermediate values for individual edges, increasing traffic and memory use. This paper organizes common layers into three computational families—sparse matrix multiplication, reductions, and attention—and develops GPU implementations around their data-movement requirements.

The approach reduces memory traffic and improves locality through family-specific kernels. Graph reordering helps differently depending on the mapping of work: neighbor-parallel kernels benefit more consistently than feature-parallel ones. For sparse-matrix-based layers, properly cached cuSPARSE outperforms evaluated custom baselines in most evaluations, showing that implementation choices matter alongside new kernel designs.

Reported median speedups are 1.6 times for Graph Transformer, 2.0 times for GATv2, and 2.6 times for degree-aware reductions. GATv2 peak memory falls by a median factor of six, with a maximum reduction of 76 times. Block-sparse Tensor Core variants reach up to 7.3 times speedup on locally dense graphs. The released implementations are designed as drop-in replacements.
summary.tldr: GPU implementations tailored to graph-layer memory access deliver substantial measured speed and memory improvements, with benefits depending on kernel and graph structure.

title: On Efficient Scaling of GNNs via IO-Aware Layers Implementations

abstract: Probing is widely adopted in computer vision to faithfully evaluate self-supervised learning (SSL) embeddings, as finetuning may misrepresent their inherent quality. In contrast, audio SSL models still rely on finetuning because simple probing fails to unlock their full potential and alters their rankings when competing on AudioSet. Hence, a robust and efficient probing mechanism is required to guide the trajectory of audio SSL towards reliable and reproducible methods. We introduce Convex Gated Probing (CGP), a prototype-based method that significantly closes the gap between finetuning and probing in audio. CGP efficiently utilizes all frozen layers via a gating mechanism and exposes the location of latent task-relevant information. Guided by CGP as a reliable post-hoc evaluation probe, we rework the entire SSL pipeline of current best performing audio models that use legacy implementations of prior SSL methods. By refining data preprocessing, model architecture, and pretraining recipe, we introduce Better Audio Transformer (BAT), and establish new SOTA on audio benchmarks.

paragraphs: Evaluating a pretrained audio representation is difficult when the evaluation itself changes the model. Finetuning can obscure the quality of the original features, while simple probes may fail to extract information already present. The paper identifies this problem in audio self-supervised learning, where probing can change model rankings relative to finetuning on AudioSet.

The authors introduce Convex Gated Probing, a prototype-based evaluator that draws on all frozen model layers. A gating mechanism determines how to use these layers, helping expose where task-relevant information resides. This substantially narrows the performance gap between probing and finetuning while keeping the underlying representations fixed.

The probe then serves as a guide for revising the broader training pipeline. The authors change data preprocessing, architecture, and the pretraining recipe to produce Better Audio Transformer, or BAT. They report new leading results on audio benchmarks. The contribution therefore combines a stronger way to assess existing representations with a model whose development is informed by that assessment.
summary.tldr: A probe that combines information across frozen audio-model layers guides the development of BAT, which achieves leading audio benchmark results.

title: BAT: Better Audio Transformer Guided by Convex Gated Probing

abstract: Evaluating a new model on an existing benchmark is often necessary to understand its behavior before deployment. For modern evaluation frameworks, generating and evaluating a response for all queries can be prohibitively expensive. In practice, responses from previously-evaluated models are often cached – creating a potential opportunity to use this additional information to decrease the number of queries required to accurately evaluate a new model. In this paper, we introduce an approach for predicting benchmark performance that leverages cached model responses based on the Data Kernel Perspective Space (DKPS), a method for quantifying the relationship between models in the black-box setting. Theoretically, we show that DKPS-based methods are query-efficient under certain conditions. Empirically, we demonstrate that DKPS-based methods achieve the same mean absolute error as baselines with a substantially decreased query budget. We conclude by proposing an offline method for selecting a set of queries that maximizes the goodness-of-fit on reference models, improving prediction accuracy over random query selection.

paragraphs: Evaluating a new model on every benchmark query can be expensive because both generating responses and assessing them require resources. This paper uses information that evaluation pipelines may already possess: cached responses from previously tested models. The goal is to predict a new model’s benchmark performance using fewer fresh queries.

The approach relies on Data Kernel Perspective Space, or DKPS, which measures relationships between models in a black-box setting. Those relationships let the evaluation method use reference-model responses when estimating performance. The authors prove query efficiency under certain conditions, providing theoretical support for when cached information can reduce the amount of new evaluation needed.

Empirically, DKPS-based methods match baseline mean absolute error with substantially smaller query budgets. The paper also introduces an offline query-selection method that chooses queries to maximize goodness-of-fit on reference models. This improves prediction accuracy over random selection. Together, the findings show how previous evaluation work can support both performance estimation and the choice of which questions to ask a new model.
summary.tldr: Cached responses from earlier models help predict a new model’s benchmark performance accurately with substantially fewer queries.

title: Query-efficient model evaluation using cached responses

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently hallucinate, limiting their reliability in critical applications. Conformal Prediction (CP) addresses this by calibrating error rates on held-out data to provide statistically valid confidence guarantees. Recent work extends CP to LLM factuality: outputs are decomposed into subclaims, each assigned a risk score, and a calibrated threshold filters out risky claims to guarantee hallucination rates below a user-specified level (e.g., 10%). While prior methods treat claims independently, Coherent Factuality extends to multi-step reasoning by representing outputs as dependency graphs and jointly validating claims with their logical ancestors. A key limitation is that Coherent Factuality is not differentiable, requiring hand-crafted scorers that at high reliability levels remove nearly 60% of true claims. We introduce Differentiable Coherent Factuality (DCF), a fully differentiable relaxation that enables learning improved scorers while provably recovering the original algorithm’s guarantees. Experiments on two reasoning datasets demonstrate DCF achieves up to 141% improvement in claim retention while maintaining reliability guarantees, representing a significant step towards reliable conformal LLM systems.

paragraphs: Conformal methods can filter language-model claims using thresholds calibrated on held-out data, providing statistical control over hallucination rates. For multistep reasoning, however, individual claims also depend on earlier claims. Coherent Factuality addresses this by representing an answer as a dependency graph and checking claims together with their logical ancestors.

The difficulty is that the original procedure is not differentiable, which prevents directly learning better scorers through that procedure. Its hand-crafted scorers can remove nearly 60% of true claims at high reliability levels. This paper introduces Differentiable Coherent Factuality, a differentiable relaxation that makes scorer learning possible while provably recovering the original algorithm’s guarantees.

On two reasoning datasets, the authors report up to 141% improvement in claim retention while maintaining reliability guarantees. The practical benefit is keeping more of an answer’s useful content under the same kind of reliability requirement. The contribution connects training with structured factuality checking: it improves the scoring component while preserving attention to dependencies between claims, rather than treating every statement as an isolated decision.
summary.tldr: A differentiable factuality filter learns to retain more reasoning claims while preserving conformal reliability guarantees.

title: Differentiable Conformal Training for LLM Reasoning Factuality

abstract: Existing referring video object segmentation (RVOS) is largely built on passive perception and assumes the target is already visible in the observed video, which limits real-world use when queries refer to objects beyond the current view. To address this gap, we introduce Referring Video Active Exploration and Segmentation (RVAS), a new task that focuses on reasoning about exploration policy and then locating and segmenting the object according to an input referring expression. To support RVAS, we build a large-scale dataset with manually annotated exploration actions and reference reasoning traces, enabling supervised training and evaluation. We benchmark representative RVOS and related video understanding baselines and find that they struggle to perform active target search and incur substantial overhead when coupled with online decision making. Motivated by these challenges, we propose LESA, a baseline framework that introduces a state controller and hierarchical memory for efficient streaming processing and sparse MLLM reasoning. LESA substantially reduces inference cost while maintaining competitive planning quality, and consistently improves segmentation accuracy on the RVAS dataset. Code is available at https://github.com/FudanCVL/RVAS.

paragraphs: Referring video segmentation usually assumes that the object described by a user is already visible. RVAS extends the problem to cases where the system must first explore to find it. Success therefore requires deciding how to search, locating the referred object, and segmenting it once the relevant view is obtained.

The authors introduce a large dataset with manually annotated exploration actions and reference reasoning traces to support supervised training and evaluation. Their benchmark shows that representative segmentation and related video-understanding methods struggle with active search, while adding online decisions creates substantial overhead. This establishes exploration as a distinct capability that existing passive perception systems do not readily provide.

The proposed LESA baseline combines a state controller and hierarchical memory for streaming processing, invoking multimodal language-model reasoning sparsely. It substantially reduces inference cost while retaining competitive planning quality and consistently improving segmentation accuracy on the RVAS dataset. The paper contributes both an evaluation setting for finding initially unseen targets and a framework that coordinates search and segmentation efficiently.
summary.tldr: RVAS introduces active search before video-object segmentation, with a dataset and an efficient memory-based baseline called LESA.

title: RVAS: Referring Video Active Exploration and Segmentation

abstract: Interpretable methods such as vision–language models (VLMs) have advanced affect analysis by aligning images with textual descriptions. However, relying on text as an intermediate proxy faces critical limitations: linguistic templates are inherently discrete, making them fundamentally incompatible with continuous valence–arousal regression, while also acting as a bottleneck for fine-grained visual nuances. Cognitive psychology suggests that human affective perception is not mediated by linguistic translation, but is grounded in perceptual resemblance to internalized visual archetypes. Motivated by this, we propose AURA, an archetype-based framework that replaces brittle linguistic proxies with a self-organizing archetype manifold. By adaptively allocating representational density according to affective complexity, AURA enables accurate continuous regression and reshapes affective taxonomies by decomposing labels into interpretable, geometrically coherent visual primitives. This paradigm offers a transparent, visually grounded decision trail and achieves state-of-the-art results across discrete and continuous tasks.

paragraphs: AURA addresses how a model can recognize affect from images while making its decisions understandable. The paper argues that translating visual evidence into textual descriptions creates a bottleneck: discrete language templates struggle to express continuous emotional variation and can lose subtle visual details. Its alternative is to organize affective understanding around visual archetypes.

These archetypes form a self-organizing representation whose density adapts to affective complexity. In other words, the model allocates more representational detail where the visual distinctions require it. It also breaks affect labels into interpretable visual components arranged in a coherent geometry. This connects predictions to visual resemblance and structure, providing a decision trail grounded in the images themselves.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on both discrete classification and continuous regression tasks. Those findings support the usefulness of the same visual representation for assigning categories and estimating continuously varying affect. The interpretability contribution is a way to inspect the visual components behind a prediction, alongside the reported improvements in predictive performance.
summary.tldr: AURA uses adaptive visual archetypes to make affect predictions interpretable while supporting both emotional categories and continuous estimates.

title: AURA: Visually Interpretable Affective Understanding via Robust Archetypes

abstract: Text-to-motion (T2M) generation has become a fundamental task, yet existing evaluation metrics often fail to capture whether a generated motion semantically matches its text description. We propose VeMo, a zero-shot evaluation framework that renders generated human motions into videos and uses pretrained video-language models (VLMs) to assess text-motion alignment. Instead of training an evaluator on scarce motion-specific labels, VeMo transfers the semantic reasoning ability of VLMs to T2M evaluation through normalized likelihood-based scoring. To reduce the effect of 3D-to-2D projection ambiguity, we introduce an entropy-driven uncertainty analysis for identifying reliable rendered views. To address the lack of rigorous standards in the field, we further contribute a test-only and human-annotated meta-evaluation benchmark, covering motions generated by multiple representative T2M models. Extensive experiments show that VeMo correlates better with human judgments than existing reference-based and reference-free metrics. Additional analyses on view selection, rendering protocols, textual prompt robustness, and computational trade-offs characterize both the promise and limitations of VLM-based T2M evaluation.

Analyses of view selection, rendering, prompt robustness, and computational trade-offs further characterize the approach. The stated benefit is better agreement with human assessment, with rendering and viewing choices explicitly examined.
summary.tldr: VeMo evaluates text-motion alignment through rendered videos and pretrained video-language models, correlating better with human judgments than existing metrics.

title: Zero-Shot Text-to-Motion Evaluation using Video Language Models

abstract: Smoothing a signal based on local neighborhoods is a core operation in machine learning and geometry processing. On well-structured domains such as vector spaces and manifolds, the Laplace operator derived from differential geometry offers a principled approach to smoothing via heat diffusion, with strong theoretical guarantees. However, constructing such Laplacians requires a carefully defined domain structure, which is not always available. Most practitioners thus rely on simple convolution kernels and message-passing layers, which are biased against the boundaries of the domain. We bridge this gap by introducing a broad class of smoothing operators, derived from general similarity or adjacency matrices, and demonstrate that they can be normalized into diffusion-like operators that inherit desirable properties from Laplacians. Our approach relies on a symmetric variant of the Sinkhorn algorithm, which rescales positive smoothing operators to match the structural behavior of heat diffusion. This construction enables Laplacian-like smoothing and processing of irregular data such as point clouds, sparse voxel grids or mixture of Gaussians. We show that the resulting operators not only approximate heat diffusion but also retain spectral information from the Laplacian itself, with applications to shape analysis and matching.

paragraphs: Smoothing typically combines a signal with information from nearby locations. On domains with suitable geometric structure, heat diffusion provides a principled version of this operation through the Laplace operator. Constructing that operator can be difficult when the domain lacks a carefully defined structure, leaving practitioners to use simpler kernels or message-passing layers that introduce boundary bias.

This paper develops smoothing operators from general similarity or adjacency matrices and normalizes them to behave more like diffusion. The construction uses a symmetric version of the Sinkhorn algorithm to rescale positive smoothing operators. It aims to recover desirable structural properties of heat diffusion without requiring the same domain construction used for a geometric Laplacian.

The resulting approach applies to irregular representations including point clouds, sparse voxel grids, and mixtures of Gaussians. The authors show that the normalized operators approximate heat diffusion and retain spectral information from the Laplacian itself. That connection supports applications to shape analysis and matching, extending the usefulness of the construction beyond smoothing signals alone.
summary.tldr: Symmetric Sinkhorn normalization turns general smoothing operators into diffusion-like operators useful for irregular geometric data.

title: Sinkhorn Normalization of Diffusion Kernels

abstract: Conventional reinforcement learning strategies for visual generation typically employ sample-wise reward functions, yet this practice frequently results in reward hacking that degrades image diversity and introduces visual anomalies. To address these limitations, we present a novel framework that finetunes generative models using distribution-wise rewards, ensuring better alignment with real-world data distributions. Unlike rewards that evaluate samples individually, distribution-wise reward accounts for the data distribution of the samples, mitigating the mode collapse problem that occurs when all samples optimize towards the same direction independently. To overcome the prohibitive computational cost of estimating these rewards, we introduce a subset-replace strategy that efficiently provides reward signals by updating only a small subset of a generated reference set. Additionally, we apply RL to optimize post-hoc model merging coefficients, potentially mitigating the train-inference inconsistency caused by introducing stochastic differential equation (SDE) in regular RL practices. Extensive experiments show our approach significantly improves FID-50K across various base models, from 8.30 to 5.77 for SiT and from 3.74 to 3.52 for EDM2. Qualitative evaluation also confirms that our method enhances perceptual quality while preserving sample diversity.

paragraphs: Rewarding generated images one at a time can encourage every output toward the same rewarded pattern. The paper connects this behavior to reward hacking, reduced diversity, and visual anomalies. Its proposed framework evaluates rewards at the distribution level, so optimization accounts for how generated samples collectively align with real-world data.

Computing such rewards can be expensive. A subset-replace strategy makes the process more efficient by changing only a small portion of a generated reference set when providing reward signals. The authors also use reinforcement learning to optimize coefficients for post-hoc model merging. This additional step could reduce the training–inference mismatch associated with introducing stochastic differential equations in conventional reinforcement-learning approaches.

Together, the results support treating the collection of generated outputs as part of the optimization target, helping address the tendency of independently rewarded samples to converge toward similar outcomes.
summary.tldr: Distribution-level rewards improve visual generation quality while helping preserve diversity during reinforcement-learning fine-tuning.

title: Optimizing Visual Generative Models via Distribution-wise Rewards

abstract: Kleinberg and Mullainathan recently proposed a formal framework for studying the phenomenon of language generation, called language generation in the limit. In this model, an adversary gives an enumeration of example strings from an unknown target language, and the algorithm is tasked with correctly generating unseen strings from the target language within finite time. Refined notions of non-uniform and uniform generation were later introduced by Li, Raman, and Tewari (2025), and a noisy model was introduced by Raman and Raman (2025), which allows the adversary to insert extraneous strings. A natural question in the noisy model is to quantify the effect of noise, by studying the impact of each additional extraneous string. We show two complementary results in this setting. We first show that for both uniform and non-uniform generation, a single noisy string strictly reduces the set of collections that can be generated, thus answering an open question in Raman and Raman (2025). Then, we show for both uniform and non-uniform generation that generation with a single noisy string is equivalent to generation with any finite amount of noise, sharply contrasting with the strict hierarchy for noisy generation in the limit shown by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (2026). Finally, we leverage our previous results to provide the first known characterization for non-uniform noise-dependent generatability.

paragraphs: This paper studies a mathematical model of language generation in which an algorithm receives example strings from an unknown language and must eventually generate valid strings it has not seen. An adversary controls the presentation of examples and, in the noisy version, can insert strings outside the target language. The question is how those extra strings change what generation is possible.

For both uniform and non-uniform generation, the authors prove that allowing even one noisy string strictly reduces the collections of languages that can be generated. They also prove that tolerating one noisy string is equivalent, in these two settings, to tolerating any finite amount of noise. The first corruption therefore changes feasibility, while further finite corruption does not create additional levels of difficulty in this characterization.

That equivalence contrasts with a previously established strict noise hierarchy for generation in the limit. Using their results, the authors also characterize non-uniform noise-dependent generatability. These are statements about formal generation guarantees, clarifying how different definitions of generation respond to corrupted evidence.
summary.tldr: For uniform and non-uniform formal language generation, one noisy example reduces feasibility as much as any finite amount of noise.

title: Characterizing the Effect of Noise in Language Generation in the Limit

abstract: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for leveraging distributed data to enhance model performance. However, existing methods predominantly rely on idealized assumptions of model homogeneity and balanced modality distributions, rendering them ill-suited for practical scenarios characterized by heterogeneous client architectures and severe modality imbalance. To address these challenges, we propose a Multimodal Federated learning Prototype-guided Bilateral Alignment (MFedPBA) framework. MFedPBA facilitates robust knowledge synergy through a dual alignment mechanism: (i) at the feature level, it aligns heterogeneous feature spaces via a projection encoder optimized by contrastive learning and the Gromov-Wasserstein distance; (ii) at the decision level, it employs an entropy-weighted aggregation of naturally aligned logit prototypes. This novel design achieves robust MFL by jointly tackling heterogeneous feature spaces and collectively aggregating decisions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under conditions of model heterogeneity and modality imbalance.

paragraphs: Multimodal federated learning combines knowledge from distributed clients that may hold different kinds of data. In practice, clients can also use different model architectures and have strongly uneven access to modalities. MFedPBA addresses these conditions, which make methods built around matching architectures and balanced modality distributions difficult to apply.

The framework aligns clients at two levels. For internal features, a projection encoder uses contrastive learning and the Gromov-Wasserstein distance to bring heterogeneous representations into alignment. For decisions, it combines naturally aligned logit prototypes using entropy-based weights. These prototypes summarize model outputs, providing a second route for sharing knowledge even when internal feature spaces differ.

The two mechanisms jointly address representation mismatch and collective decision aggregation. Extensive experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under model heterogeneity and modality imbalance. The findings support treating these as related alignment problems: clients need a way to reconcile their internal representations and a way to combine their predictions. The reported advantage applies to the heterogeneous, imbalanced conditions studied.
summary.tldr: MFedPBA aligns both features and decisions to improve multimodal federated learning across different client architectures and imbalanced modalities.

title: Prototype-guided Bilateral Alignment Multimodal Federated Learning

abstract: Planning has become a central capability for contemporary agent systems in navigating complex, long-horizon tasks, yet existing approaches predominantly rely on fixed, hand-crafted planning structures that lack the flexibility to adapt to the structural diversity of open-ended problems. To address this limitation, we introduce TodoEvolve, a meta-planning paradigm that autonomously synthesizes and dynamically revises task-specific planning architectures. Specifically, we first construct PlanFactory, a modular design space that standardizes diverse planning paradigms within a unified codebase encompassing topology, initialization, adaptation, and navigation, thereby providing a common interface for heterogeneous planning patterns. Leveraging PlanFactory, we collect high-quality planning trajectories and train Todo-14B via Impedance-Guided Preference Optimization (IGPO), a multi-objective reinforcement learning objective that encourages the generation of planning systems that are performant, stable, and token-efficient across arbitrary tasks and agent backbones. Empirical evaluations on five agentic benchmarks demonstrate that TodoEvolve consistently surpasses carefully engineered planning modules while maintaining economical API costs and runtime overhead. Our codes are available at https://github.com/EcthelionLiu/TodoEvolve.

paragraphs: Agents tackling long tasks need planning structures that fit the problems they encounter. Fixed, manually designed planners can lack flexibility across open-ended tasks. TodoEvolve addresses this by learning to construct and revise the planning architecture itself, making the organization of planning an adaptive part of the agent system.

The authors first build PlanFactory, a shared codebase and modular design space covering planning topology, initialization, adaptation, and navigation. This provides a common interface for different planning patterns. They then collect high-quality planning trajectories and train Todo-14B using Impedance-Guided Preference Optimization, a multi-objective reinforcement learning objective that encourages performance, stability, and efficient token use.

The resulting model synthesizes task-specific planning systems and can update them dynamically as planning proceeds. Across five agentic benchmarks, TodoEvolve consistently outperforms carefully engineered planning modules while maintaining economical API costs and runtime overhead. These findings support learning how to organize an agent's planning process, alongside the decisions made within that process, as a practical way to improve performance across evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: TodoEvolve learns to generate and revise task-specific planning architectures, improving agent performance while keeping costs economical.

title: TodoEvolve: Learning to Architect Agent Planning Systems

abstract: Riemannian neural networks have proven effective in solving a variety of machine learning tasks. The key to their success lies in the development of principled Riemannian analogs of fundamental building blocks in deep neural networks (DNNs). Among those, Riemannian batch normalization (BN) layers have shown to enhance training stability and improve accuracy. In this paper, we propose BN layers for neural networks on complex domains. The proposed layers have close connections with existing Riemannian BN layers. We derive essential components for practical implementations of BN layers on some complex domains which are less studied in previous works, e.g., the Siegel disk domain. We conduct experiments on radar clutter classification, node classification, and action recognition demonstrating the efficacy of our method.

paragraphs: Neural networks operating on geometric spaces need building blocks that respect the structure of those spaces. The paper focuses on batch normalization, a component whose Riemannian variants have helped stabilize training and improve accuracy. Its goal is to extend this component to networks on complex domains.

The authors propose normalization layers with close connections to existing Riemannian batch normalization methods. They also derive components needed to implement these layers on domains that have received less attention, including the Siegel disk. This implementation work matters because a geometric formulation must supply usable operations before it can become a practical part of a neural network.

Experiments on radar clutter classification, node classification, and action recognition demonstrate the method’s effectiveness across different tasks. The contribution is a way to equip networks on these complex domains with an established type of training component. It combines a connection to existing geometric normalization methods with the mathematical ingredients needed to extend their practical reach.
summary.tldr: The paper develops batch normalization layers for complex geometric domains and demonstrates their usefulness across three classification and recognition tasks.

title: Batch Normalization for Neural Networks on Complex Domains

abstract: Synthetic data generation is increasingly used in machine learning for training and data augmentation. Yet, many current strategies rely on external foundation models or datasets, which can be restricted by policy or legal constraints, especially for sensitive modalities such as human face images and videos. We propose ScoreMix, a self-contained data augmentation method to boost recognition performance by leveraging score compositionality in class-conditioned diffusion models. ScoreMix mixes class-conditioned scores along reverse diffusion trajectories, yielding domain-specific hard augmentations without external resources. We systematically study class-selection strategies and find that mixing classes that are distant in the discriminator embedding space yields larger gains, providing up to 3% additional average improvement across benchmarks over proximity-based selection. Interestingly, we observe that learned condition and embedding spaces are largely uncorrelated under standard alignment metrics, and that condition-space distances are weakly correlated to downstream gains. Across 8 public face recognition benchmarks, ScoreMix improves accuracy by up to 7 percentage points without hyperparameter search, highlighting robustness and practicality. Project page: https://parsa-ra.github.io/scoremix/ .

paragraphs: ScoreMix creates synthetic training augmentations using class-conditioned diffusion models without requiring external foundation models or datasets. Its motivation includes settings such as face recognition, where access to external resources can face policy or legal constraints. The method aims to generate challenging, domain-specific examples using resources within the augmentation setup.

It mixes class-conditioned scores along the reverse diffusion process. The authors examine which classes should be combined and find that selecting classes far apart in a discriminator's embedding space provides larger gains than choosing nearby classes. This strategy yields up to 3% additional average improvement across benchmarks relative to proximity-based selection.

The study also finds that the learned conditioning space and embedding space are largely uncorrelated under standard alignment measures; conditioning-space distances weakly predict downstream gains. Across eight public face-recognition benchmarks, ScoreMix improves accuracy by up to seven percentage points without hyperparameter search. The findings show that both score composition and the space used to choose class combinations matter for useful augmentation.
summary.tldr: ScoreMix mixes diffusion scores to create self-contained augmentations, improving face recognition by up to seven percentage points.

title: ScoreMix: Synthetic Data Generation by Score Composition in Diffusion Models Improves Recognition

abstract: Recent advancements in large multimodal models (LMMs) have driven substantial progress in both text-to-video (T2V) generation and video-to-text (V2T) interpretation tasks. However, current AI-generated videos (AIGVs) still exhibit limitations in terms of perceptual quality and text-video alignment. To this end, we present AIGVE-60K, a comprehensive dataset and benchmark for AI-Generated Video Evaluation, which features (i) comprehensive tasks, encompassing 3,050 extensive prompts across 20 fine-grained task dimensions, (ii) the largest human annotations, including 120K mean-opinion scores (MOSs) and 60K question-answering (QA) pairs annotated on 58,500 videos generated from 30 T2V models, and (iii) bidirectional benchmarking and evaluating for both T2V generation and V2T interpretation capabilities. Based on AIGVE-60K, we propose LOVE, a LMM-based metric for AIGV Evaluation from multiple dimensions including perceptual preference, text-video correspondence, and task-specific accuracy. Building upon LOVE, we further introduce LOVE-Reward to optimize T2V models through reinforcement learning, effectively enhancing both the perceptual quality and text-video correspondence of generated videos. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that LOVE achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes effectively to various AIGV benchmarks. LOVE-Reward significantly improves video generation quality. These findings highlight the effectiveness of the AIGVE-60K dataset and our proposed methods. The database and codes are available at https://github.com/IntMeGroup/LOVE.

paragraphs: This work connects evaluation of generated videos with evaluation of how models interpret those videos. Its AIGVE-60K benchmark covers 3,050 prompts across 20 fine-grained task dimensions. It contains 58,500 videos from 30 text-to-video models, with 120,000 human mean-opinion scores and 60,000 annotated question-answer pairs supporting these complementary assessments.

Built on that dataset, LOVE is a large-multimodal-model-based evaluation metric. It assesses perceptual preference, correspondence between text and video, and accuracy on the particular task. These dimensions separate whether a video is visually appealing from whether it follows the requested content and fulfills the task, allowing evaluation to capture more than one aspect of quality.

The authors then use LOVE as the basis for LOVE-Reward, which optimizes text-to-video models through reinforcement learning. Experiments report state-of-the-art evaluation performance and effective generalization across generated-video benchmarks. LOVE-Reward also improves generated-video quality and text correspondence. The overall contribution links human-annotated benchmarking, automated evaluation, and a reward signal for improving generation.
summary.tldr: LOVE combines a human-annotated video benchmark, a multidimensional evaluation metric, and a reinforcement-learning reward that improves video generation.

title: LOVE: Benchmarking and Evaluating Text-to-Video Generation and Video-to-Text Interpretation

abstract: Text-to-SQL has recently achieved impressive progress, yet remains difficult to apply effectively in real-world scenarios. This gap stems from the reliance on single static workflows, fundamentally limiting scalability to out-of-distribution and long-tail scenarios. Instead of requiring users to select suitable methods through extensive experimentation, we attempt to enable systems to adaptively construct workflows at inference time. Through rigorous theoretical and empirical analysis, we demonstrate that optimal dynamic policies consistently outperform the best static workflow, with performance gains fundamentally driven by heterogeneity across candidate workflows. Motivated by this, we propose SquRL, a reinforcement learning framework that enhances LLMs’ reasoning capability in adaptive workflow construction. We design a rule-based reward function and introduce two effective training mechanisms: dynamic actor masking to encourage broader exploration, and pseudo rewards to improve training efficiency. Experiments on widely-used Text-to-SQL benchmarks demonstrate that dynamic workflow construction consistently outperforms the best static workflow methods, with especially pronounced gains on complex and out-of-distribution queries.

paragraphs: Converting natural-language questions into SQL often involves a workflow of reasoning and processing steps. This paper argues that committing to one workflow limits performance when queries differ substantially, especially on unusual or unfamiliar cases. It studies whether a system can construct a suitable workflow while answering each query, reducing the need for users to compare methods themselves.

The theoretical and empirical analysis links the advantage of optimal dynamic policies to differences among candidate workflows. If workflows have different strengths across queries, adapting the choice can exploit that variation. The proposed SquRL framework trains a language model through reinforcement learning to make these construction decisions. It combines rule-based rewards with dynamic actor masking to broaden exploration and pseudo rewards to improve training efficiency.

On widely used Text-to-SQL benchmarks, learned dynamic workflows consistently outperform the best static workflow methods. Gains are especially pronounced for complex queries and queries outside the training distribution. The findings support query-dependent workflow construction as a way to use differing workflow strengths more effectively.
summary.tldr: SquRL learns to construct query-specific Text-to-SQL workflows, improving especially on complex and out-of-distribution queries.

title: Beyond Static Pipelines: Learning Dynamic Workflows for Text-to-SQL

abstract: Human image animation has witnessed significant advancements, yet generating high-fidelity hand motions remains a persistent challenge due to their high degrees of freedom and motion complexity. While reinforcement learning from human feedback, particularly direct preference optimization, offers a potential solution, it necessitates the construction of strict preference pairs. However, curating such pairs for dynamic hand regions is prohibitively expensive and often impractical due to frame-wise inconsistencies. In this paper, we propose Implicit Preference Alignment (IPA), a data-efficient post-training framework that eliminates the need for paired preference data. Theoretically grounded in implicit reward maximization, IPA aligns the model by maximizing the likelihood of self-generated high-quality samples while penalizing deviations from the pretrained prior. Furthermore, we introduce a Hand-Aware Local Optimization mechanism to explicitly steer the alignment process toward hand regions. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves effective preference optimization to enhance hand generation quality, while significantly lowering the barrier for constructing preference data. Codes are released at https://github.com/mdswyz/IPA

Theoretically grounded in implicit reward maximization, IPA aligns the model by maximizing the likelihood of self-generated high-quality samples while penalizing deviations from the pretrained prior. Furthermore, we introduce a Hand-Aware Local Optimization mechanism to explicitly steer the alignment process toward hand regions. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves effective preference optimization to enhance hand generation quality, while significantly lowering the barrier for constructing preference data. Codes are released at https://github.com/mdswyz/IPA

paragraphs: Animating a human image remains especially difficult around the hands, whose many possible movements make consistent generation challenging. Preference optimization offers a potential way to improve quality, but constructing reliable pairs of preferred and rejected hand animations is expensive. Frame-to-frame inconsistencies further complicate those comparisons, motivating a method that does not require paired preferences.

Implicit Preference Alignment is a post-training framework grounded in implicit reward maximization. It increases the likelihood of high-quality samples generated by the model itself while penalizing departures from the pretrained prior. This combines a signal favoring better outputs with a constraint that keeps adaptation connected to the model’s existing learned behavior.

A Hand-Aware Local Optimization mechanism directs the alignment process specifically toward hand regions. Experiments report improved hand generation through effective preference optimization while reducing the burden of constructing preference data. The contribution links a pair-free training objective with targeted local optimization, making the approach directly responsive to the animation region that motivated the work.

title: Implicit Preference Alignment for Human Image Animation

abstract: We propose GradPower, a lightweight gradient-transformation technique for accelerating language model pre-training. Given a gradient vector $\boldsymbol{g}=(g_ {i})_ {i}$, GradPower first applies the elementwise sign-power transformation: $ \varphi_ p(\boldsymbol{g}) = \left({\rm sign}(g_ i)|g_ i|^p\right)_ {i} $ for a fixed $p>0$, and then feeds the transformed gradient into a base optimizer. Notably, GradPower requires only a single-line code change and no modifications to the base optimizer’s internal logic, including the hyperparameters. When applied to AdamW (termed AdamWPower), GradPower consistently achieves lower terminal loss across diverse architectures (LLaMA, Qwen2MoE), parameter scales (66M to 2B), datasets (C4, OpenWebText), and learning-rate schedules (cosine, warmup-stable-decay). The most pronounced gains are observed when training modern mixture-of-experts models with warmup-stable-decay schedules. GradPower also integrates seamlessly with other state-of-the-art optimizers, such as Muon, yielding further improvements. Finally, we provide theoretical analyses that reveal the underlying mechanism of GradPower and highlight the influence of gradient noise.

title: GradPower: Powering Gradients for Faster Language Model Pre-Training

abstract: Score-based diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable empirical success in learning high-dimensional distributions, particularly those exhibiting low-dimensional and multi-modal structures. However, theoretical understanding of their statistical efficiency remains limited. Existing theories typically rely on strong regularity assumptions, such as uniformly bounded densities or globally smooth score functions, which fail to capture such intrinsic structures. In this work, we study the sample complexity of diffusion models for learning distributions supported on a union of low-dimensional subspaces. Assuming that the data distribution within each subspace is subgaussian, we show that diffusion models require at most the order of $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-k \vee 2})$ (up to some logarithmic factor) samples to achieve $\varepsilon$ sampling error in 1-Wasserstein distance, where $k$ is the intrinsic dimension. This near-optimal convergence rate depends only on the intrinsic dimension and significantly improves upon prior theoretical guarantees that suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Notably, our analysis applies to a broad collection of distributions without imposing smoothness, bounded-density, or log-concavity assumptions. Overall, our results show that diffusion models can statistically adapt to intrinsic low-dimensional structure while naturally accommodating multi-modal data, offering a rigorous theoretical justification for their success in complex high-dimensional learning tasks.

paragraphs: Data can have many recorded coordinates while varying along relatively few underlying directions. It can also occupy several distinct regions, creating multiple modes. This paper studies whether diffusion models can learn such distributions with a number of samples governed by their underlying dimension. The mathematical setting places data on a union of low-dimensional subspaces.

Assuming the distribution within each subspace is subgaussian, the authors establish a sample requirement of roughly epsilon raised to minus the larger of k and two, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here k is the intrinsic dimension, and epsilon measures sampling error in 1-Wasserstein distance. The resulting convergence rate is near-optimal and depends on intrinsic dimension, improving theoretical guarantees that suffer from high ambient dimensionality.

The analysis does not require smoothness, bounded densities, or log-concavity, assumptions that can exclude important forms of structured data. Its significance is a statistical explanation for diffusion models’ ability to accommodate multiple modes and low-dimensional structure. The guarantee applies under the stated subspace and subgaussian assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under subspace and subgaussian assumptions, diffusion models achieve near-optimal sample complexity governed by intrinsic dimension.

title: Diffusion Models Are Statistically Optimal for Learning Low-Dimensional Multi-Modal Distributions

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in graph analysis due to the Message-Passing (MP) mechanism, yet they struggle with heterophilic graphs where connected nodes often have distinct labels or dissimilar attributes. Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) serves as a promising approach to extract the information beyond neighboring nodes, effectively mitigating the limitations of the MP mechanism in handling heterophilic graphs. Nevertheless, GCL faces two critical challenges when applied to heterophilic graphs, i.e., the potential distribution shift from data augmentation and the loss of robustness caused by high-frequency signals. To address these problems, we propose a novel model, namely the Spectral Fusion Contrastive Learning with Topology-Adaptive Graph Augmentation (SFCLTA) for unsupervised graph representation learning. Our method dynamically adjusts graph structures via a heterophily-aware augmentation strategy, and constrains high-frequency distortions by spectral regularization. We utilize the confidence-weighted fusion to enhance the robustness. Additionally, we introduce a feature reconstruction task as a prerequisite to explicitly mitigate feature-level distribution shifts. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed SFCLTA consistently outperforms baseline models in multiple tasks. Our code is released on https://github.com/JonathanGXu/SFCLTA.

paragraphs: Graph learning becomes challenging when connected nodes have different labels or attributes. Neighbor-based message passing can struggle in these heterophilic settings. Contrastive learning can capture information beyond immediate neighbors, but its graph augmentations may shift the data distribution, while high-frequency signals can reduce robustness.

SFCLTA combines several mechanisms to address these issues in unsupervised representation learning. Its augmentation strategy adapts graph structure with awareness of heterophily. Spectral regularization constrains high-frequency distortions, and confidence-weighted fusion strengthens robustness. A feature-reconstruction task explicitly addresses distribution changes at the feature level.

These components treat graph structure and node features as related sources of potential augmentation error. The aim is to benefit from contrastive learning without allowing the generated views to distort the information being learned. Across multiple tasks on real-world datasets, SFCLTA consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines. The results support coordinating topology adaptation, spectral constraints, and feature reconstruction when learning representations from heterophilic graphs.
summary.tldr: SFCLTA improves unsupervised graph learning by combining heterophily-aware augmentation, spectral regularization, and feature reconstruction.

title: SFCLTA: Spectral Fusion Contrastive Learning with Topology-Adaptive Graph Augmentation

abstract: Connectionist models and symbolic models have long embodied two divergent paradigms: the former excel at differentiable representation learning yet struggle with transparency, while the latter deliver explicit rule-based reasoning but resist gradient-based optimization. We introduce Arboreal Neural Networks (ArbNN), a neural-symbolic framework that unifies these paradigms both computationally and conceptually. At the design level, ArbNN departs fundamentally from prior neuralized-tree models through a depth-aware routing mechanism and a topology-informed softmax aggregation, which together enable one-shot full-path gradient propagation and consequently achieving rapid and well-conditioned optimization dynamics. At the conceptual level, ArbNN reveals that decision-tree branching and self-attention routing are two realizations of the same conditional computation primitive. We prove a structural isomorphism between a decision tree and a single-query attention head, enabling a differentiable architecture that faithfully preserves symbolic decision logic. The defining property of ArbNN is Bidirectional Fidelity, ensuring that the neural module can be compiled from—and losslessly decompiled back into—a symbolic tree, yielding both ordering consistency in ranking behavior and explicit, auditable interpretability via reconstructed if-else rules. ArbNN further supports GBDT-based initialization, allowing it to inherit strong inductive biases and integrate seamlessly with existing production workflows. Empirically, ArbNN achieves state-of-the-art performance on various public tabular benchmarks and delivers consistent gains under temporal distribution shift in large-scale industrial credit-risk systems. To support realistic evaluation, we additionally construct TabCredit, a feature-rich, temporally partitioned dataset built from millions of real-world loan applications. Together, these results demonstrate that ArbNN forms a unified, reversible, and practically deployable bridge between symbolic reasoning and neural computation for high-stakes tabular domains.

paragraphs: Arboreal Neural Networks aim to combine the trainability of neural networks with the explicit decision rules of symbolic trees. The framework uses routing that accounts for tree depth and an aggregation operation informed by tree structure. Together, these mechanisms allow gradients to propagate across complete paths in one pass, supporting the rapid and well-conditioned optimization reported by the authors.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on public tabular benchmarks and consistent gains under temporal distribution shift in industrial credit-risk systems. They also introduce TabCredit, built from millions of loan applications and partitioned over time. These results support the practical value of a reversible connection between learned neural computation and inspectable tree rules.
summary.tldr: ArbNN connects differentiable neural computation with losslessly recoverable decision trees, combining strong tabular performance with explicit rules for auditing.

title: Arboreal Neural Network

abstract: As language models grow more capable, accurate capability evaluation becomes essential for safety decisions. If models can deliberately underperform on dangerous capability evaluations—a behavior known as sandbagging—they may evade safety measures designed for their true capability level. We introduce Cross-Context Consistency ($C^3$), a general framework for unsupervised black-box sandbagging detection that exploits a fundamental asymmetry: when a model truly lacks capability, its confusion manifests consistently across paraphrased questions, but when a capable model feigns incompetence, its strategic choices about how to appear weak create detectable inconsistencies. The framework is agnostic to the specific consistency metric and aggregation method; we present a simple instantiation using embedding cosine distance and mean aggregation that requires no training data or model-specific adaptation. We evaluate $C^3$ across prompted and fine-tuned sandbagging scenarios, across instructed and more naturalistic setups, maintaining a classification signal where other black-box methods fail. Our findings show the limitations of existing sandbagging detection methods, and reveal the efficacy of consistency-checking as a detection mechanism for sandbagging.

paragraphs: Capability evaluations can be misleading if a model deliberately performs below its abilities, a behavior called sandbagging. Cross-Context Consistency, or C³, investigates whether this behavior can be detected from responses alone. It compares behavior across paraphrases of the same question, using inconsistencies as evidence relevant to deliberate underperformance.

The framework is motivated by an asymmetry between genuine confusion and strategically pretending to be incapable. The latter requires choices about how to fail, which can differ across contexts. C³ allows different consistency measures and aggregation rules. The paper demonstrates a simple version that averages cosine distances between response embeddings, requiring neither training data nor model-specific adaptation.

Evaluations include prompted and fine-tuned sandbagging, with both explicitly instructed and more naturalistic setups. C³ retains a classification signal in settings where other black-box methods fail. These findings support consistency checking as a useful detection mechanism in the evaluated scenarios. The reported result is a discriminative signal from patterns across responses, rather than a claim that any single inconsistency establishes deliberate deception.
summary.tldr: C³ detects signals of deliberate underperformance by comparing how consistently a model responds to paraphrased questions.

title: Same Question, Different Lies: Cross-Context Consistency (C$^3$) for Black-Box Sandbagging Detection

abstract: Standard decoding in Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) is hindered by context rigidity: tokens are retained based on transient high confidence, often ignoring that early predictions lack full context. This creates cascade effects where initial inconsistencies misguide the remaining generation. Existing revision strategies attempt to mitigate this by relying on static confidence scores, but these signals are inherently myopic; inconsistent tokens frequently appear confident to the model itself. To address this, we propose Context-Robust Remasking (CORE), a training-free framework for inference-time revision. We introduce a new selection paradigm: rather than trusting static token probabilities, we identify context-brittle tokens by probing their sensitivity to adversarial perturbations. We formalize revision as a robust optimization problem targeting worst-case context shifts. CORE efficiently approximates this objective using theoretically bounded probability margins to expose and revise unstable tokens. On LLaDA-8B-Base, CORE delivers consistent improvements across reasoning and code benchmarks, outperforming compute-matched baselines and boosting performance on code generation (MBPP) by up to $+9.2%$, with comparable gains generalizing to the Dream-7B architecture.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models gradually fill in missing tokens, but early choices can become fixed before enough context is available. An initially confident mistake may then steer later predictions toward further inconsistencies. CORE addresses this context rigidity by reconsidering how the model decides which generated tokens need revision.

The method probes how sensitive tokens are to adversarial changes in their context. A token that looks reliable under the current context may become unstable under these perturbations, revealing a reason to revisit it. CORE formulates revision through robust optimization over worst-case context shifts and approximates that objective using probability margins with theoretical bounds. These results support contextual stability as a useful revision signal beyond a token’s confidence at a single moment.
summary.tldr: CORE improves diffusion language model decoding by revising tokens whose predictions are unstable under context perturbations.

title: CORE: Context-Robust Remasking for Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Transformer architectures have dramatically advanced representation learning and inference in deep models through self-attention mechanisms. In parallel, associative memory frameworks map representations onto energy landscapes, offering interpretable retrieval mechanisms. However, their continuous-time inference dynamics lack the biological plausibility of classical Continuous Attractor Neural Networks. To bridge this gap, we propose Controlled Dynamics Attractor Transformer (CDAT), which couples a mixture von Mises–Fisher attention energy with a Hopfield refinement energy, while augmenting energy descent with a CANN-inspired excitation–inhibition modulation. CDAT instantiates a topology-constrained dynamical system whose couplings encode relational structure among tokens, thereby linking attractor-style dynamics to modern energy-based attention. We further provide a constructive dissipation analysis to formally establish their controlled inference dynamics. Benefiting from these robust and structured dynamics, CDAT achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks in graph anomaly detection and graph classification.

The work therefore combines a mathematical account of how inference evolves with empirical evidence on graph tasks. Its biological motivation informs the architecture, while the reported performance findings concern those evaluated computational tasks.
summary.tldr: CDAT combines energy-based attention, associative-memory refinement, and attractor-inspired control to achieve strong graph-task performance.

title: Controlled Dynamics Attractor Transformer

abstract: False discovery rate (FDR) is a cornerstone of modern multiple testing. However, it often fails to guarantee the reliability of “marginal" discoveries that lie at the boundary of the rejection set, which are often crucial in high-precision applications. While recent works (Soloff et al., 2024; Xiang et al., 2025) introduced the boundary false discovery rate (bFDR) to control the error probability at the marginal discovery, their method relies on restrictive assumptions such as independence or specific prior distributions. In this paper, we first propose $k$-bFDR, a novel generalization that controls the error probability of the $k$ least significant discoveries. We then provide a systematic investigation into the theoretical relationship between $k$-bFDR and existing error metrics. Furthermore, building upon the closure principle, we develop Domino, a unified framework that guarantees $k$-bFDR control under arbitrary dependence, applicable for both p-values and e-values. We prove the theoretical validity of the proposed Domino algorithm and demonstrate through extensive numerical experiments that it consistently achieves rigorous $k$-bFDR control while identifying trustworthy marginal discoveries. Analyses of real data reveal that $k$-bFDR control yields higher-quality rejection sets with greater practical significance.

paragraphs: When many hypotheses are tested together, controlling the false discovery rate does not necessarily make the weakest accepted discoveries reliable. Those discoveries sit near the boundary between rejection and non-rejection, where precision may be especially important. This paper focuses on that boundary rather than treating the reliability of the entire discovery set as sufficient.

The authors introduce k-bFDR, which controls an error probability associated with the k least significant discoveries. They investigate how this quantity relates to existing error measures, then develop Domino using the closure principle. The central contribution is a formal way to scrutinize the edge of a discovery set even when the underlying tests are dependent.
summary.tldr: Domino controls errors among the k least significant discoveries under arbitrary dependence using either p-values or e-values.

title: Generalized Boundary FDR Control under Arbitrary Dependence: An Approach on Closure Principle

abstract: Neural network checkpoints have quietly become a large-scale data resource: millions of trained weight vectors now exist, each encoding task-, domain-, and architecture-specific knowledge. This position paper argues that model checkpoints should be treated as a first-class data modality, and that generative modeling in weight space should be standardized as a core machine learning primitive. Recent advances demonstrate that neural weights can be synthesized on demand, often matching fine-tuning performance while reducing adaptation cost by orders of magnitude. We contend that these results reflect an underlying structural fact: high-performing models occupy low-dimensional, highly structured regions of weight space shaped by symmetry, flatness, modularity, and shared subspaces. Building on this view, we organize existing methods into a five-stage pipeline, survey applications where the approach is already practical, and clarify current limits: adapter-scale and conditional generation are advancing rapidly, while unrestricted frontier-scale checkpoint synthesis remains open. Our goal is to shift the community’s default mindset from optimizing models per task to sampling models from learned weight distributions, accelerating toward an era in which AI systems routinely improve or create other AI systems.

abstract: We describe a class of causal, discrete latent variable models called Multiple Multiplicative Factor models (MMFs). A data vector is represented inthe latent space as a vector of factors that have discrete, non-negativeexpression levels. Each factor proposes a distribution over the data vector.The distinguishing feature of MMFs is that they combine the factors' proposeddistributions multiplicatively, taking into account factor expression levels.The product formulation of MMFs allow factors to specialize to a subset of theitems, while the causal generative semantics mean MMFs can readily accommodatemissing data. This makes MMFs distinct from both directed models with mixturesemantics and undirected product models. In this paper we present empiricalresults from the collaborative filtering domain showing that abinary/multinomial MMF model matches the performance of the best existingmodels while learning an interesting latent space description of the users.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Multiple Multiplicative Factor models, a class of generative models with discrete latent variables. Each observed data vector is described by hidden factors with discrete, nonnegative expression levels. Every factor proposes a distribution over the data, and the model combines those proposals by multiplication while accounting for how strongly each factor is expressed.

This product structure allows factors to specialize in subsets of items. The model's causal generative interpretation also allows it to accommodate missing data, an important property for the collaborative filtering application studied here. The combination distinguishes it from directed models that combine components as mixtures and from undirected models that also use products.

Experiments evaluate a binary/multinomial version for collaborative filtering. The reported model matches the performance of the best existing models while learning an interesting latent description of users. The result emphasizes competitive prediction together with the structure learned about users. Its contribution is the particular combination of multiplicative factor interaction, discrete expression levels, and a generative treatment that supports incomplete observations.
summary.tldr: Multiple Multiplicative Factor models combine discrete latent factors multiplicatively, matching leading collaborative filtering models while learning structured user representations.

title: The multiple multiplicative factor model for collaborative filtering

abstract: We describe and analyze a simple and effective iterative algorithm for solving the optimization problem cast by Support Vector Machines (SVM). Our method alternates between stochastic gradient descent steps and projection steps. We prove that the number of iterations required to obtain a solution of accuracy ǫ is Õ(1/ǫ). In contrast, previous analyses of stochastic gradient descent methods require Ω(1/ǫ2 ) iterations. As in previously devised SVM solvers, the number of iterations also scales linearly with 1/λ, where λ is the regularization parameter of SVM. For a linear kernel, the total run-time of our method is Õ(d/(λǫ)), where d is a bound on the number of non-zero features in each example. Since the run-time does not depend directly on the size of the training set, the resulting algorithm is especially suited for learning from large datasets. Our approach can seamlessly be adapted to employ non-linear kernels while working solely on the primal objective function. We demonstrate the efficiency and applicability of our approach by conducting experiments on large text classification problems, comparing our solver to existing state-of-the-art SVM solvers. For example, it takes less than 5 seconds for our solver to converge when solving a text classification problem from Reuters Corpus Volume 1 (RCV1) with 800, 000 training examples.

paragraphs: Pegasos is an iterative solver for the optimization problem behind support vector machines. It alternates stochastic gradient descent steps with projection steps. The paper analyzes this simple procedure and proves an iteration requirement of Õ(1/ε) for accuracy ε, compared with Ω(1/ε²) in previous analyses of stochastic gradient descent methods.

The iteration count also scales linearly with the inverse of the SVM regularization parameter λ. For a linear kernel, the stated total runtime is Õ(d/(λε)), where d bounds the number of nonzero features in each example. The runtime bound does not depend directly on the number of training examples, making the method especially relevant to large datasets with sparse examples.

The approach can also use nonlinear kernels while continuing to optimize the primal objective. Experiments on large text-classification problems compare Pegasos with existing state-of-the-art SVM solvers. One reported RCV1 problem contains 800,000 training examples and takes less than five seconds to converge. This concrete result illustrates the solver's efficiency in the reported setting alongside its theoretical scaling analysis.
summary.tldr: Pegasos combines stochastic gradient and projection steps to solve SVMs with favorable accuracy scaling and strong large-text-dataset performance.

title: Pegasos: Primal Estimated sub-GrAdient SOlver for SVM

abstract: The paper presents a kernel for learning from ordered hypergraphs, a formalization that captures relational data as used in Inductive Logic Programming (ILP). The kernel generalizes previous approaches to graph kernels in calculating similarity based on walks in the hypergraph. Experiments on challenging chemical datasets demonstrate that the kernel outperforms existing ILP methods, and is competitive with state-of-the-art graph kernels. The experiments also demonstrate that the encoding of graph data can affect performance dramatically, a fact that can be useful beyond kernel methods.

The kernel generalizes previous approaches to graph kernels in calculating similarity based on walks in the hypergraph. Experiments on challenging chemical datasets demonstrate that the kernel outperforms existing ILP methods, and is competitive with state-of-the-art graph kernels. paragraphs: Relational learning works with examples described through relationships rather than just flat lists of attributes. This paper presents a kernel for ordered hypergraphs, a representation that captures relational data of the kind used in Inductive Logic Programming. The kernel supplies a way to compare such structured examples for learning.

The similarity calculation is based on walks through a hypergraph and generalizes earlier graph-kernel approaches. Its role is to translate relational structure into comparisons between examples, allowing the chosen representation to contribute directly to learning. The contribution combines a relational data formalization with a corresponding method for measuring similarity.

Experiments on challenging chemical datasets show performance better than existing Inductive Logic Programming methods and competitive with state-of-the-art graph kernels. The experiments also reveal that changing how graph data are encoded can dramatically affect performance. This second finding matters when interpreting the first: the representation of the chemical structures is itself consequential. The authors identify this encoding effect as potentially useful beyond kernel methods, making representation choice an additional lesson of the study.
summary.tldr: A walk-based kernel for ordered hypergraphs performs strongly on chemical data and shows that graph encoding can substantially affect results.

title: Learning from interpretations: a rooted kernel for ordered hypergraphs

abstract: In many applications it is desirable to learn from several kernels. “Multiple kernel learning” (MKL) allows the practitioner to optimize over linear combinations of kernels. By enforcing sparse coefficients, it also generalizes feature selection to kernel selection. We propose MKL for joint feature maps. This provides a convenient and principled way for MKL with multiclass problems. In addition, we can exploit the joint feature map to learn kernels on output spaces. We show the equivalence of several different primal formulations including different regularizers. We present several optimization methods, and compare a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) and two semi-infinite linear programs (SILPs) on toy data, showing that the SILPs are faster than the QCQP. We then demonstrate the utility of our method by applying the SILP to three real world datasets.
