By enforcing sparse coefficients, it also generalizes feature selection to kernel selection. We propose MKL for joint feature maps. This provides a convenient and principled way for MKL with multiclass problems. In addition, we can exploit the joint feature map to learn kernels on output spaces. We show the equivalence of several different primal formulations including different regularizers. We present several optimization methods, and compare a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) and two semi-infinite linear programs (SILPs) on toy data, showing that the SILPs are faster than the QCQP. We then demonstrate the utility of our method by applying the SILP to three real world datasets.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning lets a model learn a weighted combination of kernels, each providing a way to compare examples. Sparse combination weights can also select which kernels contribute. This paper extends that idea to joint feature maps, which represent inputs together with candidate outputs, providing a principled formulation for classification with multiple classes.

Using a joint representation makes the output side part of kernel learning as well. The method can therefore learn kernels on output spaces, expanding what the learned similarities describe. The authors also establish equivalences among several primal optimization formulations, including formulations with different regularizers, connecting alternative mathematical descriptions of the learning problem.

The paper presents several optimization methods and compares a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program with two semi-infinite linear programs. On toy data, the linear-program formulations run faster than the quadratic-program formulation. Applications of a semi-infinite linear program to three real-world datasets further demonstrate the method's utility. These findings support both the multiclass formulation and the practical value of its alternative optimization routes.
summary.tldr: Joint feature maps extend multiple kernel learning to multiclass prediction and output-space kernels, with efficient linear-program optimization demonstrated experimentally.

title: Multiclass multiple kernel learning

abstract: We present a reinforcement learning architecture, Dyna-2, that encompasses both sample-based learning and sample-based search, and that generalises across states during both learning and search. We apply Dyna-2 to high performance Computer Go. In this domain the most successful planning methods are based on sample-based search algorithms, such as UCT, in which states are treated individually, and the most successful learning methods are based on temporal-difference learning algorithms, such as Sarsa, in which linear function approximation is used. In both cases, an estimate of the value function is formed, but in the first case it is transient, computed and then discarded after each move, whereas in the second case it is more permanent, slowly accumulating over many moves and games. The idea of Dyna-2 is for the transient planning memory and the permanent learning memory to remain separate, but for both to be based on linear function approximation and both to be updated by Sarsa. To apply Dyna-2 to 9x9 Computer Go, we use a million binary features in the function approximator, based on templates matching small fragments of the board. Using only the transient memory, Dyna-2 performed at least as well as UCT. Using both memories combined, it significantly outperformed UCT. Our program based on Dyna-2 achieved a higher rating on the Computer Go Online Server than any handcrafted or traditional search based program.

paragraphs: Search and learning can both estimate how valuable a game state is, but they retain that information differently. Search may build an estimate for the current move and then discard it. Learning can accumulate estimates across many moves and games. Dyna-2 brings these activities into one reinforcement learning architecture while keeping their memories separate.

Both the transient planning memory and the permanent learning memory use linear function approximation and are updated with Sarsa. This lets both learning and search generalize across states. For 9-by-9 Go, the authors use a million binary features based on templates matching small board fragments, giving both memories a shared kind of representation.

Using only transient memory, Dyna-2 performs at least as well as UCT in the reported comparison. Combining both memories significantly outperforms UCT. The resulting program also achieves a higher Computer Go Online Server rating than any handcrafted or traditional search-based program. These findings support the practical value of combining accumulated learning with temporary planning in this Go setting.
summary.tldr: Dyna-2 combines separate temporary planning and persistent learning memories, significantly outperforming UCT in the reported 9-by-9 Go comparison.

title: Sample-based learning and search with permanent and transient memories

abstract: Nonparametric latent feature models offer a flexible way to discover the latent features underlying the data, without having to a priori specify their number. The Indian Buffet Process (IBP) is a popular example of such a model. Inference in IBP based models, however, remains a challenge. Sampling techniques such as MCMC can be computationally expensive and can take a long time to converge to the stationary distribution. Variational techniques, although faster than sampling, can be difficult to design, and can still remain slow on large data. In many problems, however, we only seek a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of the latent feature assignment matrix. For such cases, we show that techniques such as beam search can give fast, approximate MAP estimates in the IBP based models. If samples from the posterior are desired, these MAP estimates can also serve as sensible initializers for MCMC based algorithms. Experimental results on a variety of datasets suggest that our algorithms can be a computationally viable alternative to Gibbs sampling, the particle filter, and variational inference based approaches for the IBP, and also perform better than other heuristics such as greedy search.

paragraphs: Indian Buffet Process models can discover underlying features without requiring their number to be specified in advance. The difficulty is inference: sampling can be expensive and slow to converge, while variational methods can be difficult to design and remain costly on large datasets. The paper targets applications that only need a high-probability feature assignment.

For these applications, the authors use beam search to obtain fast, approximate maximum a posteriori estimates of the latent feature assignment matrix. The goal is a likely configuration under the posterior, rather than a collection of posterior samples. When samples are needed, the resulting estimates can instead provide sensible starting points for Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms.

Experiments across several datasets suggest that these search procedures offer a computationally viable alternative to Gibbs sampling, particle filtering, and variational inference for IBP models. They also perform better than heuristics such as greedy search. The findings support approximate MAP search as a useful option when that form of inference matches the application's needs.
summary.tldr: Beam search provides fast approximate MAP feature assignments for Indian Buffet Process models and useful starting points for posterior sampling.

title: Beam Search based MAP Estimates for the Indian Buffet Process

abstract: Fitting probabilistic models to data is often difficult, due to the general intractability of the partition function and its derivatives. Here we propose a new parameter estimation technique that does not require computing an intractable normalization factor or sampling from the equilibrium distribution of the model. This is achieved by establishing dynamics that would transform the observed data distribution into the model distribution, and then setting as the objective the minimization of the KL divergence between the data distribution and the distribution produced by running the dynamics for an infinitesimal time. Score matching, minimum velocity learning, and certain forms of contrastive divergence are shown to be special cases of this learning technique. We demonstrate parameter estimation in Ising models, deep belief networks and an independent component analysis model of natural scenes. In the Ising model case, current state of the art techniques are outperformed by at least an order of magnitude in learning time, with lower error in recovered coupling parameters.

paragraphs: Fitting probabilistic models can be difficult when computing the normalization factor, or partition function, is intractable. This paper introduces parameter estimation that avoids both that computation and sampling from the model's equilibrium distribution. It does so by studying a very short evolution of the observed data distribution.

The method defines dynamics that would eventually transform the data distribution into the model distribution. Its objective minimizes the KL divergence between the data distribution and the distribution reached after an infinitesimal amount of time. This focuses learning on the initial change induced by those dynamics. The authors also show that score matching, minimum velocity learning, and certain forms of contrastive divergence are special cases.

Demonstrations cover Ising models, deep belief networks, and independent component analysis of natural scenes. For the Ising experiments, the method learns at least an order of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art techniques compared, while recovering coupling parameters with lower error. That quantitative result concerns the Ising case; the broader contribution is a common estimation framework linking several existing approaches.
summary.tldr: Minimum probability flow estimates probabilistic models through infinitesimal distribution dynamics, avoiding intractable normalization and equilibrium sampling.

title: Minimum Probability Flow Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of sparse variable selection in nonparametric additive models, with the prior knowledge of the structure among the covariates to encourage those variables within a group to be selected jointly. Previous works either study the group sparsity in the parametric setting (e.g., group lasso), or address the variable selection problem in the nonparametric setting without exploiting the structural information (e.g., sparse additive models (SpAM)). In this paper, we present a new method, called group sparse additive models (GroupSpAM), which can handle group sparsity in nonparametric additive models. We generalize the l1/l2 norm to Hilbert spaces as the sparsity-inducing penalty in GroupSpAM. Moreover, we derive a novel thresholding condition for identifying the functional sparsity at the group level, and propose an efficient block coordinate descent algorithm for constructing the estimate. We demonstrate by simulation that GroupSpAM substantially outperforms competing methods in terms of support recovery and prediction accuracy in additive models, and also conduct a comparative experiment on a real breast cancer dataset.

In this paper, we present a new method, called group sparse additive models (GroupSpAM), which can handle group sparsity in nonparametric additive models. We generalize the l1/l2 norm to Hilbert spaces as the sparsity-inducing penalty in GroupSpAM. Moreover, we derive a novel thresholding condition for identifying the functional sparsity at the group level, and propose an efficient block coordinate descent algorithm for constructing the estimate. We demonstrate by simulation that GroupSpAM substantially outperforms competing methods in terms of support recovery and prediction accuracy in additive models, and also conduct a comparative experiment on a real breast cancer dataset.

paragraphs: GroupSpAM addresses variable selection in nonparametric additive models when prior knowledge groups related covariates together. The objective is to encourage variables within a group to be selected jointly. This combines two capabilities that the abstract describes as separate in earlier approaches: group sparsity in parametric models and variable selection in flexible additive models.

The method extends the L1/L2 penalty to Hilbert spaces, allowing the sparsity penalty to act on functions grouped together rather than only on finite parameter vectors. The authors derive a thresholding condition for determining sparsity at the group level. They also provide an efficient block coordinate descent algorithm for computing the model estimate.

In simulations with additive models, GroupSpAM substantially outperforms competing methods in both support recovery and prediction accuracy. These outcomes concern identifying relevant variables as well as predicting responses. The paper also includes a comparative experiment on a real breast cancer dataset. Its contribution is a way to use known group structure while preserving the flexibility of nonparametric additive modeling.
summary.tldr: GroupSpAM combines nonparametric additive modeling with group-level variable selection and reports improved support recovery and prediction in simulations.

title: Group Sparse Additive Models
